A zombie crowd does both: on rows generated for RFD66606-2321’s bench, sent that way and compressed with zstd at level 3, 64 such walkers cost 0.47 bytes a row. Pedestrians who stop, start, ease their pace and walk in pairs cost 2.16, about four and a half times as much, and tracked heads and hands cost 3.96. A budget sized on zombies would be too small for the people the game actually holds.

    The game holds pedestrians, players and props, not zombies (operator, 2026-10-19). Network tests use pedestrian motion, recorded where a recording with a clean licence exists, and report every class apart.

    Git Bash is blocklisted on the Windows desk, and what it rewrites is why

    Git Bash sits between a command and the Windows program it starts. It rewrites path arguments, and it re-quotes arguments a second time on the way through. A command that works typed into cmd.exe can fail there with no error naming the shell.

    Two failures were measured on the desk on 2026-10-31. --body-file /tmp/pr.md reached gh as written, and gh could not open the path. elixir aborted at boot from Git Bash with Failed to load module 'elixir', and the same Elixir 1.20.5 over OTP 29 ran check_prose_tropes.exs --self-test to all 17 controls through cmd.exe /c elixir.bat. Neither failure names the shell, so a reader blames the tool.

    The two workarounds in use cost a line each: MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*' for /-switches, and a .cmd file for start "". A workaround that every command needs is the shell being wrong.

    Windows commands run in Nushell. Linux builds run in the desk’s WSL Ubuntu 22.04 (operator, 2026-10-31).

    NLI models are blocklisted as a judge of RFD text, and a language model does the job

    The two natural-language-inference models tried on the RFD dependency task are MoritzLaurer/DeBERTa-v3-large-mnli-fever-anli-ling-wanli and facebook/bart-large-mnli. Both are MIT-licensed. The objection is not licence. It is that a language model does this job better, and an NLI model adds a second kind of checkpoint to fetch, pin and license-check for a worse answer (operator, 2026-11-02).

    What was measured on 2026-11-02, so the next reader does not repeat it:

    • On 400 ANLI round 3 items DeBERTa-v3-large scored 0.63 and bart-large-mnli scored 0.30. On 400 MNLI matched items they scored 0.897 and 0.89.
    • Asked whether an RFD’s paragraph says it uses a capability that another RFD provides, DeBERTa separated the 36 declared edges from 587 other pairs with an AUC of 0.63. Lemma overlap alone scored 0.62. Four wordings of the question scored between 0.54 and 0.64.
    • RFD prose rarely states a dependency in one sentence, so entailment of “RFD X depends on RFD Y” almost never holds, even for an edge that is declared.

    Substitute: a language model for the judging step. The spaCy parse and the lemma overlap that find candidate pairs do not use an NLI model and stay.

    Carve-outs. None. A model that is trained for entailment and scored on an NLI benchmark is an NLI model for this rule, whatever its name.

    Hilbert curve is blocklisted for zone codes, and Morton is why

    Operator directive, 2026-11-07. The Hilbert curve for zone assignment, authority and spatial indexing was the hardest part of the fabric zone, and the math did not stay cheap to keep: a correct forward code and inverse (fixed in lean-spatial-oracle 2, gated at build time, per the space-filling-curve logbook), and the run-extent bound — a run of L consecutive codes fits in a box of side 2·L^(1/3)−1 — which was the reason to pay for the curve. The operator went back to Morton and did not ask to keep the bound.

    • What is blocked: the Hilbert curve for zone work, and everything derived from it: zone assignment, authority, the DisjointRanges invariant, and the spatial-index bucketing. That is hilbert3d, hilbert3d_inverse, hilbert_of_aabb, hilbert_cell_of, entity_hilbert, zone_for_hilbert, the ghost_hilbert field, the node hilbert field, and anything that derives authority or zone membership from a Hilbert code.
    • Replacement: Morton coding for the same work. Morton is a bit permutation (GF(2)-linear; its butterfly overlay is the Cayley graph of (ℤ/2)ⁿ), cheap to compute and invert, and needs no hand-rolled inverse or build-time gate.
    • Still on Hilbert (code search, 2026-11-07): fz/src/zone/ — pbvh_adapter.h (hilbert3d, hilbert3d_inverse, hilbert_of_aabb, hilbert_cell_of, the node hilbert field and the 4-pass LSD radix sort), zone_core.cpp (entity_hilbert, ghost_hilbert, zone_for_hilbert, the pbvh_tree_insert_h insert), zone_core.h (the entity_hilbert declaration), zone_types.h (ghost_hilbert), relativistic_zone.h (zone_for_hilbert, HilbertRange, the DisjointRanges invariant, the “authority is a pure function of Hilbert code” invariant line), and predictive_bvh.h (the Lean HilbertBroadphase reference). Each moves to Morton. Until then, a fix is not new code.
    • Not affected: the thirdparty geogram spatial partitioning in zone-backend/c_src/thirdparty, a vendored library outside this directive.
    • Consequence, from the space-filling-curve logbook: the Hilbert curve carried the run-extent bound it was measured as worth (a run of L codes fits in a box of side 2·L^(1/3)−1); Morton has no such bound at any L. Zone geometry keyed on Morton can span more than the code range suggests, so zone size and zone count are next to measure, not assume. Any persisted Hilbert code or zone assignment derived from one is invalidated by the switch; the forward code and its inverse move together, or both go stale.

    Source: BLOCKLIST.md

    Key points

    The goal manifest weftspun/weftspun-keypoint is named for a label, not for a model and not for a corpus. A keypoint is the annotation the whole goal converges on: 104-keypoint wholebody detection, trained from ANNY renders, with pose-consensus refereeing what a pose actually was.

    Naming the goal after the label rather than after the detector is what lets unrelated-looking projects sit in one manifest and still be one goal. default.xml says so in its own header: the sinew motion-capture projects are checked out beside the corpus “because motion capture produces keypoints, which is the same label this corpus supervises”. A renderer that draws bodies, a detector trained on them, a referee that checks them, and hardware that measures them are four apparatus around one annotation.

    The sibling goal was named the same way. weftspun/weftspun-mesh-latents was everything that turned an image into geometry, and its header stated the relationship between them: “The corpus is shared rather than copied. Both goals render from the same assets and both record into the same logbook.” The two manifests overlapped heavily and were not a fork of each other — a project serving one goal and not the other was the exception.

    That manifest was archived on 2026-08-22, and the overlap is why the archiving cost little. Because the corpus was shared rather than copied, absorbing the image-to-geometry projects into this manifest was a matter of listing them, not of moving anything. So there is one live goal manifest and still two goals.

    They were to sit under refs/tags/mesh-latents/v0.1.0-dev.1, a tag saying which goal they came from. That tag was never cut, and this paragraph asserted it for four days. They are pinned at bare commit SHAs instead, which name a revision and not a goal.

    Three things carry this name and are not each other

    The word is overloaded across the workspace, and one of the three is a trap:

    name what it is
    c:\keypoint a checkout of the goal manifest — a directory, replaceable
    weftspun/weftspun-keypoint the goal manifest itself: what is in the goal, and on which side
    weftspun/rf-detr-keypoint-data blocklisted for training. Validation only

    The third is the one to keep straight, because it is the one whose name reads like a keypoint training set. It is not: it carries the entire blinded holdout, and 78% of it is licence-dirty. The blocklist entry in CLAUDE.md has the counts. A keypoint training set is built, not filtered out of that one.

    2026-08-20 — the manifest reference, fixed twice

    CLAUDE.md pointed placement at default.xml in weftspun/weftspun. That repository is archived; the manifest was split per goal. Two references were stale.

    Two agents working the same workspace each found it and each opened a pull request, within the same hour and without seeing each other: logbook#9 and logbook#10. The work was duplicated in full.

    The measurement, and why one of the two was wrong. A fixed population is enumerated, not sampled, so the sweep was an enumeration: across the keypoint checkout, weftspun/weftspun appeared exactly twice outside .repo/, and after the fix, zero times. That number is correct and it answered the wrong question. The sweep ran inside one goal checkout, so it could only see one goal, and #9 accordingly rewrote both references to name weftspun/weftspun-keypoint alone. #10 named both live manifests and left the rule general. The split is org-wide; a workspace-scoped sweep cannot see that, however exhaustively it enumerates.

    #9 is closed as superseded. It is recorded here rather than deleted quietly, because the failure is not the duplicated effort — that cost an hour — it is that an enumeration returning a true count reads exactly like a complete answer.

    A second thing worth not repeating. The .logbook checkout inside a repo-managed workspace sits on a detached HEAD, and #9 was authored by creating a branch directly in it, in a workspace another agent was working in at the same time. A branch in a shared checkout is not a claim anybody else can see, and an uncommitted edit in one is less than that. The fix was a decoupled clone outside the workspace and the shared checkout restored to the detached HEAD it was found on. State that travels between agents has to be a pushed branch or a pull request; nothing in a working tree qualifies.

    Source: KEYPOINTS.md

    Recurring failure modes

    Each entry names a way this system goes wrong, what it costs, and the guard that catches it. Every one holds for real code in these repos rather than in general. Most recur at three or more sites, which is why they live here rather than in memory.

    Written in the present per RFD66606-2172: a mode that stops applying is a line to delete rather than a line to date. Ordered by cost.

    1. Bugs live at interfaces, never inside components

    Every defect in this system sits at a boundary between two things:

    boundary cost
    ANNY gender 0=male against GNM FEMALE=0 flips sex on 800k images
    ANNY Z-up/metres against SOMA-2603.16858 +Y-up/centimetres 100x scale, or a body on its side
    “local Z” against the bone’s roll axis measures a bend and calls it a twist
    rest_bone_heads against vertices 55 mm on an adult, 500 mm on a child
    lowerarm01 / lowerarm02 weight boundary the forearm twist defect
    twist bones against LabRCSF’s joint list 12 ANNY bones carry no canonical name
    forearm / hand mask boundary mesh mean understates finger error 4x
    train / val split contamination
    BVH bind orientation against ANNY’s 29.6 deg per-limb offset; blocks the poses relation

    Components get tested because they are easy to name. Interfaces belong to nobody.

    Guard: interface_audit.py names 17 interfaces. Each resolves to OK, HAZARD, or UNCHECKED — never absent.

    2. A check that passes on known-broken input certifies the defect

    The forearm-twist gate reaches honesty on its third form. The first two pass on a rig that does not transmit twist:

    1. a dominance-share proxy — passes outright
    2. a distal-band reading driven from the twist bone — 66.9 deg of an ideal 78.8, passes, and measures an interface nothing crosses: capture supplies the wrist, never a twist bone
    3. a distal-band reading driven from the wrist — still lenient, because a dispersed stock rig reads 67 deg near the wrist while its mid-forearm stays flat

    Scoring the profile’s linearity separates all three: stock 52.8, dispersed 24.0, shipping 3.6.

    Guard: every gate carries a negative control asserting that broken input fails. test_preflight.py red-tests 10 corruptions. check_readme_claims.py answers its own red test — falsifying two claims trips exactly those two.

    Naming convention for spread-and-threshold gates: ship the companion mode as a CLI switch --negative-control on the same script that computes the number. Two shapes seen in anny-keypoint-anchors:

    1. Re-run with the known-bad selector. face_anchors.py --negative-control calls the same builder with the pre-rework region selector (a per-target 1.5 mm floor over the union, no excluded-vertex filter) and asserts the spread gate rejects the result. The pre-rework worst comes in at 22.4 mm (about a nickel) against a 13 mm cap. A gate the pre-rework selector’s output does not fail is a gate that does not measure what the rework changed.
    2. Re-run the placement check against the previous artifact. check_keypoint_anchors.py --self-test reads face68_v2_snapshot.pth (v2 weights preserved as evidence per rule 10) and asserts the same placement priors that pass on face68.pth fail on the snapshot. v2 fails six priors (jawline monotone-X, chin at min-Z, eyes lateral, mouth corners flanking the nose tip); v3 passes all. A gate whose new build passes it and whose known-broken build passes it too is not a placement gate — it is decoration.

    Both shapes name the same rule: the gate must reject the known-broken input. Both survive review the same way: a green gate is not evidence until the negative control turns red.

    3. A silent skip reads exactly like a pass

    Three checks in this system produce no output and look clean while doing nothing:

    • split-contamination nested under if "scenes" in tables, so it sits out identity generation — the phase that creates contamination
    • dimorphism, when both sex subgroups come out empty
    • child stature, when the sample holds no children

    Guard: an unmet precondition fails rather than skipping. interface_audit.py counts UNCHECKED and names each. check_readme_claims.py reports an unregistered claim as UNVERIFIED and counts it against the total.

    4. The convenient proxy lies

    Five pairs, where the left column is the one that is easy to read:

    proxy measurement that settles it
    joints.csv name coverage silhouette survival
    Godot’s API surface the source
    phenotype parameter percentiles decoded stature in metres
    centroid limb direction (thigh “+9.7 deg”) recovered joint angle (2.2 deg)
    joint-position residual (BVH “153 mm”) limb direction, which is scale-free

    5. A number without a baseline is not a measurement

    A 153 mm BVH retarget residual reads as damning until a control scores two rest skeletons at 139.7 mm: the posed figure sits 13 mm above an unmeasured floor. The verdict drawn from it does not hold.

    The thigh figure has the same shape — 19.7 deg raw, of which 10.0 deg is static body-shape difference, so the raw number overstates by 2x.

    Guard: the floor appears first, in the same table. bvh_retarget_probe.py prints the rest-vs-rest control above its results.

    6. A sampled check claims more than it sees unless it states its floor

    A sample of n catches defects larger than roughly 3/n. At --sample 300 that floor sits at 10,000 ppm: nothing below 1 identity in 100 is certified, a defect touching 23 identities (800 of 800k images) escapes 95% of the time, and the audit prints all-PASS.

    A full decode of 23,000 identities costs 95 seconds.

    For a fixed population, enumeration replaces estimation. Estimation belongs to unbounded streams.

    Guard: preflight_audit.py prints its detection floor and fails when asked to certify below what its sample resolves.

    7. A denominator that does not track reality flatters the result

    Whole-mesh mean error reads 9.2 mm during a forearm pronation, because 1,356 torso vertices sit at exactly 0.00 mm and dilute it, while the fingers sit a golf ball out. The average understates the part that matters 4x.

    The shape matches a dashboard counting 500s against a fixed denominator: the quiet datacentre looks healthy because traffic sleeps, not because the failure rate moves.

    Guard: corpus_defect_rate.py reports an exceedance rate against a stated tolerance, over the region that moves, against a baseline. A rate without a threshold is not a measurement; an absolute rate without a reference does not interpret.

    8. Conventions are data — parse them

    • BVH channel order is per-joint and declared. 100STYLE writes Yrotation Xrotation Zrotation; a positional read transposes every rotation.
    • ANNY’s local-ref rotation axes are world-aligned. The local-to-world map is the identity, so “local Z” is world Z, 55 deg off the forearm.
    • An identity pose_parameters is not the rest pose.
    • rest_bone_heads pairs with rest_vertices, never with vertices.
    • Up axis and units differ per model and per rig.

    Guard: rotation axes come from probing — rotate 10 deg about each local axis, read the world axis the skin turns about, invert. The probe reads descendant vertices, because a bone’s own vertices blend under LBS and fitting them displaces the recovered rotation centre by 33 mm.

    9. Documentation rots silently, and rotted documentation misleads worse than none

    Two live examples in this system:

    • a README headline asserting Godot’s twist disperser as the solution, while the shipping answer is zero twist bones — a reader following the headline builds the wrong thing
    • a docstring asserting Delta Mush is “available here”, where grep finds zero occurrences

    Guard: README numbers are tagged claims that check_readme_claims.py re-derives from live code, so drift fails a command. Superseded findings occupy a SUPERSEDED section rather than vanishing under an edit, so dead ends stay visible.

    10. Retractions belong beside what they retract

    Claims in this system that do not hold: the twist ratio sweep and its “no ratio works” conclusion; the soma/game_engine “frame hazard”; the 9.7 deg thigh error; the “neither BVH formulation transfers the pose” verdict; the claim that Delta Mush is implemented in anny_rig.

    Each sits next to the thing it corrects. A reader who knows the dead ends is better off than one who knows only the current answer, which is the reason this file exists.

    11. Rebase-and-force-push in a tight loop deadlocks under a merge storm

    The failure pattern seen against weftspun/request-for-discussion on 2026-09-03:

    • Ruleset requires branches up to date before merging, and requires all status checks green.
    • Many small PRs land in a short window; main advances every few minutes.
    • A green PR shows mergeStateStatus: BEHIND; a rebase-and-force-push is the mechanical answer, but it resets prek from scratch, and by the time prek finishes, main has moved again. The PR never catches up.
    • --force-with-lease starts rejecting because the remote has shifted between the local rebase and the push.

    Cost: unbounded rebase loop that keeps a green PR open indefinitely; wasted CI minutes; a human eventually admin-merges to break the loop.

    Recovery: gh pr merge <N> --repo <r> --admin --merge bypasses the up-to-date requirement for one stuck PR.

    Guard: GitHub’s merge queue, which serialises PRs into a merge_group event, runs checks on a temporary branch that already has main’s tip merged in, and merges in order. .github/workflows/checks.yml declares merge_group: as a trigger, so the workflow side is ready. gh pr merge --auto --merge adds to a queue rather than firing immediately.

    The queue is ruleset 23145233, created 2026-09-13 on the default branch: MERGE method, ALLGREEN grouping, a 60-minute check timeout, batches of up to five, and a pull request required with zero approvals.

    Require only checks that run on merge_group. Seven of the nine jobs in checks.yml do; rfd-canary and rulesets guard on pull_request alone. A required check that never runs holds the queue for the whole 60 minutes and then fails it, so the required set is read off each job’s if: condition rather than assumed from the list of jobs.

    scripts/check_rulesets.py reads the ids named in CLAUDE.md and this file and fails when the repository does not carry them, so a claim cannot go stale in silence.

    When not to enable, and why that changed. A repo with a single committer and rarely-concurrent PRs gains serialisation with no contention to serialise, which still argues against a queue here. The second condition no longer holds: every pull request on 2026-09-11 and 2026-09-12 sat queued on starved runners, several beyond half an hour, so a queue would have converted a slow check into a blocked merge. On 2026-09-13 checks completed in seconds, which is what made the queue affordable.

    12. A timeout is not a state

    The hosted door’s cluster credentials took four runs to land on 2026-09-07, and every failed run ended in a timeout standing in for a state nobody had read:

    1. op read from a background process reported authorization timeout. The state was “a human has not approved the prompt”, and no retry from that process could change it.
    2. bao’s listener answered tls: certificate required. The state was “no client certificate presented”: the script carried three of the credential helper’s four variables.
    3. flyctl on Windows exits 1 after a clean ssh console -C. Under pipefail the script stopped after the leaf was minted, and its cleanup trap deleted the material, silently.
    4. fly secrets set triggered a deploy whose health checks never passed. The state was a crash loop on a priv path resolved at compile time, which the log states plainly as max restart count of 10.

    A fifth, while measuring: a log poll matched BENCH-DONE in the line that echoed the command it was waiting for, and reported done before the download had finished.

    Guard: a multi-step operation is a state machine over observed states. Each step names the state it needs and the state it leaves behind, checks the artifact rather than the tool’s exit status (a leaf that verifies against its chain, a cluster string with an @, the four secret names in the list, a health body that says primary), and a failure names the state. Minted material is placed before anything optional runs and is never deleted by a later step’s failure. A human approval is a state the human’s own process reaches (! <command> in the session), not something to wait out. A packaging defect faults the release (operator, 2026-09-07: “it must fault”); only an unreachable cluster degrades. scripts/issue_cluster_credentials.sh in transport-taskweft-acp is the shape, and rule 3 above (a silent skip reads like a pass) is the same guard for a script’s silent stop.

    13. A rename applied to prose changes facts, not names

    Renaming GRAFCET to FBD across interactor-taskweft ran a find/replace over comments and docstrings as well as identifiers. Identifiers are ours to rename. Prose carries facts about the world, and three of them were rewritten into falsehoods in one pass:

    1. IEC 60848 GRAFCET became IEC 60848 FBD in two moduledocs. IEC 60848 is GRAFCET; FBD belongs to IEC 61131-3. The file now paired a standard with a notation that standard does not define.
    2. Project-AGRAFE/GRAFCET-static-analysis became Project-AGRAFE/FBD-static-analysis. That is somebody else’s project name. A citation naming a thing that does not exist is worse than no citation, because it reads as checkable.
    3. The same file cites IEC 60848 four more times, correctly, describing firing semantics. Those are about GRAFCET and had to survive a rename away from it.

    Nothing would have caught this. The code compiles either way, no test reads a moduledoc, and the comment-density gate counts lines rather than claims. It surfaced only because a later question — whether the IEC number would be a better name than FBD — sent someone grepping for 60848.

    Guard: a rename touches identifiers, not citations. Before a bulk substitution, list what the old word names: our module, or a standard, an upstream project, a notation, a person. The first is renamed; the rest are facts and stay. Where the two appear in one line, the line gets rewritten by hand. After the pass, grep for the things the old name was attached to — the standard numbers, the upstream URLs — and read what they say now, because a substitution that produced valid prose is exactly the one no tool will flag.

    14. A godot-sandbox guest reads its arguments and its physics by convention, not by name

    Two conventions crossed a guest boundary silently this session, each producing a plausible-looking wrong answer rather than an error.

    A Godot float argument crosses the godot-sandbox unboxed ABI as a C++ double, not a float. A guest entry declared float proximity read the argument register as a 32-bit value and got garbage: a capsule radius of 0.01 came through as 44564, every capsule swelled to a sphere, and every stroke pair “crossed”. The already-shipped mjc_hold(double angle), registered as "float angle", is the pattern — the C++ type is double. A multi-argument entry also has to mirror an entry known to work (two PackedArray plus one double, as cg_cycles does); a fourth argument tacked on garbled the earlier ones.

    MuJoCo filters a collision pair whose two geoms share a weld id. Two bodies with no joint are both welded to the world, share weld id 0, and never report a contact, so strokes encoded as jointless bodies returned zero crossings. A free joint per body makes each its own weld and the inter-body pairs collide. The failure reads as “the collision found nothing”, not as “the model was filtered”.

    Guard: at a guest boundary, take the argument types and the model conventions from an entry that already works, not from the host-side name. A Godot float is a C++ double; a new entry’s signature copies a proven one before adding arguments. For a physics model, assert the contact count on a fixture with a known answer before trusting a zero — a filtered pair and an empty scene both report none.

    15. A DOI missing from Crossref is not a missing DOI: validate against DataCite and Crossref

    Crossref and DataCite are separate DOI registries, and a reference checked against only one is wrongly reported as unverified or wrongly given no DOI:

    source registry example
    arXiv preprints (prefix 10.48550) DataCite 10.48550/arXiv.2609.35426, Crossref 404
    ACM, IEEE, Elsevier, JAIR, Springer Crossref 10.1145/3453483.3454080
    IJCAI before 2017 neither (no DOI issued) Alford et al. 2016, task sharing
    Machine Intelligence 5 (1970) neither (predates DOIs) Plotkin; Reynolds

    A CITATION.cff reference is valid when its DOI resolves at https://api.datacite.org/dois/<doi> or https://api.crossref.org/works/<doi>, and its title, authors, year, venue, volume and pages match that record field by field. A work in neither registry is cited without a DOI and says how it was checked (a proceedings abstract page, a volume’s table of contents). cffconvert --validate also refuses two identical author entries, so authors who share a family name (Liu, Dong; Liu, Zheng) need their given names.

    Guard: query both registries before writing “no DOI”; run cffconvert --validate on every CITATION.cff change.

    Source: PITFALLS.md

    RFDs

    RFD66606-2493: a zone relay only routes

    State: discussion Feature: a zone hands each member the others’ frames and reads none of them. Scope: the presence slice’s zone relay: its rule for taking a frame, its sockets, its gates.

    Can a zone carry four people’s bodies to each other without simulating, decoding or judging anything, and without trusting the clock of anyone who sends to it?

    A zone that simulates is one more party to trust. The first relay built here avoided that and still trusted something it should not have: it opened each sender’s turn on a tick of its own clock. Run on real sockets for the first time, it refused 7 honest frames of 320. A client’s clock is not the relay’s, and a send that drifts across the relay’s tick lands twice in one turn and not at all in the next. The model’s gate had passed, because its clients and its router shared one clock.

    • A zone relay hands each member’s two frames to the other members as they came. It does not simulate, decode, compress or judge, and it holds no key (operator, 2026-11-13).
    • A half of a slot is open again 5 ticks after the frame it last took, counted on the relay’s own clock from that frame and from nothing else. A frame that comes sooner is counted and not stored, so a flood makes the relay do less.
    • The half of a datagram is the socket it arrived on: first frames go to one port and second frames to the next. Nothing is added to a frame and nothing travels beside it.
    • The relay is plain C with no heap and no engine, held to a model in SafeGDScript by replaying a recorded trace of every call and every answer.
    • Liveness is the relay’s and safety is not: it can drop or delay, and it cannot forge.

    Drive the relay’s state machine with four clients whose clocks are offset, skewed and jittered, for 19,200 ticks. It passes when no honest frame is refused and every flood frame is.

    Where it lives

    The parts are repositories of their own in our organisation, each started anew on 2026-11-13.

    • The model is the zone router guest, interactor-zone-router-guest: router.sgd and the script that writes its trace.
    • The relay is transport-zone-relay: src/zone_relay.c is the state machine, src/zone_net.c puts it on two sockets and a 64 Hz tick, and src/zone_load.c is the load generator.
    • The gates that run four clients through the model, with a planted zone, sender and viewer, are in interactor-presence-gates, beside the ledger of what each rung moved.

    The rule and what it replaced

    The rule before opened slot s where the relay’s now % 6 was 0, 1, 3 or 4. That put the senders on different ticks, which is good, and tied a sender’s turn to the relay’s clock, which is not. The rule now needs no shared clock. Five ticks and not six, so that a frame one tick early is still taken. A flood gets at most six frames through in five intervals.

    Clients still send on different ticks of the six. That is a courtesy that spreads arrivals, kept by the clients. The relay enforces no slot.

    What was measured

    The same fixed sequence was given to the rule in use and to the old rule, kept as a planted build. Four clients start at different moments, run 1,000 and 100 parts in a million fast and slow, and arrive up to 0.4 of a tick early or late.

    Rule Honest frames sent Honest frames refused Flood frames refused
    open 5 ticks after the last frame 25,602 0 128 of 128
    open on a fixed tick of the relay’s clock 25,602 1,894 128 of 128

    On sockets, four client threads on one machine: 0 honest frames refused of 960 over three runs, where the first run under the old rule refused 7 of 320. A Linux runner printed the same figures as the development machine.

    Gates and controls

    Each gate prints a result line, and each control plants a defect that must be caught.

    • Trace: the C relay answers every one of 1,469 recorded calls as the model did. Controls: five planted models, each of which must fail at the record where it first differs.
    • Opaque: the relay’s source touches a frame only to store it and to send it. Control: one planted read of a frame byte.
    • Clocks: the table above. Controls: the old rule, and a flood.
    • Sockets: no viewer gets a frame that differs from what was sent, or its own, or one from the socket of the other half. Controls: a relay that sends from the wrong socket, and 6 ms of planted work in every tick, which must move the median tick by at least 5 ms.

    What it does not guarantee

    • It can drop or delay, and honest clients cannot route around it.
    • A relay that is handed one pair key can alter a frame for that one viewer under a valid tag. The honest majority then names that viewer and not the relay.
    • A person here is an address. The home server’s member table, and a datagram refused because its address was never named, arrive with the transport step.

    What is not known

    • The cost of one datagram. The development machine charges about 0.4 ms for a loopback datagram, so its times compare one run with the next and nothing else. No number of people is claimed.
    • Whether a ring of submissions on Linux beats one send a datagram. That is a later rung, on a Linux machine of ours.
    • How the relay shares a viewer’s frames among more than four people. The frame budget and its levels of detail by Morton prefix depth are a later rung.

    The problem

    The relay had been made blind to frames and was still not blind to time.

    The tuples

    rfd-2493--provides--router-only-zone
rfd-2493--spends--elf-guest-native-translation
rfd-2493--is-a--zone-relay

    Related

    • RFD66606-2436, presence, the slice this relay serves.
    • RFD66606-2443, the entity server it was first built beside, which this narrows.
    • RFD66606-2442, the latency budget that is where its tick is going.
    • RFD66606-2492, the predictor that makes what it carries smaller.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2493-a-zone-relay-only-routes.exs

    RFD66606-2492: the motion matching guest predicts a body on the wire

    State: discussion Feature: a sender states a clip and a time and sends only what the guest cannot predict. Scope: the presence slice’s frame codec: a predictor under Zstandard, its gates and controls.

    Both ends of a presence stream hold the same clips and the same motion matching guest. How many bytes of a body does a sender still have to send?

    A person’s body goes on the wire as 21 entity Packets of 100 bytes, in two frames of 12, once every 6 ticks of a 64 Hz clock. Each frame is coded alone against one fixed dictionary. Measured on 62 clips, that stream is 8,693 bytes a second at level 19, which is 6% over the sustained budget of 8,192. A dictionary cannot close the gap: coding a frame against the send before it saves 3%. But the body is not free motion. The stick feeds mm_step, which answers a clip and a time, and the body is that clip’s pose placed in the world. A viewer that runs the same guest on the same clips can make most of that pose itself.

    • The predictor is the motion matching guest, mm.elf (operator, 2026-11-13: “he motion matching guest yes.”). No learned model is brought in before this has been tried.
    • The predictor sits in the frame codec, under Zstandard. A decoded frame is still 12 whole Packets of 100 bytes, so the Packet layout does not change and the observers hash the same frames as today.
    • The clip and the time travel in the payload of a Packet that is already sent. Nothing travels beside the Packets.
    • Every send states its own clip and time. A frame stands alone, and a lost send does not make the next one unreadable.
    • The hash of the clip set and of the guest joins the hashes of the dictionary and of the part table as one protocol version. A viewer with another version is refused.

    Run the frame size tool on the 62 clips with the predictor in the codec and without it. The rung passes when the bytes a second with the predictor are below the 8,693 of the fixed dictionary on the same sends, the decoded frames equal the frames that were sent, bit for bit, and each of the four controls below is caught.

    Start here

    This RFD is written so that a session with no memory of the work can begin from it. Read these in order before writing anything.

    • The gates repository, interactor-presence-gates in our organisation. Read docs/wire.md for frames and Packets, docs/frame-sizes.md for the measurement this RFD must beat, docs/ledger.md with ledger.tsv for how a rung is recorded, and tools/frame_sizes.exs, the tool that measures any recorded stream. The parts it joins are repositories of their own beside it; the Packet codec is interactor-packets-guest and RFD66606-2493 names the rest.
    • The motion matching guest’s repository, interactor-motion-matching-guest, which the workspace checks out on its interactor side. Its README has mm_add_clip, mm_bake and mm_step(dt, vx, vz, facing, mode, jump), which answers a clip, a time, the character and the clip root for each frame.
    • The packet contract, contract-entity-packet. A Packet is 100 bytes: gid at 0, position in micrometres at 4, velocity at 28, acceleration at 34, the tick at 40, rotation at 52 and 40 bytes of payload at 58.
    • The avatar follower, interactor-anny-follow-guest. follow.sgd and data/drive.tsv hold the 21 bodies of the muscle skeleton that drive ANNY. Their order on the wire is data/parts.tsv of the codec’s repository, a whole coarse body in the first frame.

    What was measured

    The 62 clips that pass the retarget gates, 29 minutes of motion, were played at the tick and written as the frames one person would send. Half the clips built the dictionary and sends of the other half were measured.

    Cadence Dictionary Level Bytes a send Bytes a second
    6 ticks none 3 982 10,476
    6 ticks fixed, 64 KiB 3 947 10,100
    6 ticks fixed, 64 KiB 19 815 8,693
    6 ticks the send before 19 791 8,436
    8 ticks fixed, 64 KiB 19 814 6,510

    The row to beat is the third. The fourth shows why a better dictionary is not the way: the best possible one, the send before, gains 3%.

    Why a predictor should work here

    A body in this slice is made in a chain. The left stick sets a wanted ground velocity. The motion matching guest picks a clip and a time. The clip’s pose at that time is placed in the world, and the muscle skeleton takes it. So for a sender whose body follows the guest, clip, time and root placement fix the pose of most of the 21 parts. What they do not fix is what the guest cannot know: the tracked head and hands, and what physics adds.

    No number is claimed for the saving. A rough bound, if only the head and two hands carried information beyond clip, time and root, is 150 to 250 bytes a send against 815. It is a guess until the first rung measures it.

    Loss is another matter

    Zstandard is not an error-correcting code and is not used as one. Compression removes redundancy and a code for errors adds it. Loss is concealed by the curve a viewer already draws: one lost send costs nothing, and after three a part moves 7% over its top speed for one segment. A third interval of playback delay is the first remedy if loss hurts. RFD66606-2327 has the gait phase the guest matches by, and RFD66606-2363 the controllers that feed it.

    The ladder

    Each rung is held to the rung below it and not to the budget. The budget is where the ladder ends.

    Rungs are climbed in this order and none is skipped. A rung is the run of the rung below with one thing changed. It is run on the development machine before anything is pushed, and it passes when its number is better than the rung below while its controls are caught.

    1. Run tools/frame_sizes.exs as it is on the 62 clips. Nothing has to improve: it must give 8,693 again, so that the baseline is this session’s own.
    2. The guest’s digest on four hosts, as the MuJoCo guest has. Hosts that agree on mm_step go from 0 to 4.
    3. Residual frames: each Packet’s fields less the predicted pose, for clips played back as they are. Bytes a second go below rung 0.
    4. Clip and time in a payload, and the decoder that rebuilds the frame from them. Frames rebuilt bit for bit go from none to all.
    5. A body that strays from the clip: head and hands on a recorded track. Bytes a second are set against rung 2 and reported as they are.
    6. The codec as a sandbox guest beside curve.sgd. Its bytes equal the tool’s.

    Rung 1 comes before any coding because a predictor that differs between two machines by one bit makes every decoded frame wrong. The MuJoCo guest already has a digest on Linux x86_64, Linux arm64, Windows x86_64 and macOS arm64, with the in-process JIT switched off, and that check found a defect on its first day.

    Gates and controls

    Each gate prints a RESULT: line, and each control plants a defect that must be caught and named.

    • Round trip: every frame that is coded decodes to the bytes that were sent. Control: one bit of the residual flipped.
    • Alone: a frame decodes with no other frame at hand. Control: a decoder that keeps the clip and time of the send before, which must fail when a send is withheld.
    • Version: a viewer whose clip set differs is refused by name. Control: one clip altered.
    • Bytes: the stream is smaller than the rung below on the same sends. Control: a predictor that answers the rest pose, which must give no saving.

    Rules a new session must keep

    • The Packet stays 100 bytes and a frame stays 12 Packets. New data goes into a payload.
    • New guest code is SafeGDScript first. Tools are .exs and gates are .gd. No new Python.
    • Comments are at most 3% of a file’s lines. The explanation goes into documentation.
    • Commits are authored as the operator, in sentence case, with no trailer and no agent credit.
    • No file names the reference social VR platform.
    • CI confirms and does not find out: one finished pull request at a time, after the gate and its controls have passed on the development machine. No draft pull requests.
    • Meshes are OpenUSD only. The clips come from a private repository whose release awaits a provenance check, and they are cleared for this work.

    What is not known

    • Whether mm_step is bit-identical across the four hosts. Nothing has run.
    • How far a real player strays from the clips. Only play in a headset shows it, and the bytes of rung 4 are a first estimate.
    • The time to code a frame with the predictor. The tick has about 1.8 ms to spare on the interpreted tier, so the codec may have to run off the tick.
    • Whether rotation needs its own residual form. The Packet carries rotation in a swing-twist code, and a small error there may not be a small number.

    The problem

    The stream is over its budget, the dictionary is spent, and the chosen cadence was kept twice by the operator. What is left is to stop sending what both ends already know.

    The tuples

    rfd-2492--provides--motion-predicted-frames
rfd-2492--spends--elf-guest-native-translation
rfd-2492--is-a--frame-codec

    Related

    • RFD66606-2436, presence, the slice this codec serves.
    • RFD66606-2442 and RFD66606-2443, the latency metric and the server that carries the frames.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2492-the-motion-matching-guest-predicts-a-body-on-the-wire.exs

    RFD66606-2491: Bonsai 2 runs a RISC-V machine in its own layers

    State: discussion Feature: a Bonsai 2 server answers a calc tool call from inside its own artifact: eleven Gated DeltaNet layers hold a 32-bit RISC-V processor, and the server’s recurrent state is its memory Scope: the chip tower as a component of the Bonsai 2 .ninfer artifact, the qwenputer compiler that writes it, the ninfer-all converter and engine that store and run it, and the calc firmware

    Can Bonsai 2 answer an arithmetic tool call with no program outside its own weights?

    A tool call leaves the model: the host parses it, runs a program and writes the answer back. A compiler can instead write a processor as transformer layers, and then no host runs anything.

    The Bonsai 2 artifact carries a chip tower: an RV32IM processor with the Zba extension, compiled by qwenputer into eleven Gated DeltaNet layers of Bonsai 2’s head geometry. The tower is its own component beside the text tower. The ternary body is stored unchanged, object for object.

    The server runs every token through the tower. The tower names the next token where it owns the position, and the body names it everywhere else. A firmware is a recurrent state the server loads, selected with --chip. The first firmware is the calc tool (operator, 2026-11-13).

    Export the tower, check it against the reference machine, convert, then run the witnesses.

    How the machine sits in the model

    qwenputer (MIT) compiles a circuit into the two sublayers of a Gated DeltaNet layer. An MLP unit is a lookup, and a recurrent head is a table whose rows a one-hot key overwrites. No weight is trained. The processor’s registers, ROM and RAM are the heads’ state rows.

    A run looks like this in the token stream. The body writes a tool call in its own syntax. The tower copies each token of the call into a text buffer. At the closing tag the tower takes over and emits chip tokens, one record per instruction. Each byte the firmware prints comes back as the body’s own token for that byte, so the body reads a tool response it wrote itself. Chip tokens run through the tower only. The body’s layers, cache and positions see the text alone.

    Why the tower is a separate component

    Upstream widens the host model and puts the processor in the added residual dims. Bonsai 2 cannot take that route:

    • The body is Hadamard-rotated ternary in 1024-column blocks. Zero padding, mute columns and rescaled norm gains do not survive that packing word for word.
    • The engine’s kernels are registered for the body’s hidden size.
    • The chip token rows hold values such as 2^40, which are not ternary.

    So the tower keeps its own residual stream of 1280 dims, its own token table and its own states, and the body stays byte-identical. This is upstream’s own fast decoding path, which already runs the chip layers as a second view with a second cache.

    The circuit is compiled for Bonsai 2’s head geometry (16 key heads, 48 value heads, head dim 128, conv kernel 4), so the engine’s recurrent kernels run it. The MLP is cut from the body’s 17408 units to the 8576 the circuit uses.

    The tower export

    chipformer.rv.export_tower in the qwenputer fork reads the host’s config and tokenizer and writes a directory: config.json with architecture ChipTower, and model.safetensors with the eleven layers under their usual names, the token table and each firmware’s parked state. A host token keeps its id and chip token t has id 248320 + t. Every tensor passes the compiler’s bf16 check on the way out.

    The converter

    --source chip=DIR and --components ...,chip add the tower to recipe bonsai2_27b_ternary. Tower parameters are stored in direct formats (bf16, and fp32 for the states and the decay constants) by method exact_direct, which refuses a value the format would round. Each parameter is its own object. The converter refuses a tower whose head geometry or token offset differs from the text model’s.

    The published artifact

    The artifact with the tower is models/chip/bonsai2-27b-heretic-chip.ninfer in the public dataset that holds the artifact of RFD66606-2311. Its SHA-256 is in models/chip/SHA256SUMS beside it. The tower’s source and the golden stream are in sources/tower-27b/. The dataset’s NOTICE names qwenputer and the libraries the calc firmware is linked with.

    The conversion reads the tower from a path inside the checkout, so the artifact and its report name no host directory, and the job that publishes them stops if one does. Every object of the published file equals the object of the file the served witness ran on.

    The steps an operator follows are v-sekai/chip-tower-sop.md in the ninfer-all fork.

    Ternary planes

    Every tower matrix is a sum of ternary planes: weights in {-1, 0, +1} with one scale per row and group of 128 columns, or per column and group of 128 rows where that needs fewer planes. Each weight sits in one plane, so the sum equals the matrix bit for bit. Of the 89 matrices, 82 need at most two planes and none needs more than seven.

    The scales are not binary16 values: they range from 2^-41 to 2^125. A ternary tower therefore needs a plane format with bf16 scales and no Hadamard rotation, which the artifact container does not have yet. Until it does, the tower is stored dense.

    Witnesses

    Each one carries a control that must fail.

    • Compiled. The circuit for Bonsai 2’s geometry has eleven layers, and every emitted tensor is a bf16 value. Control: a weight that is not a bf16 value raises.
    • Reference tower. In stock Qwen3.5 modules, the residual after the chip layers equals the circuit evaluator’s on every kept dim at every position, token by token and as a chunked prefill, with the firmware state loaded after the prompt as a server loads it. The output code names the reference machine’s next token wherever the machine owns the position. Measured with the calc firmware: 17,387 positions token by token and 261,213 positions as a prefill, each with no inexact position and no wrong token. Controls: one flipped ROM word, one flipped MLP weight, and fp16 recurrent state each fail.
    • Planes. The planes of every matrix sum back bit for bit. Control: one flipped sign fails.
    • Converted. Every tower object reads back word for word, and every text, vision, MTP and DFlash2 object hash equals the one in an artifact converted without the tower. Measured: 1,513 parameters compared and none differs, and all 178 tower parameters hold their source’s words. Control: one planted bit in a text object fails.
    • Engine ops. One token at a time through the engine’s public ops, the kept dims equal the golden file bit for bit over 17,792 positions. Controls: fp16 tower state fails, and one flipped weight bit fails.
    • Engine runtime. The tower loaded from the converted artifact by the engine’s own loader gives the same result: no inexact position, 17,104 owned positions, no wrong token. The same two controls fail.
    • Served. ninfer-serve --chip calc-bridge at temperature 0, twelve arithmetic prompts: 21 bursts and 80,468 chip tokens, each served token equal to the reference machine’s when it is fed the model’s own call tokens. All twelve values equal Python’s, and a power too large for the firmware returns its error. Controls: without --chip the call comes back unanswered, and with the ROM word the parked machine runs next spoiled in a copy of the artifact, every burst differs from the reference.
    • Body unchanged. A prompt with no tool call gives the same temperature-0 answer hash with --chip, without it, and on the engine before this work, for the same prompt text.

    Serving

    --chip NAME selects a firmware and adds the calc tool to a request that declares none. The answered call is returned inline in the content: the call, the tool response the firmware printed, then the model’s answer. --chip-trace FILE writes each burst’s tokens.

    A --chip server has one request lane, one device and no drafter. Any other combination stops at startup. A request whose echo is cut by the output limit ends with the limit reason.

    On one RTX 4090 a burst runs at 500 chip tokens per second. Text decodes at 105.1 tokens per second without --chip and at 71.6 with it, both without a drafter.

    Open questions

    • A drafter is refused beside the tower, so a --chip server runs without DFlash2. Drafting is not shown safe: a drafted round could commit tokens after the closing tag.
    • Each prompt token steps the tower by itself on every request, also on a prefix-cache hit. Chunked calls would cost less, and whether the chunked ops are bit-exact on the tower is unmeasured.
    • A burst runs inside one engine unit, so a cancel is seen only after it.
    • Thinking mode, streaming, the other endpoints, structured output and histories that hold earlier calls have not run with --chip.
    • How often Bonsai 2 writes a well-formed calc call on its own is unmeasured.
    • The tower is stored dense. The plane format above is not built.

    The problem

    Bonsai 2 cannot do exact arithmetic on its own, and a host tool adds a round trip and a second program to trust.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2311 (Bonsai 2 serving), whose artifact and server this extends.
    • RFD66606-2462 (the prism llama.cpp branch), a second runtime the same export can feed.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2491-bonsai-2-runs-a-risc-v-machine-in-its-own-layers.exs

    RFD66606-2490: What the fabric is for, and what it is not

    State: discussion Scope: the whole RFD board: its purpose and its non-goals.

    Does a new RFD on this board serve the open, self-hosted campus, or does it drift toward a walled garden?

    The 2020 charter asked for an open, remixable, self-hosted VR space. Most of it still holds. The targets and the trust model have moved on.

    The fabric is an open, remixable, self-hosted collaborative space built on Godot. People in one room can see each other. Hearing each other is a charter intent that the first beta does not ship (RFD66606-2447). The board-wide non-goals below bind every RFD on this board (operator, 2026-11-11).

    Check a new idea against the non-goals in the details. A match is refused, not argued again.

    Charter digest

    The 2020 Mozilla MVP application (https://v-sekai.github.io/manuals/decisions/20200608-vsekai-charter.html) set out these intents.

    • Kept: a remixable, self-hosted, collaborative VR environment on Godot Engine.
    • Kept: openness and communication as the basis of the platform.
    • Kept: an open alternative to walled-garden social VR.
    • Kept: users keep power over their data and can run the platform privately.
    • Kept: easy to compile and modify.
    • Kept: baseline presence, people in a room who can see each other (beta 1). Hearing each other is not in beta 1 and is not on this board’s current plan.
    • Kept: a neutral host for events, and for business meetings where privacy matters.
    • Superseded: Windows SteamVR and Oculus Quest as targets. The targets are the Mac, the Steam Frame and the Steam Deck. The Frame and the Deck build natively (operator, 2026-11-12). The Mac’s native build is unknown.
    • Superseded: decentralized authentication through a GPG web of trust. OpenBao is the identity and secret store (operator, 2026-11-11; see RFD66606-2146 and RFD66606-2202).
    • Superseded: BitTorrent and IPFS distribution. Content ships from a standard CDN through HTTP range requests, chunked so that desync-compatible tools can fetch it (operator, 2026-11-11).
    • Dropped: the 2020 stack (k3s, CentOS 8, Digital Ocean Spaces), the eight-week Gantt chart, team bios and user-count estimates.
    • Not promised here: end-to-end encryption between users. OpenBao does not provide it, and nothing in this board commits to it.

    Board-wide non-goals

    A non-goal on this board is abandoned, not deferred. A new RFD that matches one is refused, and the list is not argued again.

    • A paywall at the door: no licence, sponsor or membership check in the client or the server.
    • A client for a phone or a web page.
    • Fly as a host for any server piece (operator, 2026-11-12).
    • FEX, the x86 emulation layer, as a runtime for any build (operator, 2026-11-12).
    • Proton, the third-party compatibility layer (operator, 2026-11-12).

    Beta-only non-goals in RFD66606-2360

    These stay beta-only non-goals in RFD66606-2360 (operator, 2026-11-11). They are not on the board-wide list.

    • Real-money purchases.
    • A leaderboard or achievements.
    • Campuses or worlds built by players. This pulls against the remixable intent in the charter.
    • Moderation, reporting and blocking tools.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2360, the campus beta, which points here for its non-goals.
    • RFD66606-2447, beta 1: see each other.
    • RFD66606-2146, bao is the secret store.
    • RFD66606-2202, ReBAC role tuples enforced via Bao identity groups.
    • The 2020-06-08 V-Sekai charter, at https://v-sekai.github.io/manuals/decisions/20200608-vsekai-charter.html.

    RFD66606-2489: Extracting body measurements from the base model

    State: ideation Feature: body measurements are re-readable from the base model mesh along labeled loops Scope: base model mesh, waist and collar vertex labels, geodesic measurement

    What numbers should the base model’s body carry so clothing fits and the net can be checked?

    The base model is the body base (the reference rig everything else hangs from). GarmentCodeData v2 (the CC BY 4.0 garment dataset) stores body measurements beside the waist and collar vertex labels. Those labels plus the mesh are all a garment needs to sit on the body. So the measurements must be re-readable from the base model alone.

    The base model’s body measurements come from the mesh itself. Circumference is the perimeter of a labeled cross-section loop. Length is a geodesic distance between two landmarks. GarmentCodeData v2 supplies the waist and collar vertex labels that anchor them. RFD66606-2488 (cage-wrapped surface net) reproduces those same labels. So measuring the base model is also a check that the net read the parts correctly.

    Read DETAILS for the loop definitions and the first gate.

    The problem

    The base model is the reference body mesh, the static rig everything hangs from. It must be measured so garments fit it and the net can be checked. Hand-measured numbers are the only source today and they do not round-trip to the mesh.

    How measurement is made

    • Circumference is the perimeter of a labeled cross-section loop.
    • Waist and collar are the loops GarmentCodeData v2 already labels.
    • Length is a geodesic distance between two landmarks.

    First gate

    Re-derive the stored body measurements from the base model mesh alone. The recovered numbers agree with GarmentCodeData v2 within tolerance in the model-explorer viewer.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2488, the cage-wrapped surface net whose part labels this RFD reads.
    • RFD66606-2424, the anthropometric keypoint fit whose landmark vocabulary this inherits.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2488: Cage-wrapped segmentation net and independent garment bodies for VRM spring-bone rigs

    State: ideation Feature: net segments garment and body; everything else becomes a VRM spring-bone chain Scope: cage guest, diffusion-net, spring-bone addon, Cassie VBD, and the two datasets

    Can a garment become independent bodies that swing on their own?

    The product avatar wears clothes. Hair, skirts, belts and scarves are separate parts with cavities and non-manifold edges. A plain surface net cannot see across disconnected components. Garments must move independently. Skin weights attach; they do not swing the cloth.

    The cage-wrapped net segments the body and garment into per-vertex part and panel labels. Every part that is not the body base becomes a VRM spring-bone chain. SkinTokens gives the body base skeleton and weights; the chains swing on their own. Rest lengths come from the mesh; spring stiffness and damping are tuned.

    Read DETAILS for the part-to-body mapping and the first gate.

    References

    • CageNet, SIGGRAPH 2025. doi 10.1145/3721238.3730654
    • DiffusionNet, ToG 2022. doi 10.1145/3507905
    • SkinTokens, arXiv:2602.04805.

    The problem

    The product avatar wears clothes. Hair, skirts, belts and scarves are separate parts. They must move independently: a belt swings, a skirt drapes, a tail and hair dangle.

    The two layers

    • The segmentation net: CageNet builds a manifold cage; DiffusionNet runs on the cage; the mapping operator P projects per-vertex part and panel labels back to the messy mesh.
    • The independent bodies: VRM spring-bone chains for every part that is not the body base.
    • Stiff parts (belt, collar, hat) use short chains or a rigid pivot at the attachment bone.
    • Soft fabric (skirt, dress, sleeves) is a cloth approximated by spring-bone chains that Cassie VBD drives.

    Why the cage

    DiffusionNet alone does not communicate between distinct components. The single manifold cage lets one net see across hair, clothes and eyes. So it is the part-label engine for the garment and the body.

    Part-to-body mapping

    • Body base: SkinTokens skeleton and weights; the static rig everything hangs from.
    • Everything else: a VRM spring-bone chain.
    • Belt, collar, skirt, dress, sleeves, shawl, hair, tail, scarf.
    • Each chain carries bones with rest lengths from the mesh, tuned stiffness, damping and collision shapes.

    Data

    • GarmentCodeData v2 (CC BY 4.0): the garment mesh, per-vertex panel segmentation, waist and collar vertex labels, the sewing specification, and body measurements. The segmentation is the carving; the scrappy path uses it directly without the net.
    • Articulation-XL 2.0 (CC BY 4.0): models, skeletons, meshes, skins and point clouds. Feeds SkinTokens evaluation, which was trained on it.

    What we already have

    The cage.elf guest ships the cage build and the bind. Its self test and property test assert every target vertex lies inside the cage. The VRM addon runs SpringBoneSimulator3D with per-bone stiffness, damping, limits and collision shapes. Cassie cloth emits VBD soft-body code with adjacency, gather and project springs.

    What is new

    The DiffusionNet stage on the cage, and the mapping operator P, which segment the garment and body into parts. The rig: a SkinTokens base skeleton, and spring-bone chains for everything else.

    The licence line

    The CageNet paper is non-commercial; we implement the cage and DiffusionNet (MIT) on our own code. SkinTokens is permissive and in-house; we adopt it for the base skeleton and weights.

    First gate

    A production garment is carved into labeled parts and rigged as VRM spring-bone chains. Its belt, skirt and hair move independently while the body moves, in the model-explorer viewer.

    Related

    • RFD66606-1029, mesh segmentation and the part model it replaces.
    • RFD66606-1030, the See-Through split the net feeds.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2487: Walk mode’s clips should rejoin the AnimationMixer ecosystem

    State: discussion Feature: the motion-matching guest’s pose database is built from a real AnimationLibrary, not from raw per-clip files copied into the pack by a build script. Scope: the motion-matching guest’s bake step, the walk mode viewer’s clip loading, and the release pipeline steps that currently move clip files around.

    Why does a clip the guest needs sometimes never reach the shipped package, with nothing catching it until a user opens the app?

    A release once shipped walk mode with its clip data missing. Two fixes were tried and withdrawn: a loader change and a pack allowlist change, each disproven by planting a real clip in a fresh export and watching it come through fine either way. The honest cause is narrower: the one script step that copies clip files into the project before packing wrote nothing, once, and nothing in the resource system noticed, because raw files carry no such check. The guest’s own data loader already changed shape once for this port: a comment in the guest’s pose code says clips arrive as flat transforms instead of animation tracks, changed only for the sandboxed port. Upstream’s own baker reads a real AnimationLibrary directly, built from a mixer and a skeleton.

    • Build one AnimationLibrary resource per clip set, keyed one track at a time, in place of the flat transform files and the clip list file.
    • Decide whether the guest bakes its own pose database from that library over the sandbox’s existing calls into engine objects, or whether baking happens once on the engine side and only the finished flat arrays cross into the guest, as they do today.
    • Drop the three script steps whose only job is moving clip files between repositories and into the exported package once the library carries the same data as a tracked resource.

    Clip data for a shipped package is as safe as any other imported resource: if it is still missing, the package itself failed to build, not merely to work once launched.

    Current data flow

    Clip data is produced as a set of per-bone transform arrays, a clip list file, a skeleton description and a parent list, one set of files per clip. A release step copies these files from the source repository into the project, where an editor setting is relied on to carry them into the exported package as plain files. The guest reads its own copy of these files at run time and parses the transform layout itself to build its pose search structure.

    Where the raw layout came from

    The guest is a port of an existing engine plugin whose pose database is built directly from an AnimationLibrary, over a real mixer and skeleton, using the engine’s own animation tracks. The port’s own comment records that clips were changed to arrive as flat transforms “instead of Godot Animation tracks”, changed for the sandboxed port alone.

    Target data flow

    A build step reads the same source transform arrays once and writes one AnimationLibrary resource, one Animation per clip, each built by adding a track and inserting a key at a time rather than copying bytes. That resource is tracked and imported like any other project asset, so the normal export path carries it with no special allowlist. The guest reads pose data through the sandbox’s existing calls into engine objects rather than through a file.

    Open question

    Two shapes remain undecided. In one, the guest keeps baking its own pose search structure, now reading the AnimationLibrary’s tracks over the sandbox’s calls into engine objects instead of a file, closest to the original plugin’s design. In the other, baking moves to the engine side entirely, producing the same flat arrays the guest reads today, handed across once rather than read from a file. The guest’s own search code stays as it is. The choice needs a measurement of how much the sandbox’s call overhead costs when pulling every key of every clip once at bake time, not at the frame rate the search itself runs at.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2382, which names the datasource store these release steps also move data for.

    RFD66606-2486: Tri2d cli shared algorithm repo

    State: prediscussion

    A validated 2D constrained-Delaunay triangulation already backs a Python dataset pipeline and a godot-sandbox guest. Which repo should carry it?

    tri2d_cli wraps Geogram’s real CDT2d behind a JSON stdin/stdout contract. GarmentCodeData v2’s orig_lens pipeline (Python, replacing CGAL) shells out to it, and the sketch-mesh guest ported the same call sequence into its own curvenet guest as a native function.

    See DETAILS.md for the full argument.

    Check that the new repo exists, builds standalone with plain cmake . && make, and that neither GarmentCodeData nor the sketch-mesh guest vendors its own copy of the CLI source.

    The problem

    Where does a triangulation two unrelated consumers share live?

    Context and problem statement

    tri2d_cli existed only as scratch files on two machines, this Mac’s local port and the Windows desk’s build, never committed to a repo. It wraps Geogram’s real CDT2d (constrained Delaunay triangulation with hole removal) behind a small JSON-over-stdin/stdout CLI, validated against a known-area control case (see confirmation below).

    It has two independent consumers. GarmentCodeData v2’s orig_lens regeneration pipeline (Python) shells out to the built binary in place of CGAL. The sketch-mesh repo’s curvenet godot-sandbox guest ported the same point-flattening, constraint-insertion and hole-removal sequence into C++ as a native guest function, vmcall-verified on the Windows desk, reading native float vectors instead of JSON. Each consumer’s repo serves a different domain from the algorithm itself.

    Decision drivers

    • The validation is the control case checked in confirmation. It should be proven once, in one repo, not re-proven inside each consumer.
    • GarmentCodeData is a Python dataset-generation repo. Its only other caller is a Godot guest ELF, so a C++ triangulation library sits outside its domain.
    • The sketch-mesh repo is a godot-sandbox guest repo. The standalone-CLI build path (cmake . && make, JSON-over-stdio) serves only the Python side, so it sits outside that repo’s domain too.
    • The vendored Geogram subset (BSD-3-Clause, Inria) needs to stay distinct from our own MIT code wherever it lands. Vendoring it twice doubles the licensing surface for no benefit.

    Considered options

    • Commit tri2d_cli into GarmentCodeData’s own repo, and have the sketch-mesh guest re-derive its native function from scratch each time it drifts.
    • Commit the CLI into the sketch-mesh repo and have GarmentCodeData’s pipeline depend on that repo as a submodule.
    • Place it as its own repo: the validated CLI, its vendored geogram-subset subtree, and the control test, with both consumers treating it as an external, versioned tool.

    Decision outcome

    Chosen option: its own new repo. The algorithm and its validation belong to neither consumer, and a shared repo lets both read the same validated source instead of two copies drifting apart.

    The new repo carries:

    • tri2d_cli.cpp and boolean_expression.cpp (MIT, ours).
    • a vendored geogram-subset tree (Geogram 1.9.9, BSD-3-Clause, Inria), with its own LICENSE and CITATION.cff kept inside that subtree.
    • A CMakeLists.txt that builds standalone with plain cmake . && make, no GarmentCode or Windows-desk directory assumptions.
    • A README stating the JSON contract and the control case from confirmation as its smoke test.

    GarmentCodeData’s pipeline and the sketch-mesh guest keep their own ports of the call sequence, a Python subprocess call and a native C++ guest function. This repo is where the algorithm itself is proven once.

    Consequences

    • Good: one validated triangulation, read by two consumers, instead of two copies that can silently diverge.
    • Good: the BSD-3-Clause vendor subtree is licensed once, correctly scoped, instead of twice.
    • Good: GarmentCodeData and the sketch-mesh guest each stay focused on their own domain. Neither carries the other’s build path.
    • Bad: a third consumer, or a fix found in one port, still has to be manually checked against this repo’s tri2d_cli.cpp. The guest’s C++ port is a separate translation, not a build dependency on this repo.

    Confirmation

    • The new repo exists, public, MIT-licensed for its own code, with the vendored geogram-subset tree kept under Geogram’s BSD-3-Clause.
    • cmake . && make on a clean macOS or Linux checkout builds tri2d_cli with no other directories present.
    • The control case: a 10x10 square boundary, a 2x2 hole, and 2 interior points, piped into the built binary, sums to area 96.0, with no triangle centroid landing inside the hole.

    More information

    Relates to the sketch-mesh repo’s guest port of this same call sequence, and to GarmentCodeData v2’s orig_lens regeneration pipeline, the Python consumer this CLI replaces CGAL for.

    Related

    See DETAILS.md for the full argument.

    RFD66606-2485: Find what produces the 100 ms to 730 ms commits

    State: prediscussion Feature: a probe isolates whether FoundationDB, macOS scheduling, or cluster-wide pauses produce the slow commits seen in every benchmark arm so far. Scope: a plain fsync probe, trace-event correlation and a RAM-disk cluster arm, run against the bare libfdb_c commit loop.

    What produces the commits from 100 ms to 730 ms seen in every benchmark arm so far?

    results-contention-matrix5.log (commit 6be7ddb) ran a bare libfdb_c loop with no SQLite and no VFS (the SQLite-on-FoundationDB virtual file system), so the VFS is not the cause. Slow-commit clusters (events within 0.25 s of each other) numbered 24 across 12 cells: 14 touched more than one process and 10 touched one, correcting an earlier report that every cluster touched more than one process. A lone process stalled in 2 of 3 repeats, so sharing alone does not explain the stalls. Server CPU stayed near half a core, ratekeeper reported limited_by=workload throughout, and the scratch trace logs held one SlowTask event in total and no disk-stall events.

    • Run a plain C loop of write plus fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) on the same volume as the scratch cluster, recording the maximum latency, both alone and alongside a commit loop; if it stalls the same way, FoundationDB is cleared as the cause.
    • Correlate the wall-clock start of every slow commit against fdbserver trace events and against production fdbmonitor log activity; sample fs_usage or iostat during the cells; run a RAM-disk cluster arm on the Mac and the desk arm from the sibling scheduling probe.
    • Run the two controls: SIGSTOP a scratch fdbserver for 300 ms and confirm the detector reports a multi-process cluster; run with no load and confirm no stalls are reported.
    • Keep the three candidates separate and untested until a control decides each: the scratch tlog’s fsync sharing the Mac’s SSD with the production cluster, macOS scheduling of client processes, and a cluster-wide pause. Do not cite the commit-proxy latency lines in status json per cell; they are cluster-wide windows, repeated across cells.

    A cause counts only if a control reproduces or suppresses the stall on demand; otherwise it stays undetermined, with what was ruled out, built from log files.

    Data so far

    results-contention-matrix5.log (6be7ddb), bare libfdb_c loop, no SQLite and no VFS, so the VFS is not the cause:

    • Slow-commit clusters (events within 0.25 s of each other): 24 in the 12 cells. 14 touched more than one process, 10 touched one.
      • N=1: 8 clusters, all single-process. N=2: 4, all multi. N=4: 3, all multi. N=8: 9, of which 7 multi and 2 single.
      • An earlier report said every cluster hit more than one process. That was wrong, and this table corrects it.
    • A lone process stalled in 2 of 3 repeats (5 and 4 commits over 100 ms), so sharing alone does not explain the stalls.
    • Server CPU stayed near half a core. Ratekeeper said limited_by=workload throughout.
    • The scratch trace logs held one SlowTask event in total and no disk-stall events.
    • The commit-proxy latency lines in status json are cluster-wide windows, repeated identically across cells. Do not cite them per cell.

    Candidates, kept separate and all untested

    1. The scratch tlog’s fsync sharing the Mac’s SSD with the production cluster.
    2. macOS scheduling of the client processes.
    3. A pause across the cluster.

    Method

    • Cheap decisive probe: a plain C loop of write plus fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) on the same volume, recording the maximum latency, run alone and alongside a commit loop. If it stalls the same way, FoundationDB is cleared.
    • Correlate the wall-clock start of every slow commit with fdbserver trace events (trace format with timestamps) and with production fdbmonitor log activity.
    • Sample fs_usage or iostat during the cells.
    • A RAM-disk cluster arm on the Mac.
    • The desk arm from the sibling scheduling probe.

    Controls that must be able to fail

    • SIGSTOP a scratch fdbserver for 300 ms: the detector must report it as a multi-process cluster.
    • A run with no load must show no stalls.

    Reading rule, fixed before the run

    A cause counts only if a control reproduces or suppresses the stall on demand. Otherwise it stays “undetermined”, with the list of what was ruled out.

    Acceptance

    One named cause, or an explicit “undetermined” with what was ruled out, built from log files.
