    RFD66606-2484: Load the challenge seed into a store once, verified by counts and hashes

    State: prediscussion Feature: the challenge seed loads once into a SQLite-on-FoundationDB store through the VFS, with its row counts and content hashes checked against the seed file. Scope: the import path for seed/feed.db into one store, and the counts, hashes and integrity check that verify the import.

    Can the challenge seed be loaded once into a store through the VFS, and verified?

    The seed file seed/feed.db is 238 MB: 50,000 users, 500,000 posts, and 2,016,005 likes, with its schema fixed by schema.sql. This table is also the 50 MB to 200 MB table that a sibling measurement needs. The seed is in WAL mode, but the VFS (the SQLite-on-FoundationDB virtual file system) needs journal_mode=MEMORY and locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE, and a 4 KiB page size, so the import cannot simply reopen the seed file as-is. The VFS already stages a commit too large for one FoundationDB transaction, which bounds one transaction to 10 MB, so SQLite’s backup API or VACUUM INTO through the VFS may do the job without hand-chunking.

    • Look first for an existing import path in datasource-store: prove_big_commit.c, sqlrun.c, weft_sql.c, tpcc.c, and fly/backup-fresh.sh; try SQLite’s backup API or VACUUM INTO through the VFS before hand-chunking with ATTACH and rowid-ranged INSERT ... SELECT sized well under 10 MB.
    • Import the seed once, not at server start, with journal_mode=MEMORY and locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE set and a 4 KiB page size; record which path ran.
    • Verify with row counts per table against the file seed, a per-table content hash over an ordered SELECT compared with the file seed (reusing the content sha256 that seed/make-seed.sh prints, if it exposes one), and PRAGMA integrity_check.
    • Run the control: drop 1,000 posts from the store after import and confirm the hash and the count both catch it; record import wall time, bytes in the store, and cluster.data.partitions_count afterwards.

    Row counts per table match the file seed, a per-table content hash over an ordered SELECT matches the file seed, and PRAGMA integrity_check passes. A planted control, 1,000 posts dropped from the store after import, must be caught by the hash and the count.

    Look first for an existing path

    Candidates in datasource-store: prove_big_commit.c, sqlrun.c, weft_sql.c, tpcc.c, fly/backup-fresh.sh. The VFS already stages a commit too large for one FoundationDB transaction (the 10 MB limit), so SQLite’s backup API or VACUUM INTO through the VFS may do the job. Hand-chunk only if nothing exists.

    Method notes

    • The seed is in WAL mode. The VFS needs journal_mode=MEMORY and locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE, and the page size must be 4 KiB.
    • Import once, not at server start.
    • If hand-chunking: ATTACH the file seed and INSERT ... SELECT in rowid ranges sized well under 10 MB, or rely on staging, and record which path ran.

    Verification

    • Row counts per table against the file seed.
    • A per-table content hash over an ordered SELECT, compared with the file seed. Reuse the content sha256 that seed/make-seed.sh prints if it exposes one.
    • PRAGMA integrity_check.

    Control that must be able to fail

    A planted missing batch (drop 1,000 posts from the store after import) must be caught by the hash and the count.

    Record

    Import wall time, bytes in the store, cluster.data.partitions_count afterwards, and which path was taken.

    Acceptance

    Counts and hashes match, the planted control fails, the numbers are committed, and the sibling measurement that needs this table is told it now has a table to use.

    RFD66606-2483: Find the group-commit knee: rows per SQLite transaction against commits and p99

    State: prediscussion Feature: a benchmark measures how many rows one SQLite transaction must carry to keep a FoundationDB-backed store at the challenge’s write rate. Scope: the 4-process scratch cluster’s writer loop, its batch sizes, and the commit-rate table the run produces.

    How many requests must one SQLite transaction carry so a server on this store keeps up with the challenge’s write rate?

    One SQLite transaction is one FoundationDB transaction, and a commit costs a median of about 8.4 ms, so a server that commits per request caps near 100 writes/s per store. A lone writer through the VFS (the SQLite-on-FoundationDB virtual file system) measured from 89.7 commits/s to 106.9 commits/s, and a bare libfdb_c loop with no SQLite and no VFS measured from 106.5 commits/s to 113.5 commits/s per process at N=1. The challenge’s user model is derived, not measured on this server, at about 165 writes/s at 20,000 users and about 830 writes/s at 100,000 users; re-derive from bench/load.js before quoting.

    • Run the writer on the 4-process scratch cluster (never port 4700), through the VFS, at K = 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, three repeats, in closed-loop and fixed-arrival-rate modes, and record whether any batch’s dirty pages crossed into the VFS’s staging path (FoundationDB bounds one transaction to 10 MB and 5 s).
    • Build a table from the log files with min, mean and max over the repeats; report rows/s, per-row p99 acknowledge latency, commits over 100 ms, and conflicted delta; name the knee batch size and amend PROTOCOL.md with the chosen batch window and size.
    • Run the crash-check control: a planted variant that acknowledges before the commit must show higher throughput and then fail the check; kill -9 right after an acknowledgement must still find every acknowledged row in the store.

    Run a writer that carries K row-writes in one SQLite transaction, for K = 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, three repeats, in closed-loop and fixed-arrival-rate modes. K=1 must reproduce about 100 commits/s or the probe is wrong. Rows/s must grow close to linearly in K until commit latency rises; that point is the knee.

    Data so far

    • Lone writer through the VFS: from 89.7 commits/s to 106.9 commits/s (results-contention-matrix2.log, results-contention-matrix3.log, commit 482974a).
    • Bare libfdb_c loop, no SQLite, no VFS: from 106.5 commits/s to 113.5 commits/s per process at N=1, median commit about 8.4 ms (results-contention-matrix5.log, commit 6be7ddb).
    • Derived, not measured on this server: the user model does a like with probability 0.15 and a post with probability 0.02 per iteration of roughly 21 s of think time (think-time bands of 3 s to 7 s, 3 s to 8 s, and 5 s to 15 s). That is about 0.008 writes/s per user, so about 165 writes/s at 20,000 users and about 830 writes/s at 100,000. Re-derive from bench/load.js before quoting.
    • The C leader already group-commits; this store’s writer must too.

    Reading rule, fixed before the run

    • K=1 must reproduce about 100 commits/s. If it does not, the probe is wrong.
    • Rows/s should grow close to linearly in K until commit latency rises. The knee is the batch size the server uses.
    • Report rows/s, per-row p99 acknowledge latency, commits over 100 ms, and conflicted delta.

    Controls that must be able to fail

    • A planted variant that acknowledges before the commit must show higher throughput and then fail the crash check.
    • Crash check: kill -9 the writer right after an acknowledgement and confirm every acknowledged row is in the store. An earlier measurement found a store that acknowledged before durable, and this is the failure that catches it.

    Acceptance

    A table built from the log files, with min, mean and max over the repeats; the knee named; and a one-line PROTOCOL.md amendment stating the batch window and size the benchmark server will use.

    RFD66606-2482: Build a 50-200 MB feed-shaped table before any read or cluster-shape claim

    State: prediscussion Feature: the reader bend gets re-measured on a realistic feed-shaped table, not a toy one. Scope: the scratch FoundationDB cluster’s VFS, its test table, and PROTOCOL.md’s pair cells.

    Does the reader bend survive a realistic table?

    In the pair matrix, per-pair reads fell to 0.65-0.67 of M=1 at M=8 with the writer fixed at 50 commits/s, and to 0.47-0.48 with the writer at max rate. The current test table has 2,000 rows, about 500 KB, with a total store size probably around 4 MB, which data distribution almost certainly keeps in one shard on one storage process; adding storage processes would then change nothing, so a “not the cluster” conclusion drawn from it would be wrong. Under NORMAL locking, SQLite drops its whole page cache on every head move, so each uncached page costs one round trip when the speculative get hits and two when it misses, and a 500 KB table flatters that cost. Three candidate causes must stay separate: one storage process serving every page read, the VFS re-fetching pages after each head move, and this Mac.

    • Build a 50-200 MB table with the challenge’s schema shape (schema.sql: users, posts, likes) and run a feed-shaped query against it.
    • Before reading any result, record cluster.data.partitions_count and the per-role query counters from status json, and read per-process CPU as deltas of cputime, never ps %cpu.
    • Repeat the M=1 and M=8 pair cells, three repeats, under the pre-registered reading rule in PROTOCOL.md.
    • Report a measured partitions count above one, or a stated reason it stayed at one, and the M=8 reader ratio with its confounds stated.
    • Any change to fdb_vfs.c goes on a dev/ branch of datasource-store with a probe that fails without it, and only after this question is answered.

    A measured partitions_count above one (or a stated reason it stayed at one), and the M=8 reader ratio on the feed-shaped table with its confounds stated.

    RFD66606-2477: Suit markers: structured-light decoding with anonymous corners and lattice voting

    State: prediscussion Feature: corners are placed by lattice voting, so markers read even when their id is wrong. Scope: predict_neighbours.py, the chart’s lattice, and the corner-voting gates it must pass.

    Can a corner be placed on the chart correctly even when the id painted next to it is wrong?

    Treat the board as a spatially coded pattern instead of a set of independently-read tags: detect corners without trusting their ids, place each corner on the chart by voting over offsets, rotations and instances, and recover unread markers from their read neighbours. predict_neighbours.py already exists for this but was never run, and was left out of the earlier pull requests.

    • A planted wrong offset must lose the vote, so one bad candidate never outvotes the consistent majority.
    • A blank pattern (no corners detected) gives nothing back, rather than a false placement.
    • The UV pass marks every assignment right or wrong, with no assignment left unjudged. Once those three gates pass, measure corners placed, wrong placements, and markers recovered that tag decoding alone misses, and report those three numbers together, not separately.

    Run predict_neighbours.py against planted gates before trusting any measurement from it.

    RFD66606-2475: Suit markers: tag bench and the marker frontier (variants against input families)

    State: prediscussion Feature: a tag bench and a frontier table pick tag family, marker size and detector settings. Scope: tag_bench.py, frontier_markers.py, and the detector variants they compare.

    Which tag family, marker size and detector settings give the fewest wrong reads at distance and tilt?

    The first bench run was invalid: the flat sheets rendered mirrored, so flipping the frame read 263 markers instead of the expected count, which gave 3,913 of 3,917 tags “broken” and failed the control outright. That bug is fixed in tag_bench.py. A per-tag blocklist is not a usable gate on its own, since it only reacts to tags that already failed; the frontier table has to decide tag family, marker size and detector settings up front instead.

    Ship the frontier table as the gate that selects tag family, marker size and detector settings, replacing any per-tag blocklist approach. Detector settings already show they matter at large marker scale: a window of 3 to 203 and a threshold constant of 3 recovered most of the unread markers at 220 px, and that setting becomes the frontier’s starting point rather than a fixed default.

    Re-render the bench and build the frontier table: detector variants crossed with distance and tilt, each cell holding its wrong-read count, plus a flipped-frame control that must itself read as broken.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    The mirrored-frame bug

    The flat sheets used to validate detector settings rendered mirrored left-to-right. Flipping the frame before detection recovered 263 readable markers that the un-flipped frame reported as unreadable, which inflated the broken-tag count to 3,913 of 3,917 and made the bench’s own control pass for the wrong reason. tag_bench.py now flips consistently with the render path.

    Frontier axes

    • Tag family: which marker dictionary is painted.
    • Marker size: physical size in mm (and the derived pixel count at a given camera distance).
    • Detector settings: adaptive-threshold window size and threshold constant.
    • Distance and tilt: the two viewing conditions crossed against every other axis.
    • Flipped-frame control: every cell also runs mirrored, and must report broken, not readable.

    Code

    tag_bench.py and frontier_markers.py, both in https://github.com/V-Sekai-fire/interactor-garment-proxy.

    RFD66606-2474: Suit markers: dead-on gate must read every marker

    State: prediscussion Feature: the dead-on gate reads every painted marker in perfect conditions, with no exceptions. Scope: dead_on.py, texture_markers.py, and the placed-marker set they score.

    Does every marker we paint scan dead on, with the camera square on and nothing in the way?

    Today the gate fails: 276 of 280 visible markers read (98.57%) with the original ids, 278 of 280 (99.29%) with the ids moved. Camera 74 fails with two different ids at the same spot, so that is a position fault: a sharply tilted surface strip sits beside the marker. Ids 664, 703, 1973 and 1268 fail only at some positions, so those are pattern faults, not position faults.

    Drop every marker id that fails the dead-on gate (held in DROP_IDS) and require a 100% read rate on the rest. A dropped id’s slot stays a hole on the garment rather than being refilled by a neighbour, so the drop list is stable across renders. Camera 74’s failure is tracked and fixed separately as a position fault, since it is a tilt problem in the surface strip, not a marker pattern problem, and fixing it is out of this gate’s scope.

    Run the full pass over all 2,600 placed positions once it finishes rendering, and read the gate against that pass: 100% of the markers left after dropping the failing ids must read.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    The two fault classes

    • Position fault: a marker’s own pattern is fine, but where it sits (near a seam, a sharp fold, or a tilted strip) keeps the camera from reading it. Camera 74’s dual-id read at one spot is this class.
    • Pattern fault: the marker’s pattern itself does not read cleanly regardless of where it sits. Ids 664, 703, 1973 and 1268, which fail only at some positions and not others, land here once position is ruled out.

    Where the code lands

    dead_on.py scores each rendered position against the expected id, and texture_markers.py paints the marker set onto the garment texture before render. Both are referenced from pull requests V-Sekai-fire/interactor-taskweft-persona#6 and #7 against https://github.com/V-Sekai-fire/interactor-garment-proxy.

    Open

    The full 2,600-position pass was still rendering at the time of this draft. DROP_IDS is provisional until that pass completes and confirms no additional ids fail.

    Source: rfd/2474-suit-markers-dead-on-gate-must-read-every-marker.exs

    RFD66606-2473: Planner search: heuristics for the shortest plan

    State: prediscussion Feature: the planner’s backtracking search finds the shortest plan without an exhaustive scan. Scope: the planner’s bound-raising search and the domains it solves.

    Can the planner find the shortest plan for 16 cubes without scanning every bound in turn?

    shortestOf raises a bound on the number of actions until a plan reaches its goals, through a backtracking decomposition. That search is exhaustive at each bound, so the whole search is exponential: fine for the Sussman anomaly at six actions, too slow for 16 cubes.

    Add three heuristics to the bound-raising search, each kept only if it holds plan length unchanged while cutting search time:

    • A lower bound supplied by the domain (admissible, so the rising bound starts higher and prunes branches that cannot reach a shorter plan).
    • Memoising failed (state, bound) pairs, so a branch already shown to fail at a bound is never re-explored at that bound.
    • Ordering alternatives by a heuristic, so the search tries the branch most likely to reach the goal first, before the branches it would otherwise explore in declaration order. Each heuristic ships behind its own control: a planted domain that breaks admissibility, a planted stale memo entry, and a planted heuristic that always ranks last, each of which must make its gate fail.

    Run the blocks-world domain at 16 cubes under a wall-clock budget. A plan that returns within budget, at the same length an exhaustive search would find, passes.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2473-planner-search-heuristics-for-the-shortest-plan.exs

    RFD66606-2472: KHR_interactivity: what the interpreter does not build yet

    State: prediscussion Feature: the Lean KHR_interactivity interpreter’s gap against the extension’s own text. Scope: Persona/Khr.lean, the Lean module that builds and runs a KHR_interactivity graph.

    Which of the extension’s own nodes and types does the interpreter not build yet, and which checks does it only do while a graph runs rather than before it starts?

    Persona/Khr.lean already follows the extension’s text for typed int and bool, 32-bit wrap, flow/for re-reading endIndex, socket order by string, variable/set with index-named sockets, pointer/get with isValid, and math/switch. Floats, float vectors, matrices and quaternions are not built at all, a float type simply rejects the graph, and a long list of nodes, reference template parameters and static type checking are missing too. A plan or a goal from elsewhere in this workspace can carry an unbounded integer; the extension’s own integers are 32-bit two’s complement, and that gap sits underneath every node listed here.

    Build the missing pieces in the order they block a real graph: first the float and float vector types (so a float type stops rejecting the whole graph), then flow/doN, multiGate, waitAll, throttle, setDelay and cancelDelay, then the remaining events beyond event/onStart, then variable/interpolate and pointer/interpolate, then the integer operations div, rem, sign, clamp, the shifts, clz, ctz and popcnt, then pointer/set’s err flow, matrices and quaternions, and reference template parameters including the doubled-bracket escape for a literal bracket. Move every socket type check that runs today only while a node executes to a static pass before the run starts, so a mistyped graph is refused before any node fires.

    Build one missing node, give it a positive and a negative control, and confirm a graph that used to reject it now runs it, while a graph with the wrong socket type for it still refuses.

    Already built

    Typed int and bool, 32-bit wrap, flow/for re-reading endIndex, socket order by string, variable/set with index-named sockets, pointer/get with isValid, and math/switch, each following the extension’s own text.

    Types not built

    Floats and float vectors, matrices and quaternions; a graph that declares a float type is rejected outright today rather than run.

    Nodes not built

    flow/doN, multiGate, waitAll, throttle, setDelay, cancelDelay; every event other than event/onStart; variable/interpolate and pointer/interpolate; the integer operations div, rem, sign, clamp, the shifts, clz, ctz and popcnt; and pointer/set’s err flow.

    Syntax not built

    Reference template parameters written as {name}, and the doubled-bracket escape used for a literal bracket inside a pointer template.

    Checking that runs too late

    Every socket’s type is checked only while a node runs, not before the run starts, so a mistyped graph can run partway before it is caught.

    The integer width gap underneath

    The planner’s own integers, outside a KHR_interactivity graph, are unbounded. The extension’s own integers are 32-bit two’s complement. Every node above inherits this gap until it is closed once, at the boundary, rather than node by node.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2471: MiniZinc Challenge: precedence-scheduling problems on the temporal plan

    State: prediscussion Feature: the temporal plan expresses the Challenge’s precedence-only scheduling problems. Scope: the persona’s temporal plan representation, read against four candidate problem sets.

    After the planning puzzles, can the same temporal plan express a problem that needs only precedence and durations, with no resources at all?

    Four problem families on the Challenge’s list look like a fit by name alone: project-planning (2012, 2015), road_construction (2014, 2017), ship-schedule (2011, 2012, 2014) and train-scheduling (2024). None of their models has been read yet, so fit is a guess today. The temporal plan already carries start, end and duration per step, release times and deadlines, and a critical-path total, but it has no resources, so any model with a cumulative constraint is out of reach before a single model is read.

    Read each of the four candidate families’ models, starting with the smallest, and classify each as expressible or out of reach by the same rule the planning puzzles used. For a family that is expressible, climb from its smallest instance, validate every plan against MiniZinc itself, and accept only a plan that is both valid and optimal. A family that needs a resource, an all-different, a cumulative or a packing constraint is set aside rather than forced onto a plan that cannot carry it.

    Read one family’s model in full and classify it: expressible on the temporal plan as is, or out of reach because it needs a resource, an all-different, a cumulative or a packing constraint the plan does not carry.

    The candidate families

    • project-planning (2012, 2015)
    • road_construction (2014, 2017)
    • ship-schedule (2011, 2012, 2014)
    • train-scheduling (2024)

    None of their models has been read yet; whether each is expressible on the temporal plan is a guess from the name alone, not yet a finding.

    What the temporal plan already carries

    Start, end and duration per step (an unspecified start and end are left out of a problem; a missing duration means the step is instantaneous), release times and deadlines, and a critical-path total. It carries no resources, so a model with a cumulative constraint cannot be expressed on it as it stands.

    Acceptance

    The same rule the planning puzzles used: valid and optimal, checked against MiniZinc itself, climbing from the smallest instance of a family up, never starting at the largest.

    RFD66606-2470: MiniZinc Challenge: blocks-world on the GTN blocks methods, climbing from small instances

    State: prediscussion Feature: the ported blocks-world GTN climbs from small instances to the five official ones. Scope: the blocks_gtn domain, its frontier harness, and the MiniZinc checker that grades it.

    Can a plan the GTN (goal-task network) finds for the Challenge’s blocks-world also be the minimum, checked by the Challenge’s own tool, climbing from the smallest instance up?

    GTPyhop’s blocks_gtn is already ported, with take, put and moveblocks as a KHR_interactivity graph, and shortestOf already finds the optimal six actions for the Sussman anomaly. A separate reference tool already matched a breadth-first minimum for n = 3 to 7 on 3 piles, in times climbing from about 15 ms to about 4 s, but the domain still has no pile limit, no climbing harness and no run against the real checker.

    Encode the model’s pile limit, k piles with at most k cubes on the table, in the GTN domain, then climb: generate instances at n = 3, 4, 5 and up with the model’s k, record solve time at each step, and stop at the frontier where the time makes the next step not worth running yet. Add a heuristic lower bound, for instance the count of cubes already out of place, to prune the five official instances (16 cubes on 4 piles), which are far past what iterative deepening alone can reach. Validate every plan against MiniZinc itself, installed locally, rather than against the reference tool alone.

    Install MiniZinc, replay a solved instance through it, and confirm the checker accepts the plan as valid and minimum; a plan with one move removed must be refused by the same checker.

    Already in place

    • tests/gtpyhop/blocks_gtn/ ports GTPyhop’s blocks_gtn: actions take, put and moveblocks as a KHR_interactivity (the Khronos node-graph behaviour format) graph.
    • shortestOf, iterative deepening over the backtracking decomposition and exported as persona_plan_shortest, finds the optimal six actions for the Sussman anomaly, and refuses a smaller bound by name as limit.
    • On branch parked/minizinc-blocks-frontier, tools/minizinc/ holds an instance generator, an independent breadth-first minimum, and a replay against the model’s rules. For n = 3 to 7 on 3 piles, 20 random instances each matched the minimum and replayed validly, at a cost climbing from about 15 ms at n = 5 to about 4 s at n = 7.

    What still has to land

    • The model’s pile limit, k piles and at most k cubes on the table, encoded in the GTN domain itself rather than assumed.
    • The climbing harness: generate n = 3, 4, 5 and up at the model’s k, record solve time, and stop at the frontier; the stopping point teaches which bound or heuristic to add next.
    • A heuristic bound, such as a lower bound on cubes out of place, to prune the rising search enough to reach the five official instances, each 16 cubes on 4 piles.
    • MiniZinc itself, installed locally (brew install minizinc; there is no cask by that name, and minizincide is the IDE, not the checker) so a plan is validated for real, not only by the independent breadth-first tool.
    • A local clone of the MiniZinc/mzn-challenge archive, about 570 MB at depth 1, to read the 2022 blocks.mzn model this domain targets.

    RFD66606-2469: StableHLO: match XLA CPU’s summation order in reduce and dot_general

    State: prediscussion Feature: reduce and dot_general reproduce XLA CPU’s own order of summation, not only its sum. Scope: the StableHLO lowering in guest/pjrt-rd/stablehlo.cpp and its generated test cases.

    Can the lowering reproduce XLA CPU’s own order of adding floats, not only the value that order happens to land on?

    Eight cases are not bit-equal on the RTX 4090 today: dot_batched, mlp_pre, mlp_f32, reduce_sum_random, mean_last, softmax_f32, rms_norm_f32 and causal_attention. Each stays within the functional bar, a rel-L2 around 1e-7 and at most a few dozen ulp, but none is bit-equal. reduce with add sums in an irregular tree that changes with the shape, and dot_general runs as a fusion whose accumulation tree also depends on the shape; cases with the order written out, or whose partial sums are exact, are already bit-equal, so the gap is the order, not the arithmetic.

    Reveal XLA’s accumulation tree for each reduce and dot shape the five graphs use, on the Zen 2 desk with this jax build, and record the trees in a table keyed by shape. Emit each tree as a sequence of slices and adds, or as a kernel that takes the tree as data, and fall back to today’s order, with the case kept in XFAIL, for any shape the table does not cover. The table is tied to one CPU and one XLA build, the way rsqrt_zen2 already is, so it records both.

    Reveal one new shape’s tree, add it to the table, confirm that shape’s case turns bit-equal, and confirm removing the table brings the old difference back.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    The eight cases

    dot_batched, mlp_pre, mlp_f32, reduce_sum_random, mean_last, softmax_f32, rms_norm_f32 and causal_attention: each is within the functional bar today, a rel-L2 around 1e-7 and at most a few dozen ulp, but not bit-equal. pinned_sum_tree, softmax_pinned and causal_softmax_pinned already pin the order and are already bit-equal, which is the evidence that order, not arithmetic, is the whole gap.

    The two trees to reveal

    • reduce with add: an irregular summation tree that changes with the shape, matching an unrolled chain of adds reassociated by LLVM. tools/reveal_sum_order and the notes in STABLEHLO.md describe how it is read back out.
    • dot_general: a fusion whose accumulation tree also depends on the shape, revealed the same way, on the same desk and jax build.

    Acceptance

    • The eight cases above are bit-equal on the GPU, or each keeps a measured reason in XFAIL.
    • Removing the table brings back the old differences; that is the control this decision must fail without.
    • The added cost in dispatches and time for the five graphs is measured and written down.
    • All 11 desk gates still pass.

    Source: rfd/2469-stablehlo-match-xla-cpu-s-summation-order-in-reduce-and-dot-general.exs

    RFD66606-2468: StableHLO: run-time i32 arithmetic

    State: prediscussion Feature: run-time i32 values become i32 tensors on the device instead of a refusal. Scope: the StableHLO lowering in guest/pjrt-rd/stablehlo.cpp and its generated test cases.

    Can an i32 value computed at run time reach the device, instead of being refused because it was not already known when the graph was compiled?

    Today an i32 value is folded away on the host whenever the compiler already knows it, and refused the moment it is computed at run time: an argument, or anything derived from one. Gather’s index arithmetic and dynamic masks need those values on the device, not on the host, and the five graphs the probes run (qwen, dit, sconv and the two Kimodo layers) all touch one.

    Hold run-time i32 values as i32 tensors on the device, and add element-wise kernels under XLA’s wrapping semantics: add, subtract, multiply, compare, select, clamp, and convert to and from f32. Lift each refusal that exists only for lack of one of these kernels, case by case, so that every case in the generator is either bit-equal on the GPU or carries a measured reason in XFAIL, with all 11 desk gates kept green throughout.

    Run the generated cases, including zeros of both signs, infinities, NaN and denormals, against XLA CPU’s own output from the Zen 2 desk as the reference, and confirm a case built to fail does fail.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Cases and reference

    tools/gen_stablehlo_cases.py exercises the special values a run-time i32 path must survive: zeros of both signs, infinities, NaN and denormals. XLA CPU’s own output, taken from the Zen 2 desk, is the bit-equal reference for every case; there is no other oracle in use here.

    What ships

    • Run-time i32 values held as i32 tensors on the device, never folded away because they were not known at compile time.
    • Element-wise kernels: add, subtract, multiply, compare, select, clamp, and conversion to and from f32, each under XLA’s own wrapping semantics rather than a saturating one.
    • Refusals lifted only where one of the kernels above now covers the case; a case no kernel covers keeps its refusal unchanged.

    Acceptance

    • Every case in tools/gen_stablehlo_cases.py is bit-equal on the GPU, or carries a measured reason recorded in XFAIL.
    • A case built to fail does fail; a gate that cannot fail proves nothing.
    • All 11 desk gates still pass after the change lands.

    Source: rfd/2468-stablehlo-run-time-i32-arithmetic.exs

    RFD66606-2461: Store: B-tree cursor reads on hot read paths (secondary transfer from rust-iouring-kensac)

    State: prediscussion Feature: hot store reads would skip SQLite’s bytecode engine via direct B-tree cursor walks. Scope: the store’s read paths over the weft_fdb VFS, with a SQL fallback kept.

    Does skipping SQLite’s bytecode engine on the store’s hot read paths buy a real win once the read side is already network-bound?

    The same outside challenge entry that inspired the compaction thread also walks SQLite’s B-tree cursors directly inside a read transaction, skipping the SQL engine and its column copies, and decoding record bytes by hand with a SQL fallback kept for safety. The store’s reads already go through prepare and step today. The honest read is that this is a constant-factor win, not a network round-trip win: the store’s existing speculative reads and read-ahead already save roughly a round trip per read and turn two hundred fifty six pages into about two round trips, so the entry’s trick can add at most something like five to fifteen percent, and only if profiling shows the SQL engine’s overhead is real.

    • Profile the store’s hot read paths before writing any cursor-reading code, to confirm whether the SQL engine’s prepare and step overhead is actually a measurable share of read latency.
    • If profiling supports it, add a cursor-based reader that walks the B-tree directly inside a read transaction and decodes record bytes by hand, with the existing SQL path kept as a fallback rather than removed.
    • Treat any win here as a constant-factor improvement on top of the already network-bound read path, not a replacement for the speculative-read and read-ahead work already in place.
    • Do not spend further effort on this transfer unless the profiling step above actually shows engine overhead large enough to matter.

    Profile the hot read paths first; only build the cursor-based reader if profiling shows engine overhead worth the complexity, and keep the existing speculative read and read-ahead engineering untouched either way.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2461-store-b-tree-cursor-reads-on-hot-read-paths-secondary-transfer-from-ru.exs

    RFD66606-2460: Store: off-the-loop passive compaction thread (transfer from rust-iouring-kensac)

    State: prediscussion Feature: the store’s compaction moves off the write loop onto its own passive, timed thread. Scope: the store’s fold and compact path in fdb_vfs.c, ported from a challenge submission.

    Can the store’s compaction run on its own thread, on a timer, so a write caller never pays a fold’s cost on its own latency?

    A winning entry in an outside challenge, rust-iouring-kensac, already runs its checkpoint and compaction off the write loop on a second, low-priority thread, so write callers never wait on it. The store’s compaction today is demand-driven: a call to weft_compact_due blocks whichever caller happens to ask for it. That is exactly the kind of tail latency a day-long benchmark is built to catch, since it measures the slowest save a day reaches rather than a p99.

    • Add a dedicated, lower-priority compaction thread that opens its own FoundationDB connection and runs folds passively on a timer once the log grows past a threshold, instead of folding on demand inside the caller’s path.
    • Change weft_compact_due from a blocking fold into a cheap call that wakes the thread when the log is already short, so the write loop never performs the fold itself.
    • Bound the hold time the compaction thread may take per pass, following the referenced entry’s bound of at most 250 milliseconds, so passive compaction cannot itself become a tail-latency source.
    • Verify the change against the existing day-long benchmark that measures the slowest saves a day reaches, not only the median or the p99.

    Add a dedicated, nice’d compaction thread on its own FoundationDB connection, and measure whether a planted burst of writes still shows a fold cost on the write caller’s own latency.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2460-store-off-the-loop-passive-compaction-thread-transfer-from-rust-iourin.exs

    RFD66606-2457: Navigator: show the temporal route and state durations for the beta’s RFDs

    State: prediscussion Feature: the navigator should show each RFD’s earliest and latest possible time and route. Scope: the generator here, and the navigator and its planner in the persona repository.

    Can the navigator show a temporal route and state durations for the beta’s RFDs when no RFD states a duration yet?

    The navigator plans the beta’s route from the RFDs’ own token edges, a cone of 33 RFDs and 37 steps. The persona planner now produces temporal plans with a start, an end and a duration per step, a critical-path total, and, through a composite task that lists each step twice, the earliest and latest possible time for that step. The site does not use any of that yet. Without a stated duration every step collapses to zero length, so the total reads as an instant: of 44 committed RFDs, 39 landed in the PR that created them, leaving a median lead time that is useless as a stand-in.

    • Add a composite window-rfd-N method to the generator that decomposes into earliest-rfd-N and latest-rfd-N, where the latest side needs its own again methods since the held shortcut no longer applies once the steps are already done (proposed).
    • Pair each step’s two appearances in the navigator client as its earliest and latest possible time, with the problem document stating today as its origin (proposed).
    • Decide the declaration form for a duration, or a start and end per action, within the existing rebac block and with no new DSL (proposed).
    • Take the planner from the persona’s latest release, as the navigator build already does, and check that tag carries temporal plans and the shortest-plan export (proposed).
    • Draft the 33 RFDs’ durations from a reference-class estimate rather than the useless observed lead time, and report a range or a P50 or P80 finish instead of one critical-path total (proposed).

    Draft durations for the 33 RFDs in the cone, then run the navigator against the new temporal plan.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    The blocker

    No RFD states a duration, and the observed lead times are not a usable stand-in: 39 of the 44 committed RFDs landed in the PR that created them, so the median lead time is 0 days. Left unfilled, every step in the generated domain is instantaneous and the plan’s total reads as a zero-duration instant.

    The two generator changes

    scripts/pages_tree.exs needs a composite window-rfd-N method that decomposes into earliest-rfd-N and latest-rfd-N. The latest side cannot reuse the held shortcut, since by that point the steps it would shortcut are already done, so it needs its own “again” methods. site/navigator.js in the persona repository needs to pair each step’s two appearances as its first possible and last possible time, and the problem document needs to state today as its origin, or every start and end point is left out.

    The planner release

    The navigator build (site/build.sh in the persona repository) downloads the latest release tag of the persona repository, so no tag is pinned here. Whether that tag carries temporal plans and the shortest-plan export has not been checked against this work.

    Estimating durations

    The literature on duration estimates covers the planning fallacy, reference classes, three-point estimates, PERT merge bias, Monte Carlo methods and resource-constrained scheduling. These point toward a range or a P50 or P80 finish for the critical path, in place of one single total.

    RFD66606-2446: A2A hardening leaves five verification gaps open

    State: discussion Feature: a record of five checks a security pass never ran, so the pass is not called finished. Scope: the MCP-to-A2A bridge server, and the Godot editor’s MCP listener and its new A2A route.

    Can a security pass call itself finished while five of its own claims stay unchecked?

    Eight pull requests closed a prompt-injection finding, moved a bridge server and an editor listener to the Agent2Agent protocol’s 1.0 wire format, and closed a browser-origin hole in both of the listener’s protocols. Every pull request carries tests that passed on one machine.

    Five verification gaps stay open, and work on them does not resume until this record changes.

    • No diff against the operator’s own A2A listener script, which was never recovered.
    • No run on the Windows desk or inside the resident editor session the operator described.
    • No run against the Agent2Agent protocol’s conformance suite, for either system.
    • No real browser has exercised the new Origin refusal, only a forged command-line header.
    • Both systems’ test commands still force a hidden display, against the windowed-test rule.

    Read the five gaps below before picking any of this work back up, and close one gap at a time.

    The five gaps, and what closes each one

    • Godot parity. The operator ran a resident editor with an uncommitted listener script added to its MCP addon, serving A2A at one address with a card and two commands. That script was never pushed anywhere and could not be found on any branch, so the listener that shipped is a clean-room build from the protocol specification, not a check against the original. Closes when that original script is pushed to a branch and the two are diffed line by line.
    • The Windows desk. Every check so far ran on a Mac, in a real window, never headless. Closes when the same checks run once on the desk, inside the resident editor session.
    • A conformance suite. Both systems were checked against the official client library and against each other, never against the protocol’s own conformance suite. Closes when that suite is identified by name and run once against each system, with its own report kept.
    • A real browser. The Origin refusal was proven with a command-line client sending a forged header, never with a browser tab. Closes when an actual browser page, opened by a person, is shown the refusal.
    • The hidden-display test commands. Both systems’ committed test commands still pass a flag that hides the window, against the rule that a Godot test runs where it can be watched. Every check in this pass ran windowed by hand instead, by overriding the command each time. Closes when the committed command itself drops the flag and still passes.

    Related

    RFD66606-2443: EntityServer serves 64 Hz entity state beside FeedServer

    State: committed Feature: a sibling EntityServer serves 64 Hz 3D state beside FeedServer. Scope: the transport repository: entity modules, one executable, the codec, the load generator.

    Can the feed server’s ring, store and layers carry a tick loop without a second copy of any of them?

    The repository already has the io_uring glue with a provided-buffer ring, a store that opens FoundationDB through a VFS, and layered proofs. It has no tick, no packet codec and no load generator.

    EntityServer is a sibling of FeedServer in the same repository, built by the same lakefile (operator, 2026-11-07). It reuses the ring glue, the JWT layer and the store, and edits them where they must change. It adds no parallel copy.

    • State lives in memory in a flat array. The tick path does no SQLite and no disk I/O.
    • The 100 byte packet layout has one source, the entity packet contract, taken by subtree. EntityServer never re-emits the offsets.
    • The tick kernel is written in a restricted Lean subset with proofs and emitted as standalone C99 with fixed-capacity arrays and no heap. The ring loop stays hand-written C.
    • Pose goes by datagram. Join, leave and ownership go on a small reliable channel.
    • The timer uses absolute deadlines on the monotonic clock. An overrun coalesces or drops, and never queues a backlog.
    • Each client owns its own avatar entity, so pose has no write conflicts. Store writes happen behind the tick.

    The first gate: a binary ticks at 64 Hz on Linux, sends a fixed batch of 12 entities to one registered address, and prints tick-to-send percentiles.

    The problem

    The repository’s own record was partly stale. The store path through FoundationDB, its header and the subtree are on the main branch. Parity and profile figures in the divergence notes were measured on SQLite, not on FoundationDB, and the README said the submission has no FoundationDB code.

    Rungs

    • Skateboard: timer, UDP socket, fixed batch of 12 entities, tick-to-send percentiles printed.
    • Multishot receive into the existing buffer ring, and a session table keyed by address.
    • The codec from the contract, with two proofs: a decode reads no more than 100 bytes, and a batch with headers stays within 1,280 bytes.
    • Area-of-interest grid, so fan-out is users times entities in view, not users squared.
    • Load generator and sweep, with a control that fails: a planted slow handler that pushes p99 over budget.
    • Write-behind to the node’s store, then two nodes.

    Acceptance

    • The emitted C builds with strict C99 warnings as errors, and the tick object has no allocation or runtime symbols.
    • Fixtures through the Lean semantics and through the emitted C give identical bytes, and a planted bug in the C makes that check fail.
    • The tick kernel has zero unproved goals. No MISRA conformance is claimed.
    • The default feed path keeps passing its diff and smoke scripts.
    • On the CPU runner, only checks that need no cluster run. A live FoundationDB check is an integration test.

    Open

    Extend the in-house emitter, which emits only the codec header today, or vendor the Trust-Lean compiler by subtree. One source either way, never a copy or a submodule.

    • Gate evidence: the feed server, CI run 42417791013, jobs tick-budget and client sweeps (success). entity_serve.c fails a run whose p99 is over 4 ms, and the planted-defect sweeps are caught. The Lean tick kernel and its emitted-C byte check are not in the repo, so the Lean-to-C acceptance is unmet and stated as such.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2442, the latency metric that judges this server.
    • RFD66606-2044, Lean at build time and a flat C ABI at run time.
    • RFD66606-2304, the one Lean library that generates a C planner through the same compiler.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2443-entityserver-serves-64-hz-entity-state-beside-feedserver.exs

    RFD66606-2442: latency is the metric for 64 Hz entity state

    State: committed Feature: a 64 Hz 3D state server is judged by tick-to-send time at a held user count. Scope: the metric, budget, sweep and pass rule for the entity server on one droplet.

    How many users can one shared vCPU serve at 64 Hz before a tick runs late, and what would show it?

    A feed server that holds 295,000 readers at a p99 of 117 ms spends about seven and a half ticks on its tail. It serves reads, so neither its user count nor its latency says anything about a tick.

    The user count is whatever 64 Hz allows. Latency is the metric (operator, 2026-11-07).

    • The tick is fixed at 64 Hz, 15,625,000 ns.
    • The primary figure is server-side tick-to-send time, from packet received to batched datagram handed to the kernel, at p50, p95 and p99. The proposed budget is p99 under 4 ms, a quarter of a tick.
    • Tick overruns, missed deadlines and steal time from the host’s CPU counters are recorded beside it, so a hypervisor stall is attributed and not blamed on the code.
    • The rule is pass or fail, not rank. Raise users in a sweep to the knee where p99 crosses the budget. A run passes with 0% errors over a 5 minute hold.
    • Only bytes derived from the code are stated, and no network figure is measured.
    • A figure stays labelled derived until a measured one replaces it.

    The first gate: a load generator holds a fixed user count for 5 minutes and prints server-side tick-to-send p50, p95 and p99, and a planted slow handler pushes p99 over budget and fails the run.

    The problem

    The only public reference is a read-heavy feed benchmark that reports users held and request rate. Neither says whether a 15.625 ms tick completes in time.

    Derived figures

    All of these are arithmetic on the reference cost of 26 microseconds per operation, not measurements.

    • Operations per second are 128 times the user count: 64 inbound and 64 batched outbound per user.
    • One core at 100% does 38,461 operations per second. At 128 users that is 16,384, about 42.6% busy. At 150 users it is 49.9%, the floor with tail headroom. At 300 users it is 99.8%.
    • The 26 microseconds include HTTP parsing and SQLite reads, which the tick path drops.

    Bytes

    • An entity packet is 100 bytes, so inbound is 6,400 bytes per second per user.
    • Twelve entities in view make 1,200 bytes of data and 1,248 bytes with IP and UDP headers, under the 1,280 byte IPv6 minimum. Sixteen make 1,600 bytes and fragment, so more datagrams split them.
    • Outbound is users times entities times 6,400. At 128 users and 12 entities that is 9,830,400 bytes per second, about 25.5 TB in 30 days. The droplet’s transfer allowance is not verified, so egress may bind before the CPU, and the entities in view are the main lever.

    Steal time

    A shared vCPU can lose a few milliseconds to the hypervisor, a large share of a tick. Whether the droplet is one shared vCPU is assumed and not verified.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2443, the server that this metric judges.
    • The droplet here is the benchmark host. Where the ghost servers run is open: Fly is a non-goal (RFD66606-2490, operator, 2026-11-12).
    • Gate evidence: the feed server, CI run 42417791013, job tick-budget (success). It proves a p99 under 4 ms budget on a 64-tick loopback check. The 5-minute hold at fixed user counts and the sweep to the knee are not run yet, so the gate is unproven.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2442-latency-is-the-metric-for-64-hz-entity-state.exs

    RFD66606-2436: presence is an independent native slice

    State: discussion Feature: two people in one campus zone see each other’s avatars from a program that runs alone. Scope: the see-each-other beta feature as its own native program, its gate and its control.

    Can two people see each other from a program that needs nothing else in the beta?

    The beta lists seeing each other first, and nothing built yet carries it alone. A slice that needs voice, the pen and the adventure party to run depends on all three.

    • Presence ships as one native program with no editor or browser. It owns the zone’s list of people and their avatar poses (operator, 2026-11-01).
    • The slice runs with no voice, pen, adventure party or shop present. Its inputs are recorded pose streams in place of those parts (operator, 2026-11-01).
    • Native means a riscv64 guest ELF for the sandbox, run binary-translated (operator, 2026-11-01). Its gates run on the CPU guest as the parity oracle (RFD66606-2374, RFD66606-2390).
    • The host is the win64 build of RFD66606-2360, built natively for the Steam Frame and the Steam Deck, and the slice’s gates run there too (operator, 2026-11-12).
    • An avatar is ANNY on the MS-Human-700 muscle skeleton, sent as 21 entity Packets of 100 bytes. The zone only routes and four parties judge each sender (operator, 2026-11-13).
    • The work climbs one ordered ladder from what already runs, one change a rung.

    Run the sight gate against a recorded pose stream. A zone that drops one side’s poses must fail it.

    What the beta asks

    The beta’s first feature is two people in the campus zone, one in the standalone Steam Frame and one on the desktop. Each sees the other’s avatar. The slice holds that and nothing more: who is in the zone, where each avatar stands, and the pose each person sends.

    The campus

    A campus is a world, and a world runs as instances. Any player starts an instance for friends, public or invite-only. One zone server is the authority for one instance. Each instance keeps its own shop books. One campus ships first, and building a campus stays with the V-Sekai content tools (operator, 2026-10-30).

    The slice’s edge

    In: the zone’s list of people, a pose from each, and a view of the others for each person. Out: voice, outfits, seats and books, which are the sibling slices. The edge is a message shape between the zone and a client. It is the only contract the slice shares, and its first step writes it down.

    Gates and controls

    Each gate has a control that plants the defect and must fail.

    • Sight: two clients replay a pose stream, and each client’s view lists the other’s avatar at the replayed pose. Control: a zone that drops one client’s poses.
    • Alone: the program starts and passes its sight gate with every sibling slice absent. Control: a sibling’s message planted in the input, which the program must refuse by name.

    Frontier learning picks the runs

    The slice’s gates run as levels in RFD66606-2309’s sense, scheduled the way RFD66606-2323 schedules the store’s attacks. A level is an input family with fixed attributes: the number of people in the zone, the pose rate, the client side (stream or desktop), and the loss pattern in the recorded pose stream. A problem is one 5 minute replay of a pose stream with a drawn seed and offset.

    Level Planted defect Found when
    pose drop the zone drops one client’s poses a client’s view misses the other avatar
    pose order the zone swaps two poses an avatar seen at an older pose than the replay
    self echo the zone lists a person to themselves a view that lists its own avatar
    late join the zone skips the list for a late client a late client sees nobody
    sibling input a sibling’s message planted the program accepts it

    Each level runs on the slice as it is and on the slice with that level’s defect planted. On the planted target, success is the defect found. Regret 1[s ≥ 1] − s/n over the last eight runs is high when a level finds its defect only some of the time. Mutation moves one attribute and is kept only when the planted find rate rises. A clean run counts only after its level found the planted defect in each of its last eight runs. A finding on the real slice is never averaged into a rate: it stops the lane and becomes a level that runs every time. The runs are guest ELF runs on the CPU guest, which is the parity oracle, so no gate here needs a GPU.

    Where the code lands

    Each slice is a repository of its own in our organization, named for what it does with no game name, and pinned through the repo manifest. It arrives as an ordinary pull request. V-Sekai repositories stay read-only.

    Since 2026-11-13 each part of this slice is a repository of its own too, started anew: the Packet codec, the zone router model, the observer, the curve, the replica, the avatar follower, the relay in C, and the gates that join them on a real body. RFD66606-2493 says where the relay’s parts are.

    What has run

    One real body has crossed the wire inside one process. A clip moves the muscle skeleton, its 21 parts go as Packets through the router model, the observers and the curve, and a second ANNY is posed from them 12 ticks behind. All 21 parts were drawn and no honest frame was refused. A part was 0.21 mm from the sender’s on average and 9.1 mm at worst, and its rotation up to 185 milliradians off, because a rotation has no rate on the wire. Three planted defects each made the largest error at least forty times worse.

    A position is whole micrometres on the wire and is never a float, so a body 8 billion kilometres from zero comes back within a micrometre, under a hair (operator, 2026-11-13).

    Not yet run: four bodies with the judgement of four parties, the clients as separate programs through the relay, feet that the floor carries, and a stick in place of a clip.

    What is not known

    • How a rotation should be drawn between two sends. The shortest arc does not follow a fast hand.
    • Whether a zone holds the pose rate for two people. Nothing has run, and no number is claimed.

    The problem

    RFD66606-2360 lists four features and names no way to build one without the others.

    The tuples

    rfd-2436--provides--see-each-other
rfd-2436--spends--binary-translated-only-timings
rfd-2436--spends--elf-guest-native-translation
rfd-2436--is-a--native-slice

    RFD66606-2435: a garment is repaired as a distance-field surface

    State: discussion Feature: a garment that crosses itself starts the cloth-fit solve as one clean surface. Scope: the proxy garment that the cloth-fit solve fits, and how its result returns.

    Can a garment that crosses itself start the cloth-fit solve clean?

    The pants cross themselves 1316 times across 53 shells. The solver takes one connected manifold mesh with no crossings, and a union of those shells did not give one. A surface of the garment’s distance field might.

    • The garment is repaired as a proxy. The original keeps its UVs, skin weights and materials.
    • The proxy is a level surface of the unsigned distance to the garment. Open edges close and layers closer than the distance merge (operator, 2026-11-01).
    • The proxy takes skin weights from the garment through the robust weight transfer guest. The fitted displacement returns to the original through the cage stage.
    • The repair uses no CoACD hulls and no CSG union of the shells (operator, 2026-11-01).

    Count the crossing pairs and the shells of the proxy. The solve takes it when they read 0 and 1, and a planted second shell must read 2.

    What the solver takes

    The cloth-fit solver’s input spec asks for an avatar of one or more closed surfaces, because the avatar becomes a signed distance field. It asks for a garment that is a connected manifold triangle mesh. The solver also refuses a start where the garment crosses itself.

    The solver’s own example solves. Its garment is one shell with no non-manifold edge, 144 open edges (a hem and a waist) and 0 crossing pairs. Its avatar is 32 shells that cross each other 1394 times between shells. So the body may overlap itself, and the garment may not.

    What an outfit piece looks like

    Measured with a throwaway script that welds at one hundred-thousandth of the bounding box and tests each edge against each triangle that shares no vertex. A planted crossing reads 1 and a planted separate pair reads 0.

    • The pants have 53 shells, no non-manifold edge, 399 open edges and 1316 crossing pairs. Of those, 1300 are between shells and 16 are inside one shell.
    • The skirt has 43 shells and 12 open loops.
    • The kimono has 346 shells, 128 open loops and 77 non-manifold edges.
    • The pants have 982 vertices that sit twice at one position, and no triangle collapses.

    What did not work

    A union of the shells did not give a clean surface. Each shell became a solid: an inner copy offset along the vertex normals, joined to the shell by a strip on every open edge. A stock CSG union then ran on all 53 solids.

    • At 4 mm, about five credit cards stacked, 24 of the 53 solids came out inside out, because the small shells are thinner than the offset.
    • At 1 mm, about one credit card, all solids were valid. The union still had 295 non-manifold edges and 30969 crossing pairs, against 1316 before.

    Convex hulls from CoACD are closed and cover the garment, but the operator ruled them out for the repair. The pants gave 9 hulls in 6 seconds.

    The distance field

    MuJoCo’s mesh compiler builds an octree of signed distances. It finds the closest triangle through a bounding-volume hierarchy. It takes the sign from the angle-weighted pseudonormal of the closest vertex, edge or face, so it casts no rays and counts no windings. MuJoCo’s GPU port only evaluates that field.

    The proxy uses the unsigned distance, so the sign never decides the surface. A level surface of it wraps every open edge and cannot cross itself. The distance is an argument that the operator picks. The solver’s contact distance is 2 mm, about three credit cards stacked.

    Rigging and carrying back

    The robust weight transfer guest takes the garment as source and the proxy as target. Its arrays are bone-major. It builds its Laplacian with intrinsic mollification (operator, 2026-11-01). With two vertices at one position, a plain cotangent Laplacian gave non-finite weights for 480 of 484 outputs on a test grid, and the mollified one stayed finite.

    The cage stage binds the original to a cage and moves it with the fitted proxy. That gives a smooth field. Copying the nearest vertex’s displacement does not.

    What is not known

    • Whether a level surface at the contact distance keeps the garment’s folds.
    • Whether it is one shell. The first step counts shells on the pants.
    • Whether the solver takes a garment of several shells. That needs the solver build on the Windows desk.
    • Whether the garments wind consistently. The unsigned field does not need it.
    • Where the nearest-triangle query runs as a guest, and its speed on a 54000-vertex piece.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2424, where a sketch is placed on the avatar before any fit.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2435-a-garment-is-repaired-as-a-distance-field-surface.exs

    RFD66606-2430: the gacha critical path is ten rungs from a prompt to a public roll

    State: discussion Scope: the ten rungs of the gacha path and its runtime motion source.

    Ten rungs take the gacha from a language prompt to a public, hosted roll button.

    Each rung produces an output the next rung consumes, so a rung with no output leaves the next one nothing to take.

    Ten rungs, each producing an output the next rung consumes:

    0. Language prompt → image           (OmniGen2, Q4 GGUF + Flow LCM LoRA GGUF)
1. Image → mesh                      (Pixal3D, Q4 GGUF)
2. Mesh → judged                     (EditScore over Qwen3-VL-8B Q4 GGUF)
3. Judged → repaired                 (VoxHammer, procedural, N-attempt bound)
4. Repaired → skinned                (skin-tokens.cpp against ANNY, GGUF)
5. Skinned → tagged (SAM2 or rf-detr-Seg + OmniGen2 per RFD66606-2183, all GGUF)
6. Tagged → VRM                      (portable character)
7. Prompt list → pool                (~50 VRMs, judged, seed-reproducible)
8. Pool → roll button                (native Godot binary head per RFD66606-2210)
9. Public                            (hosted with sponsor link)

    Follow the ten rungs in order, from the language prompt to the public hosted roll page, and check that each consumes the output of the one before.

    Runtime motion

    Runtime motion: motion-bricks.cpp (already ggml/GGUF) generates keyframe-driven animation from the shipped VRM. Apache-2.0 code, NVIDIA Open Model License on weights (same license class already accepted for Kimodo-SOMA-* per RFD66606-1028). The model has 183M params. Runs alongside rungs 7-9 as the animation source for the pool preview and hosted roll page. Loaded through the shared modules/ggml/ module per RFD66606-2230.

    RFD66606-2428: every model follows a six-step migration recipe

    State: discussion Scope: the six steps that move one model onto the shared ggml runtime.

    Every model moves to the shared ggml runtime by the same six steps, one row per consumer.

    Which quantization does a vision model get? Q4_K_M only if it produces a measurable EditScore win over Q4_0 on held-out inputs.

    • Every model follows the recipe RFD66606-2229 named as the interchangeable-parts consolidation shape, one row per consumer.
    • The six steps are Q4 quantize, GGUF conversion, ZSTD-SQLite bundle, the Ggml.load_model() GDExtension call, GDScript adapter, and Docker image.

    Run the six steps in order for each new model, from the Q4 quantize to its Docker image. Mark the model “port needed” in RFD66606-1102 when upstream has no GGUF conversion.

    Migration recipe (per model)

    Same recipe RFD66606-2229 named as the interchangeable-parts consolidation shape, one row per consumer:

    1. Q4 quantize, QAT if we train the model, PTQ per the CLAUDE.md Post-training-quantization blocklist exemption (a vendor’s own runtime is exempt from the QAT-only rule) otherwise. Target Q4_0 for text models, Q4_K_M for vision if the K-quant produces a measurable EditScore win over Q4_0 on held-out inputs.
    2. GGUF conversion, via llama.cpp’s convert_hf_to_gguf.py for HF-hosted models, per-model script for non-HF checkpoints. Ports for Wan-VACE, Pixal3D, MoGe-3, rf-detr-Seg, LaMa, Qwen3-TTS, Parakeet, Voxtral, wav2vec2, allosaurus, WavLM all follow this step.
    3. ZSTD-SQLite bundle, RFD66606-2214 shape, sqlite3_open() on local disk. One .zstd.sqlite per model bundle, install-time download via the release channel.
    4. Ggml.load_model() GDExtension call, RFD66606-2230 surface, the native modules/ggml/ module hands bytes to ggml.
    5. GDScript adapter, per-model .gd file at res://adapters/<name>.gd, extends GgmlAdapter, defines format_prompt / decode_output / apply_lora per model quirks.
    6. Docker image, per RFD66606-1036 /health + /predict shape still applies, the container binary is now the native Godot binary + shared modules/ggml/ + the model’s ZSTD-SQLite bundle + adapter .gd. One model per image (packaging stays RFD66606-1036), one runtime across images.

    RFD66606-2427: frontier learning picks the garment handover timing runs

    State: discussion Scope: how the garment handover timing runs are chosen as levels, with a planted defect each.

    Each timing level runs clean and with its defect planted, so a pass means something.

    A level that finds its planted defect only some of the time has a result that is luck.

    • The timing runs are levels in RFD66606-2309’s sense, scheduled the way RFD66606-2323 schedules the store’s attacks.
    • Each level runs on the rung as it is and on the rung with that level’s defect planted.
    • A clean run on the real rung counts only after its level found the planted defect in each of its last eight runs.
    • A finding on the real rung is never averaged into a rate: it stops the lane and becomes a level that runs every time.
    • The percentiles the pass limits come from are read only from calibrated levels, so a limit is never set from a load that could not see a slow leg.

    Check a new timing level against the rule. Run it on the rung as it is, then on the rung with that level’s defect planted.

    Levels and problems

    A level is a load template with fixed attributes: players, the recorded replay, the zone’s distance from the store, the commit group size, and the injected round trip and loss. A problem is one 5 minute run with a drawn seed and replay offset.

    The planted defects

    Level Planted defect Found when
    store commit leg a delay added to each commit that leg’s 95th percentile moves
    confirm order confirm sent before the commit a garment seen before its commit
    tick isolation the tick waits on the store a tick over its budget
    paused players a short idle timeout a reconnect during a pause
    replay limit the replay host throttled the replay named as the limit

    Success, regret and mutation

    On the planted target, success is the defect found. Regret 1[s ≥ 1] − s/n over the last eight runs is high when the level finds its defect only some of the time, so its result is luck. Mutation moves one attribute, kept only when the planted find rate rises.

    The tuples

    rfd-2427--provides--handover-timing-planted-levels
rfd-2427--spends--per-leg-handover-timing
rfd-2427--is-a--experiment-record

    Related

    • RFD66606-2309, the sense of a level. RFD66606-2323, how the store’s attacks are scheduled.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2426: the garment handover is timed per leg

    State: discussion Scope: the timed garment handover, its legs, its load and its checks.

    The garment handover is timed leg by leg, so a slow leg shows up where it happens.

    The round trip from a player’s desk to the store’s region measured 22 to 28 ms. Which leg of the handover spends it?

    The store and the backend stay together in one region, and the zones run on a server near the players (operator, 2026-10-23). The handover is the step that crosses the round trip, and the rung times it. The measure is per server and per leg, never a count of servers to minimise (operator, 2026-10-23).

    The time runs from the worker zone finishing the garment to its ghost drawn in the players’ zone, split by leg: the store commit, the ownership handover, and the fetch by hash. The load is a replay of recorded pen strokes with the players’ recorded head and hand tracks, pauses included, never scripted motion. It holds for 5 minutes and is judged on the 95th and 99th percentiles, never on a mean.

    Run the timed handover: replay the recorded pen strokes for 5 minutes and read the 95th and 99th percentiles of each leg.

    Why several servers

    Running several servers is expected: a system that tolerates faulty or lying members needs more machines to match one machine’s reliability, so the measure is per server and per leg.

    Rules of the run

    • A zone confirms a handover only after the store commits it. Writes may group into one commit, and every waiter waits for that commit.
    • The zone’s tick never waits on the store.
    • A player who pauses keeps their session. The replay’s pauses must not cause a reconnect.
    • The report names what stopped the run: tick time, memory, the store commit, or sessions.
    • The first run on a new host repeats a reference build, so a change of machine is not read as a change of code.

    Checks and controls

    Checks, each with a control that must fail:

    • The legs add up to the measured total. A control that adds a delay to the store commit must show up in that leg and nowhere else.
    • No player sees a garment confirmed before its commit. A control that confirms first must be caught.
    • The replay is not the bottleneck: the replay host’s own load is reported beside the zone’s, and a control that throttles the replay must be named as the limit.

    Pass limits

    The pass limits are not set yet: the first sustained run measures them, and the operator sets them from it.

    The tuples

    rfd-2426--provides--per-leg-handover-timing
rfd-2426--spends--worker-zone-dispatch
rfd-2426--spends--fdb-sqlite
rfd-2426--is-a--experiment-record

    Related

    • RFD66606-2287, where this rule lived before the split.

    RFD66606-2419: Git Bash on Windows runs slash-switch commands under a path-conversion guard

    State: discussion Scope: how a desk runs slash-switch commands from Git Bash on Windows.

    What happens when Git Bash rewrites your switches into paths? And when an empty title arrives as \"\" and start tries to run \?

    From Git Bash on Windows, a command with /-switches runs under MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*', so the switches are not rewritten into paths.

    The start command and Godot priority

    start "" ... goes in a .cmd file: passed inline, the empty title arrives as \"\" and start tries to run \. Godot raises its own process to above-normal priority, so a desk run lowers it by PID once started.

    RFD66606-2408: dev.1: one person visits the station

    State: discussion Scope: the dev.1 prerelease, where one person walks the ported station.

    dev.1 lets one person walk from the plaza toward the station, snap turn and teleport.

    The persona did not reach the platform or climb the stairs, and past the four modules the terrain is open.

    • The pen’s v20261001-dev.1 tag marks dev.1, and the prerelease carries the double engine v20260930-double.1, the addon v20260930-addon.1 and the five guest ELFs, each against SHA256SUMS.
    • The four ported modules (environment, station, plaza, sakura), each a faithful port of the pinned original, send their 1089 primitive colliders and the terrain height field to the MuJoCo guest as the original’s physics.js calls make them.

    Run gate_locomotion in the pen’s double.yml and check that each control fails.

    The station port is abandoned

    RFD66606-2384, the module-by-module port, is abandoned (operator, 2026-11-11). The plaza’s assets and tech stay in use, and baking goes through slughorn.

    The walker and world grab

    A walker ported from the original’s player.js (radius 0.3 m, height 1.7 m, step 0.45 m) runs on the guest’s ray and contact queries, read through rx’s stick movement and rotation components, with a 30 degree snap turn and teleport; there is no jump. World grab is off by default and sits in a three-wedge radial (hold B or Y, tilt, release: world grab, recentre, exit).

    Gates

    Gates: gate_colliders in entities-sakuragaoka-station (4-entities/sakuragaoka-station) (every collider matches the original’s, with drop_one and shift as controls), run by hand because that repository has no CI. And gate_locomotion in the pen’s double.yml (walk, step-up and the refused 1.25 m ledge, the handrail stopping the walker, snap turn, teleport landing and refused, and bit-identical poses across two runs), with the controls step_high, no_resolve, solid_land and ulp, each of which must fail.

    Playable, and the gap

    Playable, as the persona run on 2026-10-02 showed: walk from the plaza toward the station, snap turn, teleport, reach the forecourt, and toggle world grab from the radial. The persona did not reach the platform or climb the stairs. The locomotion gate climbs the six treads headless. Past the four modules the terrain is open where the town’s houses and shops stand in the original. The logbook names that gap and counts five others.

    RFD66606-2400: the worker zone dispatches and a sidecar computes

    State: discussion Scope: the worker zone, its GPU sidecar, and the garment’s one owner.

    The tiny worker zone owns and dispatches the garment while a sidecar with a GPU computes it.

    What if one byte of one chunk is flipped on the way back? The worker verifies every chunk against its id, so the flip is caught there.

    • The worker zone is tiny and has no GPU, so it owns and dispatches and does not compute. zone.elf in worker mode (zone 1) keeps the job queue, the garment’s ownership and the asset index.
    • The GPU stage runs on a sidecar, a client that has a GPU and the pen’s sandbox (this Mac in this rung, the Frame when it is idle), which registers with the worker over a CH_JOB stream when it connects.
    • When no sidecar is attached the worker runs the CPU target of the same Lean-emitted kernels (kernels/cassie/cpp, the slangc cpp emits under slang-rt, one source two targets) itself, slower and the same answer within RFD66606-2269’s intervals.

    Run the two-client gate and check that it counts exactly one owner of the garment every tick.

    The sidecar path

    On strokes_ready the worker sends the stroke set to one sidecar. The sidecar’s stages/sidecar_stage.gd runs curvenet.elf on compute-rd, then asset_store through asset.elf, and streams the .caibx and the chunks back on CH_ASSET. The worker verifies every chunk against its id (guest/asset: parse_caibx, the buzhash chunker, sha512_256, decompress_and_verify_chunk, assemble_from_caibx, lifted from fabric_mmog_asset.cpp onto std types. HTTP, keychain and ACL dropped), writes them under the server’s store, records the index hash in its journal, then zone_garment_spawn(hash) and zone_handoff(eid, 0). The ghost carries the index hash. Each client fetches by it and assembles.

    Check and controls

    Check: the two-client gate counts the garment’s owners every tick and finds exactly one. A garment the sidecar made lies inside the CPU oracle’s intervals (RFD66606-2269). The Lean chunk property stores random data up to 1 MiB, verifies every chunk and assembles the input.

    Controls: one byte of one chunk flipped with the expectation kept must be caught at the worker. A sidecar kernel built with -ffp-contract=on falls outside the interval and is named. The worker with no sidecar makes the garment itself and the gate records both times.

    The tuples

    rfd-2400--provides--worker-zone-dispatch
rfd-2400--provides--gpu-sidecar-compute
rfd-2400--is-a--guest-runtime
rfd-2400--spends--zone-core-open-tick

    RFD66606-2399: the zone journal lives in Bao over FoundationDB

    State: discussion Scope: where the zone journal lives, how it is written and read back.

    The zone journal leaves the guest for Bao over FoundationDB, so a restarted zone resumes.

    What if a zone restarts and its journal stayed in the guest? One owner per entity would hold only across a hand-off.

    The journal does not stay in the guest. OpenBao -> fdb -> s3 is the placement. stages/zone_stage.gd drains zone_journal_export under the write capability every tick that changed a row and hands the rows to the host’s Bao client, which runs the catalogued execs append_mutation and append_snapshot on the database zone-<id>. A zone that restarts loads its last snapshot back through query/zone-<id>/latest_snapshot into zone_load_snapshot.

    Run bao read for a row the zone wrote and check that its entity id and tick match.

    The placement

    The placement is service-openbao (7-service/openbao) on FoundationDB, datasource-store (6-datasource/store)’s fdb_vfs.c giving SQLite pages that live in the same cluster, and service-bao-sqlite-fdb (7-service/bao-sqlite-fdb) answering bao read <mount>/query/<name> and bao write <mount>/exec/<db>/<name> from a startup catalog and nothing else.

    The write and the schema

    The host’s Bao client is the desk’s agent identity over Tailscale, RFD66606-2142’s shape. The schema is fabric_zone_journal.cpp’s two tables, entity_mutations and entity_snapshots, in a schema "zone-*" block.

    The restart and the garment index

    So one owner per entity holds across a restart as well as across a hand-off. The garment’s index hash is a row in the same journal, so step 6’s fetch has a record a session later.

    Check and controls

    Check: a row the zone wrote is read back by bao read with the same entity id and tick, and a restarted zone resumes at its last snapshot’s tick. Controls: an export with no write capability is refused by capability.gd before any Bao call. An exec name not in the catalog is refused by Bao. The plugin’s own --self-test plants a fenced database opened without its fence.

    The tuples
