    RFD66606-2397: the transport step puts a certificate authority and capabilities in guests

    State: discussion Scope: the transport and lock-down step: zone and voice guests, the CA and capabilities.

    Two guest repositories carry the transport, a certificate authority and capabilities for zones.

    A certificate from another CA is accepted by the null verifier, and a transfer with no capability goes through a table that skips the bit test.

    • Two repositories shaped like interactor-lasso (3-interactor/lasso), placed after it: interactor-fabric-zone (3-interactor/fabric-zone) and interactor-voice (3-interactor/voice).
    • zone.elf has a player mode, as FabricZone::is_player does, so there is no client.elf.
    • picoquic lives only in zone.elf. ca.elf carries mbedTLS only.

    Run the Lean tests over the compiled C++ with an in-memory UDP pair, and make each control fail.

    The guests and the host

    • guest/transport: quic_picoquic_backend.cpp rewritten without picoquic_packet_loop and its thread: picoquic_incoming_packet and picoquic_prepare_next_packet_ex, driven by tick(now_us). Entropy and clock come from the host (net_seed, zone_tick’s wall time). The null verifier is replaced by ptls_mbedtls_get_certificate_verifier over the session root DER, thirdparty/webtransportd/frame.c verbatim.
    • guest/ca: a root key made in guest memory at ca_open, ca_issue(csr, name, now) issues one-hour certificates for names matching ^[a-z0-9-]+\\.zone\\.fabric\\.internal$. ca.elf has no transfer entry point at all.
    • guest/capability: macaroons as an HMAC-SHA256 chain with caveats vm, verb, object, expires, epoch. The host (stages/capability.gd) holds the root key and hands each VM a derived key, so ca.elf, which gets none, can verify no transfer. The per-VM bit in the godot-sandbox host-call table lands in entities-godot-sandbox (planned on 4-entities).
    • Host: stages/zone_stage.gd owns a PacketPeerUDP, drains it into net_rx, sends net_tx, calls zone_tick once a frame. Enrolment is a CSR on an ENROL stream the desktop hands to ca_stage.gd, then a reconnect with mTLS. The root DER passes out of band as a launch argument.
    • Vendored at riscv64 from the fabric tag by tools/vendor/from_godot_fabric.py: picoquic without its socket loops and other TLS backends, picotls’s four files, mbedTLS with FS_IO, THREADING, NET and SSL off, SQLite as OS_OTHER on spmemvfs, zstd’s three directories. Each directory with a CITATION.cff naming the tag.

    Check and controls

    Check, Lean tests over the compiled C++ with an in-memory UDP pair: a certificate from another CA is refused (control: the null verifier accepts it). An expired one is refused (control: the clock frozen at issue accepts it). An out-of-pattern name is not issued (control: a suffix check issues a.zone.fabric.internal.evil.com). A transfer with no capability is refused and goes ahead once minted (control: a table that skips the bit test lets it through. A macaroon with one caveat altered still verifies).

    RFD66606-2390: every ELF guest ships with its native translation

    State: discussion Scope: native binary translation of every ELF guest on every platform.

Xtools/build.exsdoes the same on a desk. The Windows leg is in progress. Until its.dll` loads, a Windows guest is untranslated and the gate below names it.

    The Windows segfault of 2026-09-23 (the setting on with no library present) is reproduced on the double build, its backtrace logged, and fixed in the placed addon source, not avoided. guests.yml and the release carry the libraries beside the ELFs with their sha256s.

    RFD66606-2387: GitHub Actions builds every double binary

    State: discussion Scope: the workflow that builds and releases the double engine binaries.

    GitHub Actions builds every double binary a rung runs or ships, so none of those is built by hand again.

    The release lands on the assembled engine, not on a side repository, so a binary names the exact tree it was built from.

    • GitHub Actions builds every double binary that a rung runs or ships. A build on a desk from a dev branch is not covered (operator, 2026-11-03).
    • Releases go on entities-zone (operator, 2026-11-03). The workflow lives on the engine branch dev/double-release of entities-godot (4-entities/godot-cineform), and entities-assembly merges it into r0-base, so every release carries it. The workflow changes only through that branch and the assembler (operator, 2026-11-03).
    • The engine fork keeps upstream’s nine workflows off and pays no runner minutes for them.

    Check a double binary that a rung runs or ships against the rule: it comes from a release on an entities-zone release tag.

    The double.yml matrix and the release

    .github/workflows/double.yml runs on each v0.0.0-<UTC time>-<commit> tag the assembler pushes to entities-zone, and on a dispatch with release_tag set. It builds the tagged tree in a matrix of windows-x86_64 (llvm-mingw 20260922, use_mingw=yes use_llvm=yes), linux-x86_64 and macos-arm64, each at precision=double for target=editor and target=template_release (debug_symbols=yes on the Windows template, for the fault below), with sccache on the runner’s cache. It publishes the six binaries and their sha256s as a release on the tag.

    Replaying a job on a desk

    The escript in service-godot-build (7-service/godot-build) takes --precision and --extra, so the Windows job replays on a Windows desk when a runner is not at hand. The pen’s CITATION.cff records the engine commit, the toolchain, the flag line and each sha256. The Frame pulls the Windows release with curl over ssh frame into ~/rfd2287/godot-dbl. This Mac pulls the macOS one.

    RFD66606-2381: a Windows host answers four system calls as Linux does

    State: discussion Scope: what a Linux guest needs from the emulator’s Windows host.

    A Linux guest runs on the Windows host once four system calls answer as they do on Linux.

    A Rust guest linked against static glibc failed on the Windows host, translated and interpreted alike, and so did the released addon. The first three fixes left the crash in place.

    The emulator’s Windows host answers four system calls as its Linux host does:

    • brk keeps the new break.
    • clock_gettime writes the 64-bit guest’s two 64-bit fields.
    • Error numbers map to the Linux numbers in one header.
    • sched_getaffinity reports one CPU, as the Linux and macOS hosts do.

    Check that the Windows host answers brk, clock_gettime, error numbers and sched_getaffinity as the Linux host does.

    What went wrong

    The emulator’s Windows host answered four system calls differently from its Linux host:

    • brk did not keep the new break. Static glibc puts the main thread’s thread-local block at the first break, so the heap handed out memory inside it and, later, an address in read-only data. This was the crash.
    • clock_gettime wrote the host’s own timespec, a 32-bit nanosecond field with padding, where the 64-bit guest reads two 64-bit fields.
    • Error numbers above ERANGE follow the Windows C runtime (ENOSYS is 40, where Linux has 38). glibc chooses its rseq and clone3 fallbacks on ENOSYS, so the host now maps errors to the Linux numbers in one header.
    • sched_getaffinity was missing. The Linux and macOS hosts report one CPU, and the Windows host now does the same.

    How the break was found

    A dump of the guest registers and the page’s permissions at the fault found the break. The fixes are in our libriscv fork, and the addon takes them with Linux’s ENOSYS for an unknown system call.

    The tuples

    rfd-2381--provides--windows-host-four-syscalls
rfd-2381--is-a--guest-runtime

    Related

    • RFD66606-2294, where this rule lived before the split.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2379: desktop zips ship as release assets

    State: discussion Scope: where the desktop zips ship, and what the page and the Space carry.

    The desktop zips ship as release assets, so the Space stays under its limit.

    A Space holds at most 1 GB, and the upload of three zips of 69, 84 and 91 MB was refused at the limit. Every earlier upload of the zips still counted in its history.

    • The macOS, Windows and Linux zips are assets of a GitHub release of the guest’s repository, tagged by RFD66606-2312, and the game Space links to them (operator, 2026-10-17).
    • The Space keeps the web game and the page.
    • The upload script deletes any zip from the Space.

    Upload the next zip as an asset of the guest’s GitHub release, not to the Space, and let the game Space link to it.

    The Space limit

    The upload of three zips of 69, 84 and 91 MB was refused at the limit. The Space history was squashed to one commit to free it, and the upload script now deletes any zip from the Space.

    The page and the preview

    The page shows the downloads on its first slide and the web game on its last slide, as a preview (operator, 2026-10-17). The preview starts its download only when that slide opens.

    A change to the game script

    A change to the game script alone leaves the guest and every translation hash as they were, so only the .pck of each zip is replaced. Each new zip started translated and printed RESULT PASS on its own system on 2026-10-17. The web game’s slowest frame in the first round read 139 to 145 ms before and after the change.

    A Space holds at most 1 GB, and every earlier upload of the zips still counted in its history.

    RFD66606-2378: desktop libraries build in WSL and cross-build from the Mac

    State: discussion Scope: where each desktop library is built, and how the WSL steps run.

    Build each desktop library on its named machine, and run WSL steps from a script file.

    Ubuntu’s clang 14 cannot parse the macOS SDK’s libc++ headers. Nested quoting from cmd into WSL returns empty output.

    • Linux x86_64 is built and tested in WSL Ubuntu 22.04 on the Windows desk, not in a container on the Mac (operator, 2026-10-16). The library needs glibc 2.35, the floor the Godot template already sets.
    • macOS arm64 is cross-built in the same WSL with osxcross and the macOS 15.4 SDK packed from the Mac (operator, 2026-10-16). Windows x86_64 is cross-built with MinGW on the Mac.
    • Steps that run in WSL go in a script file on the Windows side, which wsl.exe runs as root with sh from /mnt/c/.

    Put the next step that runs in WSL in a script file on the Windows side, and run it with wsl.exe as root with sh from /mnt/c/.

    The osxcross compiler

    Ubuntu’s clang 14 cannot parse that SDK’s libc++ headers, so osxcross is built with clang 18, and clang 18 is the clang on the PATH, because the osxcross wrapper calls plain clang.

    Build times

    Compiling the 32 translation units took 158 s for macOS on the Mac, 348 s for Windows on the Mac and 590 s for Linux in WSL on the desk.

    What was measured

    The same macOS translation built with Apple clang took 69.5 to 72.4 ms against 37.7 to 38.4 ms from osxcross with clang 18, so the osxcross build is the one that ships. The cause of that difference is not measured. Readings taken while another build ran on the same machine overstated the gap: Windows interpreted read 848 to 907 ms then.

    The problem

    Nested quoting from cmd into WSL returns empty output.

    RFD66606-2377: a translation links into the addon, one bake per platform

    State: discussion Scope: linking a translation into the addon, and baking its C once per platform.

    Each platform links its own baked translation into the addon, so the web game loads.

    Chrome refuses to compile a WebAssembly module larger than 8 MB on the main thread, and a game’s translation is larger. C baked on one platform does not match on another.

    • A translation can be compiled into the addon library of its platform instead of being loaded as a library at run time. On the web this is the only route that works. The desktop builds of the same game use the same route.
    • Each platform bakes its own C. The game runs once on that platform with the emitter on, and the emitted C is compiled for that platform.

    Bake the C of a platform by running the game once on that platform with the emitter on, then compile the emitted C for that platform.

    Where the objects live

    The addon keeps each platform’s translation objects in a folder of their own, src/bintr/<platform>.<arch>/.

    Why each platform bakes

    The program hash covers the machine layout as well as the program, so C baked on one platform does not match on another. Windows and Linux on x86_64 share a layout and a hash, and each still compiles its own copy. One bake of the SolidCraft guest is 32 C files, 336 MB of C for 16.2 MB of RISC-V code.

    A change to the host’s system calls

    A change to the host’s system calls leaves the guest’s translation as it was, so the compiled objects and the hash stay valid and only a relink is needed.

    The problem

    Chrome refuses to compile a WebAssembly module larger than 8 MB on the main thread, and a game’s translation is larger.

    RFD66606-2376: nothing runs in the headset unless the operator asks

    State: discussion Scope: when anything may run, restart or capture in the headset the operator wears.

    Nothing runs, restarts or captures in the headset unless the operator asks for that run.

    Nothing may capture the headset view while the operator is in a social session. X11 capture cannot see it, so a capture attempt there shows nothing.

    • Tests and gates run on the Windows desk or as renders on the Mac, not in the headset the operator wears.
    • A run, a runtime restart or a capture in the headset happens only when the operator asks for that run, and nothing captures the headset view while the operator is in a social session.
    • The headset view comes from the compositor mirror (/dev/video99) with screen sharing on. X11 capture cannot see it.

    Before a run, a runtime restart or a capture in the headset, check that the operator asked for that run, and run tests and gates on the Windows desk or as renders on the Mac instead.

    Asleep

    Asleep, the headset drops off the LAN entirely, answering neither mDNS nor ARP, so a name that does not resolve means it is asleep, not broken.

    Whose it is in the queue and the key

    The headset is the Mac desk’s in the queue, so another desk coordinates with the Mac before touching it. A key appended to its authorized_keys starts on a new line with carriage returns stripped, because the file may end without a newline and a .pub written on Windows ends its lines with CRLF.

    RFD66606-2375: the game ships to the headset as a Windows build

    State: discussion Scope: the Windows build that ships to the headset, and how it is exported and pulled.

    The game reaches the headset as a Windows build, exported on the desk and pulled as a casync repository.

    A translation generated at run time into writable executable memory does not load under the headset’s compatibility layer. A service-mode CI runner runs in session 0, which has no desktop, so it cannot export.

    • The game ships as a Windows build, run natively and through the headset’s compatibility layer, so a translation is a precompiled Windows library linked against the universal C runtime that loads under that layer, never code generated at run time into writable executable memory.
    • A Linux .so serves the Linux zone servers and never reaches the headset. The compatibility layer runs that same Windows build, so the Windows desk is where it is tested. RFD66606-2390 builds the libraries.

    Check a new translation against the rule: it is a precompiled Windows library linked against the universal C runtime, tested on the Windows desk.

    How the station ships to the headset

    The station ships to the headset as the Windows x86_64 build, run through the headset’s compatibility layer, on single-precision Godot 4.7.2 until the station’s double-precision guests are verified (operator, 2026-10-01). The export uses an export template and a real rendering device, so it runs in the Windows desk’s interactive session: Windows OpenSSH and a service-mode CI runner both run in session 0, which has no desktop. A session drives the Godot editor there through the computer-use driver, or starts the export from SSH as a scheduled task with /it. No GitHub Actions runner does it.

    The casync repository

    The build ships as a casync repository: desync, the Go implementation of casync, makes the index and chunk store, and they go into a V-Sekai-fire repository of their own. The headset pulls the title with desync’s arm64 build, or takes it over SSH as user deck with the desk’s key, as a dev title.

    RFD66606-2374: everything in a godot-sandbox runs binary-translated

    State: discussion Scope: binary translation in godot-sandbox and the timings that justify it.

    Everything in a godot-sandbox runs binary-translated, and only translated timings are reported.

    An interpreted timing reported as the result would hide the translated speed. A script that does not compile has no fallback to hide behind.

    • Everything that runs in godot-sandbox is binary-translated, guest ELFs and SafeGDScript alike, and an interpreted timing is never the one reported.
    • No .gd ships: every script, third-party ones included, ships compiled as .sgd with its translation, and a script that does not compile is a counted FAIL, not a fallback.

    Check a new script against the rule: ship it compiled as .sgd with its translation, and count a script that does not compile as a FAIL.

    What was measured

    Each target built one sphere of 672 triangles in the guest’s self-test, with the translated and the interpreted build started one after the other, twice, on a machine with no other load (2026-10-17). Times are in milliseconds.

    target translated interpreted
    macOS arm64, Mac mini, osxcross build 40.3 to 42.0 214.7 to 293.5
    Windows x86_64, the desk 61.2 to 62.0 454.2 to 491.7
    Linux x86_64, WSL on the same desk 114.4 to 131.9 583.8 to 595.3
    web, Chrome on the Mac, tab in front 79 to 110 442 to 472

    The same macOS translation built with Apple clang took 69.5 to 72.4 ms against 37.7 to 38.4 ms from osxcross with clang 18, so the osxcross build is the one that ships. The cause of that difference is not measured. Readings taken while another build ran on the same machine overstated the gap: Windows interpreted read 848 to 907 ms then.

    RFD66606-2372: heavy compute runs in a godot-sandbox guest

    State: discussion Scope: where heavy compute runs.

    Heavy compute runs in a godot-sandbox guest, never as a host pipeline or a GDScript loop.

    A native ggml engine module, a GDExtension ggml API and a standalone runtime are all off the route.

    • Heavy compute runs in a godot-sandbox guest: a riscv64 guest ELF on the CPU, which is also the parity oracle, or kernels on ggml-rd with compute-rd, authored in Lean and lowered through Slang to SPIR-V (RFD66606-2265).
    • It never runs as a host Python or C++ pipeline or as a GDScript loop.
    • ggml runs only in such a guest (RFD66606-2290).

    Check a new heavy compute job against the rule: put it in a riscv64 guest ELF or on ggml-rd with compute-rd.

    What stays allowed

    Fragment shaders that render are fine, and Python bindings serve upstream contributions and their tests, never a pipeline.

    What is off the route

    A native ggml engine module, a GDExtension ggml API or a standalone runtime is off the route, and a standalone CLI may stay as a CPU oracle for a gate.

    Diffusion

    Diffusion in ggml runs on ggml-rd with compute-rd as well, since EditScore’s decision model builds on it (RFD66606-2268).

    RFD66606-2371: a residual is fixed down a ladder, never smudged

    State: discussion Scope: how a residual in a visual diff is fixed.

    A residual in a diff is fixed down a measured ladder, never hidden by a blur or a mask.

    What if a residual vanished because an image was blurred, a threshold loosened or a region masked?

    • A residual is fixed, never smudged: nothing blurs an image before the diff, loosens a threshold or masks a region.
    • Fixes go down a ladder, each rung measured with the diff’s own metric before and after: exact fixes at the source, then missing structure, then registration, then fitted parameters.
    • What remains is reported beside its floor, and a later change may not raise it.

    Check a proposed fix against the rule: measure it with the diff’s own metric before and after, rung by rung.

    The rungs

    Registration is where a camera that does not match is fixed in the camera and never by warping an image. The last rung is parameters fitted to the oracle with contract-lbfgsb (2-contract/lbfgsb) on the GPU, coarse to fine, written back into the source assets and checked on views the fit did not use.

    What stays

    Antialiasing and distance fades that belong to the renderer stay.

rfd-2371--is-a--workspace-policy

    A sheet is composed by rendering, never by a GDScript loop over pixels, and no gate reads a sheet.

    • A visual comparison is delivered as a labelled contact sheet, the format for both vision-model review and human QA: one row per case, one column per source (original, before, after, diff), each cell labelled with its metric, failures first, and the numbers kept beside the sheet.
    • These rules hold by agreement. No gate reads a sheet.

A sheet is composed by rendering, with fragment shaders into a SubViewport, or in a godot-sandbox guest, never by a GDScript loop over pixels. Its script ships as .sgd, and its views come from sphere_hammersley_sequence.

    Each sheet carries a .cff and its <stem>.xmp sidecar (RFD66606-2240). A copy goes to lookdev-contact-sheets/ on the Desktop of the desk that made it, as <topic>-NN.png, the number rising so that no sheet is overwritten.

    RFD66606-2369: the standalone headset draws at most 700k triangles

    State: discussion Scope: the triangle budget for the standalone headset and how it is enforced.

    The standalone headset draws at most 700k triangles in view per frame, split between world and characters.

    Past 700k triangles in view the frame is over the operator’s budget, and the crowd of non-player characters is the first to drop to impostors.

    The operator’s budget for the standalone headset: at most 700k triangles in view per frame, of which world geometry gets 250k (400k at most) and characters 450k. A crowd of non-player characters holds 150k of the character share and drops to impostors first. One equal-error LOD threshold over the frame enforces it, and the LODs come from Godot’s own generate_lods on welded meshes, except the blossom cards, whose levels are the cluster LOD DAGs of RFD66606-2367.

    Check a scene against the budget: at most 700k triangles in view per frame, 250k for world geometry and 450k for characters.

    Avatars and characters cast their shadows from tapered capsules fitted per skeleton (issue 110), not from the shadow map. An untapered capsule keeps stock Godot’s height and radius behaviour.

    RFD66606-2367: the station port renders in Godot from baked meshes

    State: discussion Scope: how the Sakuragaoka Station port builds, shades and renders its geometry in Godot.

    The station port draws baked meshes in Godot, so it renders with the runtime vector shader off.

    CSG keeps UV and drops vertex colour, and it takes only manifold solids, so a geometry that fails the manifold check cannot be unioned as it is.

    The Sakuragaoka Station port (entities-sakuragaoka-station (4-entities/sakuragaoka-station)):

    • realizes every closed solid through CSG, and carries each face’s colour as a palette index in UV, since CSG keeps UV and drops vertex colour. CSG takes only manifold solids, so a geometry that fails the manifold check stays a plain surface, or goes through remesh.elf when it must be unioned;
    • shades with godot-vrm’s MToon unchanged, and a variant includes it rather than forking it;
    • renders from meshes baked from the vector materials’ data (signs, paving, bark), coarsened by LOD when over budget, so it works with the runtime vector shader off. Alpha-cut foliage cards bake too: each blossom card is its atlas cell’s outline, baked by slug.elf at 256 triangles a cell, and the cards go into cluster LOD DAGs built by remesh.elf‘s cluster_lod (meshoptimizer’s clusterlod.h), which clod_select cuts per frame, binary-translated, on both standalone headsets (operator, 2026-10-10);
    • judges alpha on the final composite of its layers: an opaque object ends with no transparency, and a transparent base-colour material writes alpha.

    Check a new station mesh against the rule: realize each closed solid through CSG, bake vector materials to meshes, and keep rasterized vector art out of the headset.

    Quality and procedural detail

    The Sakuragaoka Station port:

    • runs slughorn‘s per-pixel vector shader as a quality setting, on by default, adding detail to surfaces near the eye within the headset’s GPU budget;
    • synthesizes finer detail only where the source is procedural.

    What stays out of the headset

    No rasterized vector art or glyph outline goes into the headset. Meshes made from outlines are fine, and a glyph mesh goes through remesh.elf when its font’s winding is invalid.

    The blossom cards and the cut

    Over the 48 valid orbit views, the 53,211 cards are 13.6M triangles at full detail, and a 4 px cut for a 1760 px eye at 100 degrees draws a mean of 39k and at most 122k. With the cut, depth differs from the original on 0.16 % of the frame, and on 2.15 % without the cards. Translated, the cut takes a median 1.6 ms a view on the desk, and 4.3 ms interpreted.

    The outline

    The outline reads the mesh’s geometric normal, which the toon-ramp hook writes, not MToon’s bent indirect-light normal, and takes depth and normal from the majority MSAA sample.

    The whole stack deploys offline on one laptop, reachable on the LAN and perhaps the tailnet, with nothing needed from the WAN:

    RFD66606-2362: A prose rule ships after it runs against the corpus

    State: discussion Feature: measuring the AI-trope table before it gates Scope: tropes-removal-model, seeds/ai_trope.parquet, and the 119 RFD READMEs.

    A prose rule ships only after it has run against the corpus.

    Twelve detectors report zero on the corpus, and three of those zeros come from detectors that cannot fire, so a broken detector reads exactly like a clean corpus.

    A rule ships only after it runs against the corpus, the bar RFD66606-1124 set. Three of the table’s fifteen detectors cannot fire, so they wait on repair.

    Run --audit first, before you trust any zero; it exits non-zero while any detector is broken.

    What already exists

    This RFD proposes less than it first appears. The tropes-removal-model project holds most of the parts:

    part state
    seeds/trope.parquet 28 ASD-STE100 violation categories
    seeds/ai_trope.parquet 20 AI-writing tropes, seeded from tropes.fyi
    runtime/prose_nodes.py CommonMark prose extraction, so a gate reads no syntax
    gate.py the ASD-STE100 gate; it runs the STE table only
    a runner for the AI tropes absent

    scripts/seed_ai_tropes.py reached the same conclusion as this RFD before this RFD did. Its own docstring states that ASD-STE100 “gates the wrong things” in an essay. Two facts remain to settle, and this RFD settles them.

    gate.py does not import prose_nodes, and nothing reads ai_trope.parquet. The catalog and the parser exist and are not connected.

    runtime/prose_nodes.py imports markdown_it. pixi.toml does not declare it. The RFD gates pin markdown-it-py==3.0.0, so the two projects must agree on a version once both depend on it.

    The measurement

    scripts/measure_ai_tropes.py in tropes-removal-model reads seeds/ai_trope.parquet and runtime/prose_nodes.py. It owns no patterns and no parser, because a second copy of either would drift from the first.

    It reads all 119 RFD README.md files. The counts are exact: the population is fixed and the script reads every member, which is what CLAUDE.md rule 5 asks for.

    The table holds 20 tropes: 15 regex, 3 classifier, 2 manual. Three of the 15 find anything:

    trope documents share hits
    Compulsive Counting 6 5% 7
    Overused Adverb 2 2% 2
    Em-Dash Addiction 2 2% 2

    Three detectors cannot fire

    Twelve detectors report zero. Nine of those zeros are real. Three are not.

    --audit feeds each pattern its own recorded example_phrase, passes it through prose_nodes, and asserts the pattern still matches. A detector that cannot match its own example is BROKEN, and its zero on a corpus means nothing.

    detector fault
    Bolded Lead Clause matches **...**; prose_nodes removes the markers
    Where/What/Why Header matches #{1,6}; prose_nodes removes the hashes
    Negative Parallelism spells it'?s; its own example says “it is”

    The first two are one fault twice. Both patterns were written against raw markdown, and the extractor hands over the text a reader sees. Measured on one file: Bolded Lead Clause finds 5 in the source and 0 after extraction.

    Each repair is small. Move the two formatting rules to run before extraction, or rewrite them against the extracted text. Add it is to the third alternation.

    A zero from a broken detector reads exactly like a clean corpus. That is the failure CLAUDE.md rule 3 names, and it is why --audit runs first.

    Every hit is a false positive

    Run --inspect to see each hit in context. The inspection changes the result, so the count alone is not the measurement.

    trope what the hits are
    Compulsive Counting exact counts of items the document then enumerates
    Overused Adverb “silently”, describing a check that skipped in silence
    Em-Dash Addiction two parenthetical dashes across 119 documents

    seed_ai_tropes.py predicted this. Its docstring records that a regex is “a screen, not a verdict”, and that Compulsive Counting “fires on the phrase ‘three things’, which is sometimes just three things”. The corpus agrees: all seven hits count things the document goes on to list.

    No hit in the corpus is a true positive. Against the mechanical subset, the corpus is clean, and every firing rule needs narrowing before it gates anything.

    What no mechanical detector reaches

    tropes.fyi lists 49 tropes. The table seeds 20, and records that limit per row in its coverage column rather than in a README.

    Five of the 20 have no regex. Invented Concept Label, Premise Stacking and Enumeration As Prose need the classifier. Circular Fractal and Symmetric Paragraph Length have no automatic detector at all.

    The ASD-STE100 half splits the same way: about 18 mechanical rules as regular expressions, about 8 semantic rules through a SetFit classifier, and 2 more through a whole-document pass in runtime/cross_sentence.py. An essay gate needs the same second half, and this RFD does not build it.

    How to re-run

    cd .tropes_removal_model
python3 scripts/measure_ai_tropes.py --audit    # check each detector can fire
python3 scripts/measure_ai_tropes.py            # the AI-trope table
python3 scripts/measure_ai_tropes.py --inspect  # every hit, in context
python3 scripts/measure_ai_tropes.py --compare  # both tables, same extractor

    --audit exits non-zero while any detector is broken. Run it before you trust a zero from the other modes.

    The default path is ../.request_for_discussion, which holds when both projects sit at the workspace root. default.xml places them there.

    The problem

    The catalog and the parser exist and are not connected.

    Related

    RFD66606-1125 assigns the AI-trope table to essays. RFD66606-2361 marks each section with its gate. RFD66606-1124 gives the measure-first rule.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2362-a-prose-rule-ships-after-it-runs-against-the-corpus.exs

    RFD66606-2357: A narrow unit holds a wide number as a sum of parts

    State: discussion Feature: numeric precision for kernels on float32 and bf16 units Scope: df32 guest geometry, and f32 matrix products on bf16 units such as a TPU.

    A narrow unit gives wide precision when each number is split into parts it can hold.

    A float32 coordinate 3.8e8 m from the origin cannot hold a 1 mm step, and a bf16 unit holds 8 bits of mantissa.

    A TPU computes a float32 product as 3 or 6 bf16 passes. A df32 pair computes a wide coordinate as a high and a low float32. Both split a number into a sum of narrow parts.

    1. A kernel that needs more precision than its unit holds splits the operands into parts and sums the products of the parts, smallest first.
    2. A kernel states its part count: 1, 2 or 3 bf16 parts, or one df32 pair.
    3. Each part count carries a measured error against a float64 reference, and a control that fails when the count drops by one.

    Record the measured error of a kernel before it claims float32 or df32 accuracy.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    What the TPU library states

    The array library that drives Cloud TPU documents its matrix precision setting in its source, read from the main branch at the time of writing. The setting changes float32 computations only and leaves the input and output types alone.

    • DEFAULT: on TPU, float32 computations run in bfloat16.
    • HIGH: on TPU, float32 computations run in 3 bfloat16 passes.
    • HIGHEST: on TPU, float32 computations run in 6 bfloat16 passes.

    The dot algorithm presets name the same idea: BF16_BF16_F32_X3, BF16_BF16_F32_X6 and BF16_BF16_F32_X9 use 3, 6 and 9 operations to emulate higher precision, and a float8 preset decomposes each operand into an initial term and a residual term.

    The source does not state which products the 3 and 6 pass modes keep, and no TPU ran for this RFD. The host measurement below chooses the usual split: 2 parts keep the 3 products whose part indexes sum to at most 1, 3 parts keep the 6 whose indexes sum to at most 2, and 9 keeps all products of 3 parts.

    The split rule

    A part is the operand rounded to bf16. The residual is the operand minus the part, exact in float32. The next part is the residual rounded to bf16, and so on. Three bf16 parts hold 3 times 8 bits, which covers the 24 bit float32 mantissa.

    A product of two bf16 values is exact in float32. The sum of the kept products runs in float32, smallest products first, so the large products do not drown the small ones.

    df32 is the same split one level up. The high part is the float32 value and the low part is the float32 residual of a float64. two_sum, quick_two_sum and two_prod carry the rounding error of each operation into the low part, as RFD66606-2392 lists.

    Measured on the host

    A host emulation, not a TPU. Matrices 64 by K times K by 64, standard normal entries, 8 seeds. Error is the norm of the difference from a float64 product, over the norm of that product. Median over the seeds, with the maximum in brackets.

    product K = 256 K = 4096
    1 bf16 part 2.3e-3 (2.4e-3) 2.4e-3 (2.4e-3)
    3 products, 2 parts (X3) 4.4e-6 (4.6e-6) 4.4e-6 (4.6e-6)
    6 products, 3 parts (X6) 9.6e-8 (9.9e-8) 1.2e-7 (1.2e-7)
    9 products, 3 parts (X9) 9.6e-8 (9.9e-8) 1.2e-7 (1.2e-7)
    float32 host product 2.5e-7 (2.6e-7) 2.4e-7 (2.4e-7)

    Each step up the table lowers the error, from 2.3e-3 to 1.2e-7 over three steps. The 3 part products sit at the float32 rounding floor of 1.2e-7 (the float32 epsilon), and the ninth product adds nothing over the sixth here. The host float32 product is a blocked product with its own rounding, so a TPU accumulator can differ from every row.

    Control: the 1 bf16 part row is 520 times above the 2 part row, so a bound of 1e-5 fails a kernel that dropped to 1 part and passes the X3 row.

    df32 at the Moon distance

    A position 3.8e8 m from the origin, moved 1000 times by 1 mm. Float32 spacing there is 32 m, some 480 soda cans.

    • float32: 1.0 m after 1000 steps, about 15 soda cans. Placing 20000 random positions errs by 16 m at most.
    • df32: 9.3e-6 m after 1000 steps, 1/80 of a credit card. Placing the same positions errs by 4.8e-7 m at most.

    The float32 position did not move at all: each 1 mm step rounds away. The df32 position kept the steps. The placement error ratio is about 3.4e7 to 1.

    Method

    The bf16 round is round to nearest even on the upper 16 bits of a float32. Parts come from the residual rule above. Products and sums ran in float32 on the host with numpy. The df32 steps use two_sum and quick_two_sum on float32 scalars. The numbers above are the output of a short script that is not committed; the kernels that RFD66606-2392 lists are the place for a permanent gate.

    What is not known

    • The error of a real TPU product at each precision setting. The first step is one run on a Cloud TPU with the same shapes and seeds, compared with the host table.
    • Which products the 3 and 6 pass modes keep. The first step is the compiler’s own text for the dot, read from a lowered program.
    • Whether the part count a kernel needs follows its inputs’ range as well as its size. The first step is the same table over inputs with a wide exponent spread.
    • The cost of each part count in time. No timing ran.

    The problem

    RFD66606-2392 chose df32 for the first. This RFD adds the second and puts both under one rule with one set of measured bounds.

    Related

    RFD66606-2392 chooses df32 for guest geometry. RFD66606-1025 gives the bf16 memory arithmetic. The BLOCKLIST row on XLA and PJRT keeps the Cloud TPU route open.

    Source: rfd/2357-a-narrow-unit-holds-a-wide-number-as-a-sum-of-parts.exs

    RFD66606-2356: Workspace services stay DNS-only

    State: discussion Scope: the DNS records of every workspace service.

    Workspace services stay DNS-only, so no CDN reads their traffic.

    A proxied record puts Cloudflare between a client and the service for every request.

    CF-proxied records have Cloudflare terminating TLS at its edge, every byte plaintext at CF for the round trip. Workspace services stay DNS-only; edge cache, if needed, is Fly-side or origin-side.

    If a workspace service lands under a proxied subdomain, take the proxy flag off before it serves requests.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    No CDN proxy in front of workspace services

    Cloudflare’s proxied: true mode has CF terminating TLS at its edge using its Universal SSL cert and re-encrypting to origin. Every byte of the request headers and body is plaintext at CF for the round trip. CF is not the workspace’s tenant. That is a MITM regardless of intent, and it is not compatible with services that carry auth tokens or hostname-bound credentials.

    Records for services this workspace runs stay proxied: false. Edge caching, if it is ever needed, lives Fly-side (Fly’s own Anycast + edge) or origin-side (an in-process cache).

    One record in the chibifire.com zone as of 2026-09-01 is CF-proxied: hub-700a.chibifire.com, pointing at 173.180.240.105 / 2001:569:7e58:dd00:.... That is a personal home network endpoint, outside this workspace’s scope. If a workspace service ever lands under a subdomain that is currently proxied, the proxy flag comes off before the service starts serving requests.

    The problem

    Services here carry auth tokens and hostname-bound credentials.

    Related

    RFD66606-2146. Split from the old RFD66606-2147: RFD66606-2353 (replicas), 2354 (unseal), 2355 (cache).

    Source: rfd/2356-workspace-services-stay-dns-only.exs

    RFD66606-2355: Consumers cache Bao reads in memory

    State: discussion Scope: every consumer of Bao: DNS, R2 writes, FDB coordinator lookup.

    A consumer that holds a bearer for a few minutes keeps Bao out of its critical path.

    Every read against Bao is a Bao dependency, and DNS, R2 writes and the FDB coordinator lookup all read from it.

    Consumers cache what they can. A bearer held for a few minutes puts Bao in the critical path only at cache expiry.

    Check a consumer that reads Bao against the rule above: it caches the value in its own memory for less time than the value protects, and on a Bao error it retries rather than holding the stale value.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Consumer-side cache: what and for how long

    Every read against Bao is a Bao dependency. Two ends of the spectrum:

    • Never cache. Simple, correct, hot dependency on Bao.
    • Cache forever. Wrong for rotating secrets (RFD66606-2145 leaves at 90 days; a hot bearer at hour 720 leaks past its rotation).

    The middle: cache for a duration shorter than the shortest thing the cached value protects. For a DNS bearer that itself has a Cloudflare API-token lifetime, minutes-to-an-hour is safe. For an FDB cluster file that changes only on a scale event, an hour is safe. Cache should live in the CONSUMER’s memory, not on disk, and it should refresh on a Bao error by simply retrying rather than by holding the stale value.

    The problem

    RFD66606-2146 moved every routine credential read onto Bao, so every consumer now depends on Bao being up.

    Related

    RFD66606-2145, RFD66606-2146. Split from the old RFD66606-2147: RFD66606-2353 (replicas), 2354 (unseal), 2356 (no CDN proxy).

    Source: rfd/2355-consumers-cache-bao-reads-in-memory.exs

    RFD66606-2354: Bao unseals itself through a Seal Bao on Fly

    State: discussion Scope: the seal of every Bao, its key, and its recovery.

    Bao restarts and unseals with no person at the keyboard.

    Three Baos mean three seal states and three unseal calls per fleet restart.

    A transit seal on a Seal Bao on Fly, unwrapped from Fly KMS at boot (operator, 2026-10-30). Recovery becomes hands-off, not operator-with-1P. Superseded on 2026-11-01: Bao runs as one Fly machine and unseals from Fly KMS at boot, with an offline division of the seal key with n=1 as the last resort (operator, 2026-11-01).

    Pass the recovery test on clean hosts before prod moves; the sections below hold the steps.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Auto-unseal: KMS wrapper, Shamir stays as break-glass

    Shamir with a manual share is the right seal for one-of-one, wrong for three-of-three. Options:

    • Cloud KMS seal (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, Oracle). The key stays in the cloud KMS; Bao decrypts the master key at boot via the KMS API. Standard pattern. Cost is per-request against the KMS, measured in fractions of a cent per unseal.
    • Transit seal (a second, seed-only Bao). Chicken-and-egg unless the seed Bao is truly offline (Raspberry Pi, HSM, boot-from-USB). Adds a second thing to maintain.
    • HSM / PKCS#11. Right answer for a fleet in a datacenter with its own HSM. Overkill for this workspace’s scale.
    • HCP Vault / OpenBao managed. Not this workspace’s shape.

    Recommendation: Fly KMS, through a Seal Bao. Fly app secret keys are a first-party KMS, usable only from inside a machine of the owning app, and OpenBao has no Fly seal type, so a Seal Bao bridges the two (operator, 2026-10-30). The break-glass key for the day the KMS itself is the outage (the day RFD66606-2144 logs as its eleventh defect) is the Seal Bao’s static key, held offline as a Shamir share, whose count may be 1.

    An auto-unseal wrapper does not change the CRL-loop bug logged during the DR (Bao’s authenticated paths going flaky after a particular sequence of issuer imports). That is a separate item.

    Transit seal on Fly, unwrapped by Fly KMS

    The operator chose on 2026-10-13 to unseal the Fly instances from a small Bao, rescinded the Mac mini as its host on 2026-10-30, and chose a Seal Bao on Fly that unwraps its own key from Fly KMS (operator, 2026-10-30).

    • Encrypt and decrypt with a Fly secret key work only from inside a machine of the owning app, through the machine’s local API socket; the public API refuses. The Seal Bao’s start-up script decrypts a wrapped 32-byte key into memory and starts Bao with a static seal. Every other Bao uses a stock transit seal against it.
    • The Seal Bao runs as one machine or as an HA set of three voters. Two voters tolerate no failure, so two is not a valid setting (operator, 2026-10-30). One machine relies on a restore from backup that has been tested.
    • It listens only on its tailnet address, over TLS, and the tailnet policy lets only Bao nodes reach it. No peer reaches a localhost or public listener.
    • Each Bao has its own transit key and a policy limited to encrypt and decrypt on that key. A certificate login yields a short token, but a seal needs its token at boot, so each Bao also holds a periodic orphan token for its key: a Fly secret on the Fly instances, a file readable only by its own user elsewhere. Measured on a throwaway Bao, the seal renews that token while the Bao runs; the token expires if the Bao is down longer than its period, so the period is set to days and a longer outage needs a new token.
    • If the Seal Bao is down, a restarted Bao stays sealed until it is back. Running Baos keep serving.
    • The break-glass key is the Seal Bao’s static key, held offline as a Shamir share even when the count is 1, and never in the backup bucket. A new Seal Bao started with that key and a restored snapshot unlocks every other Bao. Each Bao’s Shamir recovery keys authorise operations such as generating a root token; they do not unseal.
    • The Seal Bao backs up to the same bucket as the others, under its own prefix, with unique object names and a retention lock; plain-text config files stay out of the snapshots and are protected separately.
    • The change is proved with a planted control: with the Seal Bao stopped, a restarted Bao stays sealed. The recovery test passes before prod moves: on clean hosts with Fly blocked, restore the Seal Bao from the offline key and the backup, then restore one other Bao through it and read back data.

    Recovery without Fly KMS

    This procedure needs no Fly account, no Fly machine and no network path to Fly. It is the one the recovery test runs (operator, 2026-10-30).

    1. Gather the materials: the offline Shamir share or shares of the Seal Bao’s static key, the Seal Bao’s configuration without its secrets, and the newest snapshot of the Seal Bao from the backup bucket.
    2. Rebuild the key: combine the shares into the 32-byte key (one share is the key itself). Check the length and the key id the configuration names before use.
    3. Start a new Seal Bao on any host with a static seal whose key is a file in memory backed storage, and with the same listener rules: tailnet address, TLS.
    4. Restore the snapshot into it. Whether the restore needs the force option under a fresh barrier is not yet measured; the recovery test settles it.
    5. Check that the transit keys, the policies and the cert roles are back, and that one other Bao unseals through the new address with its existing periodic token.
    6. Point the other Baos at the new address if it changed, one at a time.
    7. Resume hands-off unsealing by wrapping the key with a new KMS, or by leaving it manual until one exists. A Bao that stays up needs none of this; only a restart does.
    8. Write down what the restore took and which step was unclear, then amend this block.

    The key never leaves the offline store except during steps 2 and 3, and the memory copy is destroyed when the host stops.

    Alternative wrapper: a passkey

    Fly KMS is the hands-off wrapper. A passkey can wrap the same 32-byte static key when no Fly KMS is available, at the price of a person at every restart (operator, 2026-10-30). The route has not been run here; the recovery test measures it.

    • Passkey. A passkey whose authenticator offers a secret-derivation extension can derive a wrapping key from a challenge, with a touch. Support differs by authenticator and by client library, so confirm that the same credential returns the same secret on a second host before relying on it. A passkey that only signs cannot wrap anything.
    • Hardware seal in Bao. OpenBao can seal through a PKCS#11 module, but that needs a token that decrypts or unwraps with a mechanism the seal supports; whether a passkey does is not known. Until measured, the passkey wraps the static key and Bao keeps its static seal.
    • Keep two passkeys, stored apart, since one lost token otherwise ends recovery. A passkey stays out of the backup bucket and off any Fly host.

    How the key arrives, and rotating the seal

    A Bao on a static seal holds one 32-byte key. How that key reaches the process is a mode in the start-up script, not part of the seal. Every mode supplies the same key, so a node changes mode with no migration (operator, 2026-10-30).

    • tpm: a non-exportable TPM key unwraps a wrapped copy of the key at start, with no PIN and no touch. The wrapped file opens only on that machine.
    • kms: the start-up script asks the Seal Bao, or on Fly the machine’s own KMS, for the key.
    • passkey: a person touches the passkey at each start.
    • manual: the script asks a person for the key, for example from the offline Shamir shares, and then starts Bao. Bao does not start without the key, and a static seal has no manual unseal of its own. A node left in this mode starts nothing on its own.
    • A node lists the modes it has in order and uses the first that works, for example tpm, then kms, then passkey, then manual. Each node wraps the key once per mode it lists, so any one is enough (operator, 2026-10-30). The script logs which mode unwrapped the key, so a fallback shows. Splitting the key so that several modes are all required is not used: one broken mode would then block the start.
    • The plain key is held in memory-backed storage only for the start, and the file is deleted once Bao reports unsealed.
    • Changing the seal type is a different act: it is seal key rotation, run with bao operator unseal -migrate while the old seal still answers, and it needs a restart.

    Measured on the operator’s desktop on 2026-10-30, a TPM 2.0 firmware TPM: a 32-byte key wrapped to a non-exportable key unwrapped to the same bytes; a changed byte in the wrapped file, an export of the private key and a deleted key were each refused. A Bao with a static seal fed by that unwrap initialised, restarted and unsealed with nobody typing, and a wrong key left it sealed. Not measured: a reboot, a copy of the wrapped file on another machine, and the kms, passkey and manual modes. The Steam Deck shows a TPM 2.0 device that systemd-creds cannot use without root; the Steam Frame is unchecked.

    Migration to the transit seal

    Stand up the Seal Bao on Fly and pass its recovery test, add a seal "transit" block to the Fly config, and migrate with one last Shamir unseal (-migrate). The Shamir key stays offline as the recovery key.

    Sub-decisions open

    • The seal provider: a Seal Bao on Fly, unwrapped from Fly KMS (operator, 2026-10-30).
    • Whether the Seal Bao runs as one machine or as three voters; both are allowed.
    • Where the offline copy of the Seal Bao’s key is kept.
    • Whether to write the CRL-loop fix (a separate bug) into this rollout or before it.

    Sources

    • Vault auto-unseal precedent for the KMS wrapper pattern (cloud kms auto-unseal, applies unchanged to OpenBao forks).
    • RFD66606-2144 (its eleventh defect: the without-auto-unseal failure mode).

    The problem

    Bao was one machine, Shamir seal single share, operator+1P recovery per restart. Shamir with a manual share is the right seal for one-of-one, wrong for three-of-three.

    Related

    RFD66606-2144, RFD66606-2145, RFD66606-2146. Split from the old RFD66606-2147: RFD66606-2353 (replicas), 2355 (cache), 2356 (no CDN proxy).

    Source: rfd/2354-bao-unseals-itself-through-a-seal-bao-on-fly.exs

    RFD66606-2353: Bao runs three replicas on the FDB machines

    State: discussion Scope: weftspun-bao and the weftspun-fdb machines it runs on.

    Bao runs as three replicas, one beside each FDB machine.

    Bao was one machine, and every consumer now depends on it: every routine credential read, coordination write and policy check routes through Bao, so one outage stops them all.

    ha_enabled = true, coordinated over FDB (operator, 2026-10-13). The weftspun-bao app retires once the three instances serve. Superseded on 2026-11-01: Bao runs as one instance beside a single-node FDB cluster on one Fly machine, restored from the R2 backup, with ha_enabled = false (operator, 2026-11-01).

    Deploy the image to the three weftspun-fdb machines one at a time and unseal each, then destroy the weftspun-bao app once the three serve.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Why HA now, not before

    RFD66606-2140 chose ha_enabled = "false" when Bao was one machine and one operator. Under that arrangement, Bao being down meant one thing was down: the Bao API. Everything else routed around Bao by holding its credentials in Fly secrets or 1P.

    RFD66606-2146 turned that inside out. Every consumer now authenticates to Bao with its per-service cert, reads its credentials from Bao at runtime, and coordinates state through Bao’s KV. When Bao goes down, the DNS-editing path goes down, the R2-write path goes down, the FDB coordinator info lookup goes down, and any new spend gate that follows the same pattern goes down with them. The single-machine posture that was fine as a convenience store is not fine as the switchboard.

    Colocated on the FDB machines

    The operator chose on 2026-10-13 to run Bao on the three weftspun-fdb machines instead of in its own app. The Fly plan in use includes three shared-cpu-1x 256 MB machines and 3 GB of volumes; three FDB machines plus a separate Bao machine overran both, and the separate machine bought no redundancy. FDB keeps double redundancy and three coordinators, so one machine may still be lost.

    Each machine runs fdbserver, the backup agent, Bao, tailscaled and sshd, at 512 MB. Measured on 2026-10-13 at 256 MB: an FDB machine used about 130 MB, and the Bao machine about 130 MB, of which Bao was 77 MB, tailscaled 26 MB and the plugin 18 MB. The two together do not fit in the 207 MB a 256 MB machine leaves usable.

    • The weftspun-bao app retires once the three instances serve. Its volume held no secrets: Bao’s storage is FDB, and the volume kept the tailnet identity, the SSH host key and renewed listener certificates.
    • Each instance advertises its own machine address as api_addr and cluster_addr, so standbys forward to the active instance. Standbys forward every read to the active instance.
    • Clients keep verifying the listener as weftspun-bao.internal; the name in the certificate does not move with the app.
    • One machine carries the existing tailnet state and keeps the weftspun-bao node; the others join under their own names.
    • The SSH tunnel port is balanced across all three machines, so they share one host key, held as a secret rather than generated per volume.
    • The change is proved on a throwaway three-machine app before weftspun-fdb is touched: an initialised test Bao, a secret written and read back, one machine restarted and unsealed while the others keep serving.

    Replicas: 3 in sjc, coordinated over FDB

    OpenBao’s FDB backend supports HA by leader election over the same storage the writes go to. One instance runs on each FDB machine, so Bao spreads across the same three zones FDB does.

    Standby replicas can either serve reads directly or forward every request to the leader. Read-serving standbys would suit the read/write ratio the cert-auth path establishes (many reads per one write); until the fork is shown to serve reads from a standby, standbys forward.

    The 3-machine scale exposes one wrinkle: three machines mean three seal states, three unseal calls per fleet restart. This is the reason auto-unseal stays the goal.

    Migration path

    Enabling the replicas on the live cluster is:

    1. Update service-openbao/config-fdb.hcl: ha_enabled = "true".
    2. Build one image carrying the FDB server and Bao, and deploy it to the three weftspun-fdb machines one at a time, unsealing each.
    3. Stop the weftspun-bao app, then destroy it once the three serve.

    A desk reaches the active instance

    Read on 2026-10-16. The three instances elect one leader, and only the leader answers a login; a standby redirects to the leader’s <machine>.vm.weftspun-fdb.internal address, which no desk resolves. Two of the three carried tailnet names that day (weftspun-bao-3, weftspun-bao-4), both unsealed standbys, and the leader, the third machine, had none, so a desk asking the tailnet found no leader and the desk helper exited without a word.

    The route that worked: read sys/leader from any instance (no token, mTLS only), take the machine id out of leader_address, and run fly proxy 8200:8200 <id>.vm.weftspun-fdb.internal -a weftspun-fdb as a background process. The desk then uses BAO_ADDR=https://127.0.0.1:8200 with BAO_TLS_SERVER_NAME=weftspun-bao.internal and its agent certificate. The proxy exits on its own after some minutes; a connection refused on 127.0.0.1:8200 means restart it, not that Bao is down.

    The retired weftspun-bao app still exists, stopped. fly proxy -a weftspun-bao fails with host was not found in DNS because nothing runs there, and starting its machine brings up a second Bao against the same FDB storage, which stops again within a minute. It was started twice that day by mistake before the route above was found; it is not started again, and its deletion is an open item.

    Sub-decisions open

    • Delete the retired weftspun-bao app and its volume, so a desk cannot start a second Bao by mistake.
    • Every instance joins the tailnet under its own name, or the leader’s name is published where a desk can read it without a Fly login.
    • 3 replicas, one per FDB machine (operator, 2026-10-13).
    • Standbys serve reads (disable_performance_standby = false) vs forward to leader. Read-heavy workload argues for serving.
    • The FDB and Bao data machines run as one machine or as an HA set; the one-machine form relies on tested backups (operator, 2026-10-30).

    Sources

    • OpenBao HA storage docs (FDB backend supports HA via leader election on the shared FDB cluster).
    • RFD66606-2140 (Bao on FDB, this raises its ambition), 2145 (leaf and CA rotation cadence this HA has to survive), 2146 (the capability topology this now underwrites).

    The problem

    RFD66606-2140’s ha_enabled = "false" fit that framing. RFD66606-2146 then moved every routine credential read, coordination write, and policy check onto Bao. Every consumer now depends on Bao being up, and RFD66606-2140’s reliability budget is smaller than what routes through Bao now needs.

    The tuples

    rfd-2353--provides--bao-single-fly-instance
rfd-2353--is-a--deployment
rfd-2353--spends--bao
rfd-2353--spends--bao-fdb-storage-backend
rfd-2353--spends--bao-cert-auth-role-map
rfd-2353--spends--fdb-backup-r2-dr-tag
rfd-2353--spends--fly
rfd-2353--spends--tailscale

    Related

    RFD66606-2140, RFD66606-2144, RFD66606-2145, RFD66606-2146. Split from the old RFD66606-2147: RFD66606-2354 (unseal), 2355 (cache), 2356 (no CDN proxy).

    Source: rfd/2353-bao-runs-three-replicas-on-the-fdb-machines.exs

    RFD66606-2351: one ledger of BORING-TOKENs and INNOVATION-TOKENs for three orgs

    State: discussion Feature: a token is what the stack cannot run without: twenty, six INNOVATION-TOKENs and fourteen BORING-TOKENs Scope: the token ledger in the private working agreements and the private plan, the private blocklist, and the repos of V-Sekai-fire, chibifire-stages and the private org

    Which of the twenty tokens are INNOVATION-TOKENs, and which are BORING-TOKENs?

    The stack crashes without any of the twenty, and only six of them are new risk.

    A token is a substrate: delete it and the tech stack crashes. The name keeps it apart from a credential (operator, 2026-11-01). The ledger has twenty tokens. Each is a BORING-TOKEN, whose failures are widely known and which runs as shipped, or an INNOVATION-TOKEN, which is our own build, a fork or a use nobody has run. The INNOVATION-TOKENs are guest ELFs on the pinned double engine as row 1, which also runs the pen, zone.elf, the ggml-rd models, slug.elf, voice, the USD guest and the Lean tests, then SQLite on FoundationDB pages as row 2, FEX as row 6, the Fedora cross-build image as row 12, osxcross as row 15 and the taskweft persona engine as row 18. The BORING-TOKENs are Bao as row 3, our fork with an FDB storage backend, then Fly as row 4, which hosts the store, Bao and the KMS key that unseals Bao, then Tailscale as row 5, Proton as row 7, Windows as row 8, pixi as row 9, prek as row 10, GitHub as row 11, LLVM as row 13, llvm-mingw as row 14, SteamVR as row 16, Godot Engine as row 17, Elixir as row 19 and steamac as row 20. The operator ruled Elixir and Proton BORING-TOKENs on 2026-11-01, and Bao a BORING-TOKEN on 2026-11-12 although it is a fork. CockroachDB is retired (operator, 2026-10-18), and the guest BEAM is unship (operator, 2026-10-29). The count was three, then two INNOVATION-TOKENs, and is twenty tokens of which six are INNOVATION-TOKENs. The ledger changes between rungs, not in an open one, and the operator moved the two documents on 2026-10-30 rather than wait for a rung to claim them.

    Check a new technology against the rule: a token is a substrate, and the tech stack crashes without it. Write it BORING-TOKEN if its failures are widely known, INNOVATION-TOKEN if not.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    The measured gap

    The upstream orgs ran a second database. Of 312 repos that use a non-boring technology, 182 fit inside one INNOVATION-TOKEN when each technology is its own.

    How the ledger was found

    The operator requested it on 2026-10-18: study the three orgs and consolidate the INNOVATION-TOKENS with frontier learning, with no limit on the count. Each org is a level. Each repo that uses a non-boring technology is a problem: 298 in V-Sekai-fire, 10 in the private org (the local checkouts, because the token cannot list the org) and 4 in chibifire-stages. A problem passes when every technology it uses is in one INNOVATION-TOKEN. Repos were tagged against 33 technologies from their names, descriptions, topics and languages.

    A step tries one move, “technology X rides on INNOVATION-TOKEN Y”. The level with the most regret picks it. The move is kept only when total passes rise and at least two repos use both. Two planted moves with no relation (Ink onto OpenBao, Janet onto CockroachDB) were controls, and both were rejected.

    What it measured

    • Passes rose from 182 to 263 of 312 (58% to 84%): 23 moves kept, 11 rejected.
    • Per level at the end: V-Sekai-fire 251 of 298, the private org 8 of 10, chibifire-stages 4 of 4.
    • Kept onto the guest INNOVATION-TOKEN: the pen, zone.elf, ggml-rd (and the Python reference models and Slang kernels behind it), MuJoCo, OpenUSD, voice, Rust guests, slug.elf, the double engine with xr-pilot and CineForm, and Lean as tests.
    • Kept onto the BEAM: taskweft, MCP, holographic reduced representations.
    • Not merged, for want of shared repos: CockroachDB, the casync chunk store, OpenBao and parquet into the store. Retiring CockroachDB was an operator decision, not a measured one.

    What is still split

    • Elixir and guest code meet in 29 repos (taskweft compiled to a guest, the Godot build service, the MCP guest, the private org’s double-engine repository). That boundary decides two big INNOVATION-TOKENS or one.
    • Terraform, Ink, Janet, TLA+, gaussian splats, hypercore and Go each sit alone. Each is a candidate to retire or park.
    • The tagging reads metadata, not code. Two third-party engine scripting tags landed in the guest INNOVATION-TOKEN on a loose keyword. The moves were written by the agent. The measurement only checked them against shared repos.

    The parts added on 2026-11-01, classified

    The operator asked for the ledger to name these parts and ruled that each is a token (operator, 2026-11-01). The class of each follows the test in the decision.

    • Row 3, Bao, is a BORING-TOKEN. The zone talks to the store directly, and reaches Bao rarely, to get or renew the credential it presents to the store.
    • Row 4, Fly, is a BORING-TOKEN. Delete it and the store, Bao and the KMS key that unseals Bao go with it.
    • Row 5, Tailscale, is a BORING-TOKEN and is allowed (operator, 2026-11-12). The desk’s Bao client reaches Bao over it (RFD66606-2399).
    • Row 20, steamac (github.com/fxgl/steamac), is a BORING-TOKEN (operator, 2026-11-12). It is third party. What it runs underneath, FEX and Proton among them, is not this ledger’s.
    • Row 6, FEX, and row 7, Proton, are abandoned (RFD66606-2490, operator, 2026-11-12). The win64 build targets the Steam Frame and the Steam Deck natively.
    • Windows (row 8), pixi (9), prek (10) and GitHub (11) are BORING-TOKENs. The build and gate tools count as the tech stack.
    • The Fedora cross-build image (row 12) and osxcross (row 15) are INNOVATION-TOKENs. LLVM (row 13) and llvm-mingw (row 14) are BORING-TOKENs. Each is its own substrate, so deleting one stops a cross-build.
    • The SteamVR runtime (row 16) and Godot Engine (row 17) are BORING-TOKENs, and the taskweft persona engine (row 18) is an INNOVATION-TOKEN. Godot Engine and the pinned double engine of row 1 are separate tokens (operator, 2026-11-01).
    • Elixir (row 19) is a BORING-TOKEN (operator, 2026-11-01). It runs every gate and the ledger’s own tools, and its failure stops them, so it counts under the tool ruling.
    • GitHub’s identity-token login rides row 3, because it is a login to Bao.

    What is not known

    • How many INNOVATION-TOKENs the stack may hold. The old limit was two, and six now stand.
    • Whether the classes of the rows the operator did not rule on one by one stand as written.

    Related RFDs

    • RFD66606-2341, dev.next, where this waits; RFD66606-2309, frontier learning.
    • RFD66606-2006 and RFD66606-2075, abandoned.
    • The private blocklist, the CockroachDB row.

    CockroachDB, retired

    • The private org: a row in the private blocklist.
    • Weftspun: a manuals pull request, merged.
    • Moved to SQLite on FoundationDB, all merged 2026-10-18: the zone backend contract (its leftover CockroachDB deploy and notes), the taskweft MMOG agent and the residual FSQ recommender (both tested in CI on a real FoundationDB), and the multiplayer fabric hosting service (compose only, never run: no desk runs containers).
    • Also moved, merged 2026-10-18: weftspun-character-taxonomy. Its image no longer starts a CockroachDB node, and CI finds its test database’s keys in FoundationDB. The smoke-test scripts in the multiplayer fabric meta repo need a merge with no CI before they run.
    • Archived: the fabric’s CockroachDB service, the Dokku CockroachDB service, the vertex interactor, the fabric’s container service, the fabric gateway transport and the fabric infra service (the Terraform for the Fly app, whose daily backup found no started machine on 2026-10-18).
    • The pinned taskweft dependency still pulls postgrex.
    • The analysis script was Python in a scratch directory. It is not kept here, by the languages rule.

    The BEAM row, unship (operator, 2026-10-29)

    No guest runs BEAM bytecode, and no beam.elf exists in the tree. The only novel piece of the row is RFD66606-2330’s static riscv64 BEAM, and that is the piece to unship. Counting the BEAM as an INNOVATION-TOKEN spent the slot that merging the pen and the shared world freed.

    The two rows, moved (operator, 2026-10-30)

    • The private plan: “The three innovation tokens” is two. The ledger table’s pen row and zones row are one guest row, which absorbs the “already paid” RISC-V row, and the store row is INNOVATION-TOKEN 2.
    • The private working agreements: “There are three, and all three are spent” is two, naming guest ELFs on the pinned double engine as the INNOVATION-TOKEN the pen and zone.elf share.
    • The operator moved both on 2026-10-30, outside a rung, rather than waiting for one to claim them, and RFD66606-2341’s item left dev.next.

    The problem

    Elixir runs every tool and is a BORING-TOKEN.

    The verbs

    verb meaning
    provides the subject, once accomplished, mints the object token
    spends the subject is accomplished only by spending the object token
    is-a the subject is a kind of the object, as a subclass is of its class
    owns the subject is composed of the object, as an object owns the parts it has
    controls the subject decides what the object does
    delegated-to the subject hands its control to the object
    has-capability the subject may use the object capability
    is-member-of the subject belongs to the object group, and inherits what the group holds
    supervisor-of the subject answers for the object’s work
    partner-of the subject and the object share a goal as peers

    The tuples

    datasource-store--provides--fdb-sqlite

weftspun--owns--fdb-sqlite
weftspun--owns--guest-elf-double

    RFD66606-2349: Recording a live run: house recorder at 4K, CineForm, no FFmpeg tool

    State: committed Feature: one way to record a run where a live model plays Scope: every recording of a live run in the workspace, first the decider games

    A live run is recorded at 4K, in CineForm, with the house recorder.

    Movie Maker renders at a fixed frame rate, so the game waits for the model and the video hides its latency. A video of a live model must show the latency it has.

    A live run is recorded with the house recorder on the Mac at a 3840x2160 canvas. The recorder writes CineForm video and FLAC audio in Matroska through its custom output. The game runs on the wall clock and never waits for the model. Godot Movie Maker is blocklisted. FFmpeg never runs as a tool. RFD66606-2345’s format stands; this RFD replaces its encoder, its live recorder and its file check.

    Read RFD66606-2345 for the format this RFD amends.

    The operator’s rulings, 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-10

    • The recorder is the house recorder. Movie Maker is blocklisted.
    • The video is 3840x2160. 2K is denied.
    • A video holds at least 2 minutes of real run time. A short run is made longer by running longer, never by holding or repeating frames.
    • The game ticks on the wall clock. A late reply applies at the next tick. With no reply the game takes its default move.
    • CineForm everywhere. No ProRes is written and converted to CineForm.
    • FFmpeg never runs as a tool, and headless Godot never runs.

    How the house recorder writes CineForm

    The house recorder’s current release ships the cfhd CineForm encoder. Its custom output, built on FFmpeg, is set to Matroska with cfhd video and FLAC audio. In a still-frame test every frame decoded through the CineForm SDK at 39.4 dB against the input. The control, the same input shifted 40 px, scored 16.3 dB.

    Encoding outside the house recorder

    A render that is not a live capture encodes with the CineForm SDK through the engine’s CineForm module or the CineForm interactor. Delivery uses the AV1-in-Matroska interactor’s deliver.exs. It rewraps the frames byte for byte and checks every frame and sample.

    • A render reel records through the engine’s movie writer straight to CineForm. It writes no PNG frames to encode later (operator, 2026-10-17).
    • Large media and videos are kept on the Windows desk, not on the Mac mini, which sits on a remote network (operator, 2026-10-17). A render made on the Mac is copied to the desk, its size is read back there, and only then is the Mac copy deleted.

    How a file is checked

    deliver.exs checks every frame and every sample. av1mkv dump-frame pulls frames, and a person looks at them. The run’s length is gated from the frames’ own timestamps, and a short frame set is the control that must fail. The frames and samples are the check, whatever exit code the recorder returns.

    Still open

    • The house recorder’s custom output uses FFmpeg’s encoder inside the recorder. The ruling bans FFmpeg as a tool, and the Snake video issue records the house recorder as the route. The operator has not ruled on whether the licence reason reaches the house recorder.
    • The decider-pong recorders named in RFD66606-2345 still call ffmpeg. They move to the house recorder or the SDK route when that project is next worked on.

    The problem

    RFD66606-2345 encodes with the homebrew ffmpeg and checks files with ffprobe. FFmpeg as a tool is now banned.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2345, the video format, which this RFD amends; RFD66606-2347, the decider-pong review.
    • The private blocklist, which lists Movie Maker and FFmpeg as a tool.
    • The private manifest’s issue on the parked Snake video, which records the rulings and the house recorder test.

    RFD66606-2348: the taskweft superset workspace

    State: committed Feature: the workspace manifest places every taskweft path, opt-in, and the bootstrap opts in Scope: the private manifest’s default.xml and README.md, the private bootstrap’s bootstrap.sh and bootstrap.ps1, and the private working agreements

    One workspace checkout holds both the taskweft rows and this workspace’s own.

    The taskweft workspace and this one were two clients of two manifests. Work that needed both had no single checkout.

    The workspace manifest is a superset of the taskweft manifest, by path. Where both place a path, this workspace’s row wins, so rung pins never move through the merge. Every other taskweft row is added with groups="notdefault,taskweft", pinned to the commit its branch or tag had on the day it was added, with upstream naming that ref. The bootstrap runs repo init -g default,taskweft, so a new workspace syncs both sets. A plain repo init still syncs the workspace’s own rows only.

    Read below for the checks that passed and the work still open.

    The operator’s decisions

    1. The taskweft rows the blocklist names (the OpenBao service and the Bao on SQLite and FoundationDB service) and iceoryx2 are added as they are. They are placed for study. No workspace repo depends on them.
    2. New rows are pinned to a commit, as every upstream row here is.
    3. The rows are an opt-in group. The bootstrap opts in. WEFTSPUN_GROUPS=default gives the workspace’s own rows alone.

    Why a plain copy fails

    Taskweft rows track branches and include rows this org blocks, so a plain copy would have broken the pin rule and put blocked repos in every default sync.

    The merge rules

    The comparison is by path, because a path is what repo collides on. 11 paths are in both manifests. At the bootstrap path the two rows name different repos, and the private fork stays. The datasource store keeps this workspace’s row, so taskweft’s two linkfiles into the Bao on SQLite and FoundationDB service are not placed. GitHub rows use the one origin remote with an org-qualified name. The nine Hugging Face rows need two absolute remotes, huggingface and huggingface-datasets.

    Numbers and checks

    taskweft had 180 rows: 169 added, 21 of them already pinned by commit. The manifest went from 20 to 189 rows. Every branch and tag resolved with git ls-remote, with 0 failures. The four manifest gates passed locally, each after its self-test, and the five CI jobs passed on the pull request and on main after the merge. A scratch repo init listed 189 rows with the group and 20 with -g default, which is the control. repo list without -a shows 0 rows before a sync, so it proves nothing about a fresh client.

    Still open

    Nothing keeps the superset true as taskweft moves: a new taskweft row is absent here until someone adds it. The bootstrap repo’s workflow is active but has never run, and this repo has no workflow, so neither change was checked in CI. No pwsh was available, so the PowerShell change was not parsed. The private org is invisible to the gh wrapper; its pull requests go through the REST API with a bao-mint-github token, which prints the token and its expiry on one line.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2346, the last change that added manifest rows; RFD66606-2341, dev.next.
