    RFD66606-2347: decider-pong: a second opinion, and a model that wins

    State: committed Feature: a Pong recording whose labels match what the live model does, and a run where it wins Scope: the decider-pong interactor’s recorder_second_opinion.py, its simulators, evals and PEER_REVIEW.md

    A live Pong model wins 7-0 and 8-0, and the write-up says who does the predicting.

    The shipped video showed “a live decider” playing Pong. The model was right on 34 to 52 percent of its replies, answered “up” most of the time, and lost 0-25 in 2 minutes.

    The live paddle plays with four parts. Code predicts the y where the ball will reach the paddle by running Pong.step forward. The model answers the sign of the 10-px steps to that point. A held move stops at the target. An answer older than 15 frames hands the paddle to the teacher. With the classic angle rule on both paddles, the model wins 7-0 and 8-0 on its own points over two 5-minute runs. The teacher controls on the same seeds end 7-6 and 9-8.

    Read PEER_REVIEW.md in decider-pong, which carries every number.

    The review, in short

    The shipped prompt scored 68 percent offline, with 41 of 60 answers “up”. A held answer overshot: one “move” carries the paddle 40 px over a 4-frame reply, against a 14-px reach. One failed request froze the paddle on “stay” for the rest of a run. The drawn paddles were twice the size of the colliding ones, and the right one sat 10 px behind its hit plane. The overlap test had a wrong y term, the timecode printed hundredths, serves were seeded from the clock, and 600 frames sat in memory. The README contradicted the files on disk.

    Why the game could not be won

    Under the repo physics no paddle can win: the teacher never misses. A hit never changes the ball’s vertical speed, which stays under 4.1 px a frame. A paddle moves 10 px a frame. Teacher against teacher held 0-0 for 30 simulated minutes on three seeds. The classic angle rule, --english 8, lets the hit point change the vertical speed by up to 8 px a frame. It applies to both paddles, and teacher against teacher stays even under it.

    What each step fixed

    1. Simulation first. sim_right_paddle.py showed that even a paddle that is always right loses about 4 points a minute when it holds an answer for a 4-frame delay. Aiming at the crossing point and stopping there loses almost none, even with 60 percent wrong answers.
    2. Prompt. A two-number prompt at temperature 0 was right 98 percent of the time on spread cases, but 81 percent on gaps under 30 px, where it answered “stay”. The STEPS prompt was right on 80 of 80 close calls at a median of about 105 ms.
    3. Prediction. A mirror-reflection formula tied 2-2. It was wrong on 80 of 80 approaches, because the game pins the ball to the wall. The rollout matched the real hit-test y on 80 of 80.
    4. Staleness. The first 5-minute rollout run led 4-0, then an endpoint stall froze the paddle for about 30 s and it lost 13 points. A 1 s request timeout and a 15-frame answer limit fixed it. A planted endpoint that never answers gave 600 of 600 teacher frames, with the paddle still moving.

    Results that count

    Seed 7, 5 minutes: 0-7, all 7 points the model’s, 3232 of 3232 replies correct, p50 84 ms. Seed 11, 5 minutes: 2-8. The model’s points are 8-0, and the 2 lost came while the teacher held the paddle during 13 endpoint failures. Without the angle rule the rollout run holds 0-0, the most the physics allows.

    What the win does not show

    The model answers the sign of a small integer. A rule in code would do the same. It does not plan, aim or read the game. The next test gives the model the game state and scores the target it chooses.

    Files

    Every render is CineForm and FLAC in Matroska on the Desktop, named by mode, seed and length, with its decision log. Runs that exposed a bug keep a suffix that says so, such as _stale-reply-bug. The commits that carry this work are on decider-pong main.

    The problem

    Code does the predicting in the winning runs, and the write-up must say so.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2345, the video format; RFD66606-2346, decider-pong in the workspace.
    • PEER_REVIEW.md and evidence/ in decider-pong carry every number.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2346: decider-pong in the workspace

    State: committed Feature: decider-pong synced, pinned and mirrored like every other project Scope: the private manifest’s default.xml, the decider-pong interactor and its upstream decider interactor

    decider-pong is a manifest row, synced offline like every other project.

    The repo lived outside the workspace, on GitHub only, with its upstream as a submodule.

    decider-pong is a manifest row on the interactor side, tracking main. Its upstream, Mapika/decider (Apache-2.0), is a second row beside it, pinned to a commit. It was a git submodule; it is not any more. Both are in the local mirror, and a fresh offline client syncs them with 0 failures. The OpenBao credential helper was removed from the tree.

    Read RFD66606-2341 for the two open questions, parked in dev.next.

    • The private working agreements, the org and languages sections; the private blocklist.

    The steps, in order

    1. The pending prompt change was committed in decider-pong.
    2. The submodule checkout was shallow, so the mirror refused it. It was unshallowed from GitHub, and the pinned upstream commit was pushed to a new bare mirror of the upstream. All 98 commits arrived and git fsck is clean.
    3. bin/bao-github-credential was removed in one commit, then the submodule was replaced by the manifest row in the next.
    4. A bare mirror of decider-pong was made and main was pushed to it.
    5. Two rows were added to default.xml beside the other interactors, committed and pushed to the manifest mirror.
    6. A scoped repo sync of the two paths placed both checkouts. A full sync was not run, because three projects sit on dev1 branches that the preflight would park.

    Gates run

    check_manifest_comments.py, check_manifest_xml.py --offline, check_manifest_dupes.exs and check_manifest_root.py passed, each after its self-test. check_offline.exs lists 19 projects with 0 failures, both decider rows at their pins, and its self-test fails as planted. One run reported 1 failure while a push to the mirror was in flight; three runs after it reported 0.

    GitHub and the mirror

    decider-pong’s GitHub main fast-forwards to the mirror’s and is pushed there too. The manifest was pushed to the mirror only. GitHub’s manifest carries one commit the mirror lacks, which adds a row for a repo not yet mirrored. Reconciling the two needs that repo mirrored first, and is the user’s call.

    Open questions, parked in dev.next

    The languages rule forbids project Python. decider-pong is an evaluation harness. It is either ported to Elixir or the engine, or given a named exemption. The org names repos by hexagon side; the repo should carry the interactor prefix. Only the user renames repos on GitHub. After the rename the manifest row changes by one line. The removed helper stays in history from the commit that added it; dropping it means rewriting a published branch.

    The problem

    The contract places a repo in the manifest the day it is created and pins upstreams as manifest rows. The repo also carried a blocklisted OpenBao helper. Two questions remain open: the repo is all Python, and its name lacks a side prefix.

    RFD66606-2345: Video intermediate: CineForm and FLAC in Matroska

    State: committed Feature: one intermediate format for every rendered video Scope: every tool in the workspace that writes a video file, first the decider-pong interactor

    Every rendered video is one format: CineForm and FLAC in Matroska.

    The decider-pong recorders wrote H.264 and AAC in MP4. That is a lossy delivery format, and a second encode loses more.

    Every rendered video is written as CineForm video and FLAC audio in a Matroska (.mkv) file. CineForm runs at gbrp12le, so RGB frames keep full chroma. MP4 is blocklisted as a container, and H.264 and AAC are not written as outputs. A tool that writes video refuses an output path that does not end in .mkv. Uncompressed PCM audio is accepted in place of FLAC (operator, 2026-10-23); both are lossless.

    Check a video with ffprobe, which must report cfhd, gbrp12le, 1920x1080 and the matroska format.

    Also related

    • The private blocklist, which lists MP4.
    • The decider-pong skill carries the same rule for agents.

    Why an intermediate

    An intermediate must survive re-encoding and keep sharp synthetic edges.

    Encoder settings

    The homebrew ffmpeg ships the cfhd encoder. It takes yuv422p10le, gbrp12le and gbrap12le. The recorders use gbrp12le, because their frames are RGB and Pong’s edges are one colour against another. Audio is FLAC, or uncompressed PCM, at 48 kHz, stereo. An engine movie writer receives 32-bit samples, so it writes pcm_s24le and never 16-bit.

    CineForm fails on a frame whose width is not divisible by 16 or whose height is not divisible by 8. A writer checks the size before it starts and refuses with a message that names the size, because the encoder otherwise dies mid-stream and the only symptom is a broken pipe.

    A live recorder pipes raw RGB to one ffmpeg process that writes CineForm in Matroska, then a second pass copies that video and adds the FLAC track. Nothing is held in memory past the pipe.

    Cost

    On the Mac mini, cfhd encodes a 1080p test source at about 170 frames a second, so a 30 fps live render keeps up with room to spare. A file grows by about 20 MB a second at 1080p. A 2-minute render is about 2.4 GB and a 5-minute render about 6 GB. The Desktop filled to 43 GB in one session, so superseded renders are listed for deletion and deleted only on request.

    How a file is checked

    ffprobe must report cfhd, gbrp12le, 1920x1080, flac or a pcm_s16le/pcm_s24le stream at 48000 Hz and the matroska format, with the duration the run asked for. A frame is then pulled with ffmpeg -ss and looked at. That report and that frame are the check, whatever exit code the recorder returns.

    The guard and its control

    recorder_second_opinion.py exits with an error on any --out that does not end in .mkv. The planted control asked for planted.mp4: the run exited 1 and wrote no file.

    What changed in decider-pong

    recorder_pong_v.py and recorder_second_opinion.py now write CineForm and FLAC. Four superseded recorders that only wrote MP4 were deleted: recorder_live.py, recorder_pong_live.py, recorder_pong_vector.py and recorder_realtime.py. Every MP4 the session had made was removed and re-rendered.

    The problem

    The workspace had no written format, so each recorder picked its own.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2346, decider-pong in the workspace; RFD66606-2347, the decider-pong review.

    RFD66606-2344: dev.3, the proof of dev.2

    State: committed Feature: every dev.2 claim, run under the private working agreements, with its control seen to fail Scope: the pen and the tray at the pins of RFD66606-2343; no new feature

    dev.3 runs every dev.2 claim under the private pins, with each control seen to fail.

    The pen’s gates were written on the FOSS side, several run headless, and none has run under the private pins.

    dev.3 proves what RFD66606-2343 lists and adds nothing. Each dev.2 gate runs on the pinned double editor with a real renderer, on OXRSys and flat, and each of its controls is seen to fail as planted. A claim with no passing run is a counted gap, not a feature.

    Read RFD66606-2343 for the dev.2 list that dev.3 proves.

    How every run is made

    The pinned double editor from our Godot double build, never headless: a small windowed --resolution where a gate’s own usage line says --headless. XR runs use OXRSys as the runtime and xr_pilot_mcp to see and drive. Each command, its pins and its output go verbatim into logbook/logbook-dev3.md.

    Gates and controls

    1. gate_xr_scripted.gd, XR and flat: 6 strokes, 2 cycles, 2 openings, one shell. Controls: --control=drop_seam FAILs at MESH; --expect=xr with the runtime hidden FAILs as flat.
    2. gate_replay.gd, through OXRSys and from tools/strokes/skirt.usda, and the CASSIE dress layer. Control: --control=drop_seam FAILs at MESH.
    3. gate_statue.gd: the skirt lands in the statue’s body frame and shows on it. Controls: on_monument and canvas_frame each FAIL.
    4. gate_world_grab.gd: carry 0.30 m within 5 mm, scale 2x within 2 %, one grip holds within 1 mm. Control: cold_debounce FAILs on the first grab.
    5. gate_locomotion.gd: walk, stairs, refusals, snap turn, teleport, repeat. Controls: step_high, no_resolve, solid_land, no_floor and ulp each FAIL.
    6. The tray: its tools/gate_dev1.exs, gates 1 to 7 of RFD66606-2342, each with its control.
    7. Reliability, over a 30-minute run of gate 1 in XR: at most 1 frame in 100,000 over 27.8 ms. Control: a planted 30 ms stall every 10,000 frames FAILs by count.
    8. Churn: zero pin moves and zero edits to RFD66606-2343 and this file between open and tag. Control: a planted pin bump FAILs by name.

    A gate that passes with its control also passing is decoration and counts as a FAIL.

    The playtest

    One person on OXRSys draws with the pen for 15 minutes, three sessions, rotating the user, a teammate and one trusted outsider. At minute 15: “What were you about to draw next?”, “Do you want to keep going?”, “Did anything look wrong or uncomfortable?” Every answer goes in the logbook verbatim.

    The release

    v<date>-dev.3 on the pen and the tray, logbook-dev3.md, and the counted gaps. The gaps and RFD66606-2341’s items plan dev.4.

    The pins, the same as RFD66606-2343

    Each pin is the commit or release the dev.2 logbook names.

    • Engine: our Godot build fork’s release v20260930-double.1.
    • Our meshing pen and our curvenet interactor.
    • Our XR pilot interactor: OXRSys and xr_pilot_mcp.
    • The tray’s dev.1 build.

    The problem

    Until they do, dev.2 is a list, not a result.

    RFD66606-2343: dev.2, the first playable

    State: committed Feature: what the pen holds at its pinned commit: draw, curvenet’s closed shell, the statue, world grab Scope: the pen at its pinned commit and the tray’s dev.1 build; RFD66606-2344 proves it

    dev.2 is what the pen holds at its pinned commit, and nothing more.

    The first version of this rung promised a shared world, a wardrobe, the mascot’s requests and the signs. None of them is built.

    dev.2 is what the pen holds at its pinned commit, written down and nothing more. A person draws with the XR pen, curvenet.elf closes the strokes into one shell, and the shell shows on the dress-on statue. World grab and the station walker work. RFD66606-2344 proves each of these under the private working agreements.

    Run the proof in RFD66606-2344 against each dev.2 claim: the XR pen, the closed shell, the dress-on statue, world grab and the station walker.

    What dev.2 holds

    Each line names the gate in the pen’s tools/ that already exercises it.

    • The scripted pen in xr_main.tscn, XR or flat: 6 strokes close 2 cycles and 2 openings into one skirt shell (gate_xr_scripted.gd).
    • A recorded or replayed stroke layer, through OXRSys or from .usda, meshed to its expected counts; a CASSIE session replayed to every expected cycle (gate_replay.gd).
    • The dress-on statue beside the plaza monument: the skirt drawn at the statue lands in its body frame and shows on it as a closed garment (gate_statue.gd).
    • World grab: both grips carry, turn and scale the canvas; one grip moves nothing (gate_world_grab.gd).
    • The walker on the station’s colliders in the MuJoCo guest: walk, stairs, ledge and handrail refusal, snap turn, teleport, bit-exact repeat (gate_locomotion.gd).
    • Pen strokes drawn as Line3D ribbons; every shipped guest and .sgd binary-translated on macOS and Windows.
    • The tray from RFD66606-2342: icon, popup, headset probe, the mascot idling.

    What dev.2 does not hold

    Every gate above stops at MESH. Nothing checks a garment against a body mesh, a clothing hide, or bone rest scale. No SCSS port is in the pen. No zone, no ENet clients, no FDB-SQLite wardrobe, no mascot requests, no signs, no audio cues. These wait in RFD66606-2341.

    The pins

    Each pin is the commit or release the dev.2 logbook names.

    • Engine: our Godot build fork’s release v20260930-double.1.
    • Our meshing pen and our curvenet interactor.
    • Our XR pilot interactor: OXRSys and xr_pilot_mcp.
    • The tray’s dev.1 build.

    A rung that lists unbuilt work as done cannot be verified, so this one lists only what exists.

    RFD66606-2342: dev.1, the tray icon

    State: committed Feature: a tray icon with the stand-in mascot’s face on macOS and Windows, the first dev rung Scope: the tray’s v<date>-dev.1 release

    The tray icon ships first: one Godot scene with a borrowed mascot’s face.

    Install, integrity, silence and uninstall must work before anything is drawn.

    dev.1 ships one Godot scene, built with the pinned double editor and exported with its templates for macOS and Windows. A borrowed mascot’s face is the icon. A click opens a popup with the version, a headset line, a zone line, a disabled “Draw” button and the mascot playing Idle.

    Run the gates in tools/gate_dev1.exs against OXRSys.

    dev.1: the feature

    One Godot scene, built with the pinned double editor and exported with its templates for macOS and Windows. The stand-in mascot’s face is the icon. Clicking it opens a popup with:

    • the version;
    • a “headset: connected / not found” line;
    • a “zone: none” line;
    • a disabled “Draw” button;
    • a viewport where the mascot’s glb plays Idle with its own materials.

    The tray becomes the zone host and the desktop client’s launcher in dev.2, so it comes first.

    • macOS: a menu-bar status item via DisplayServer.create_status_indicator, guarded by has_feature(FEATURE_STATUS_INDICATOR); ad-hoc signed; a DMG.
    • Windows: a system tray icon via the same API; a zip.

    The mascot is borrowed third-party work under MIT, not ours. It is the stand-in for dev.1 and dev.2, and no public asset shows it.

    The pins, frozen from open to tag

    This file names every pin when the rung opens, and nothing moves until the rung tags. Bumps happen between rungs, as one batch, recorded in the logbook.

    • Engine: our Godot build fork’s release v20260930-double.1, at the engine ref its release notes name, with the macOS arm64 editor and templates and the Windows x86_64 templates.
    • OXRSys and xr_pilot_mcp: our XR pilot interactor at the commit the logbook names.
    • The headset probe: the pen’s OpenXR probe, from our meshing pen at the commit the logbook names.
    • The mascot: the borrowed stand-in (MIT), from the private character repo.

    The reliability gate

    Every client logs frame times. At most 1 frame in 100,000 may exceed twice its budget (27.8 ms at 72 Hz), with zero crashes and zero disconnects across the playtest. It is measured on OXRSys and on the flat client. Control: a planted 30 ms stall every 10,000 frames must fail by count.

    Gates and controls

    The tray’s tools/gate_dev1.exs runs these against OXRSys.

    1. Install and launch from a fresh user account. The icon appears within 5 s. The version matches the tag. Control: a wrong version string must fail by name.
    2. Integrity. Signing waits on a signing identity, so dev.1 ships ad-hoc signed on macOS and unsigned on Windows, with one documented first-launch override. A SHA-256 per artifact is published and checked. Control: a tampered artifact must fail its hash by name.
    3. “headset: connected” only when an OpenXR session can be created on OXRSys. Control: XR_RUNTIME_JSON at a missing file must give “not found”.
    4. Zero outbound connections in a 10-minute idle capture. Control: the off-by-default update check, switched on, must show exactly one.
    5. Uninstall leaves nothing behind. Control: a planted stray file must be named.
    6. The mascot’s Idle plays in the popup, and the reliability gate holds over a 30-minute idle run. Controls: the glb removed must fail by path; the planted stall must fail by count.
    7. Churn: zero pin moves and zero edits to this RFD between open and tag. Control: a planted pin bump must fail by name.

    The playtest

    The user, a teammate and one trusted outsider each install on a Mac or PC they own, from the release page, with no help beyond the written first-launch override. Pass: three icons running at day’s end. Every install question is logged.

    Which features are likely to bring joy

    Each forecast uses the sense-of-wonder rubric of RFD66606-2412 and the tag form of RFD66606-2295.

    rung feature criteria joy
    dev.1 tray icon one override, hash-checked, silent (remote, p=0.05): plumbing
    dev.1 the mascot idles in the popup the glb plays (unlikely, p=0.20)

    The release

    v<date>-dev.1 on the tray: a private release with the artifacts and their hashes, and logbook/logbook-dev1.md in the private manifest.

    After the tag: the three installs, the logbook, the counted gaps, one batch of pin bumps, and RFD66606-2343 (dev.2) opened with its pins frozen.

    The problem

    In dev.2 the tray is the zone host and the desktop client’s launcher. So the plumbing ships first, with a face.

    RFD66606-2341: dev.next

    State: discussion Feature: the parked work that no numbered dev rung has claimed Scope: everything past dev.2 that waits for a rung of its own

    Parked work waits in one place, and no open rung changes to make room for it.

    Reducing churn is an absolute requirement. An ask added to an open rung moves its pins or edits its file, which the churn gate counts as a failure.

    dev.next holds every ask that no numbered rung has claimed. An idea that arrives while a rung is open is written here, and the open rung’s definition does not change. An item leaves dev.next when a numbered rung is planned around it.

    Write a new ask into dev.next instead of an open rung, and check that the open rung’s file and pins stay unchanged. The sections below list the parked items.

    The parked items

    • An original mascot, swapped into the stand-in mascot’s three slots (the tray icon, the popup, the requests in the world).
    • A thematic world that replaces the placeholder backstory and explains the dummy, the requests, the shared world and the persistence.
    • The vehicle story, chosen as a ladder of choices. You carry the atelier as a sample case and deploy it on any flat surface. The dress form is in the lid and the ledger is the lining. Closing the case writes the journal. Opening it replays the journal. AR comes first: the alpha blend mode with nothing drawn behind the case, which OXRSys already accepts with passthrough_enabled. VR is the same scene in the opaque mode. The case is the town (operator, 2026-10-09): opened, it holds the procedural station town the pen already vendors (MIT) as a diorama you look into, like a tabletop Japanese town built in a wooden tray. It is not a case of building pieces carried through a full-size town. This is the station RFD66606-2343 left for a later rung. The surface is found by MoGe-3 (MIT) when you set the case down. In AR it reads the colour stereo pair from the headset’s colour camera module, on the expansion port. The built-in cameras are monochrome and are not used. In a social VR world we did not build, it reads the rendered eye pair. Its metric points and normals give the plane, and the second eye checks the first. Without root, the headset’s runtime publishes one colour view as a loopback camera that the video group can read. It advertises 1920x1080 at 30 fps and measured 1.4 to 3.8 fps. Its own camera API is off by default. MoGe-3 runs as a godot-sandbox guest ELF on ggml-rd, the shape RFD66606-2272 proved for segmentation. Its weights come through the weight pump, and no Python is in the running path. It spends no innovation token: it is one more guest on the route zone.elf and curvenet.elf already use. With no confident plane, the case falls back to the controller pose. Its dense graph is 1,406 nodes. ggml-rd lacks only replicate padding and one antialiased resize. Its sparse 3D refiner has no ggml-rd kernels and is left out. Passthrough is tested sim-to-real in virtual worlds only. Two held-out sets are frozen before they render: path-traced rooms built from CC0 scanned furniture, and the station, whose build publishes every seat height. The station set matters because MoGe is unproven on stylized frames. Gate: the surface under the crosshair, scaled by the floor at the tracked eye height, lies within 3 cm of truth. Controls: a frame with no flat surface must fall back, and GGML_RD_FAULT=1 must fail the fit. RFD66606-2313 parks the full loop over colour passthrough on this surface.
    • Lookdev: style frames for the world, the mascot, Maro in SCSS and the dummy. Image generation waits for a rung.

No flap, lap panel, ruffle trim or bow covers it, and the tail is kept. The cut is the tail base’s sweep over the motion clips plus 5 mm. The tail’s long strands still cross the cardigan in motion.     RFD66606-2339: a persona answers from a planning domain

    State: discussion Feature: a persona answers from a goal-task network instead of from weights Scope: the persona repository, the planner it requires as a library, and its register row

    A persona answers from a goal-task network, so a goal gives an exact plan with no sampling.

    A request in words reaches a persona only by way of whoever authors the domain. A domain with a thin vocabulary answers a thin set of goals.

    • A persona answers from a goal-task network rather than from weights: a domain and a goal go in, an exact plan comes out, and no sampling is involved (operator, 2026-10-30).
    • The persona is the instinct model: Lean 4 code, named for its latency against a language model (operator, 2026-10-29).
    • The planner is a library, not a reference. The persona requires the RECTGTN domain over GitHub, as the character domain does, and composes in its shared GTN space.
    • Its inputs are a code or a number. A code is the vocabulary: one level count a dimension, packed mixed-radix, the shape residual FSQ stacks its stages in.
    • A code the codebook does not hold, a variable the domain does not declare, and a goal the domain cannot reach are refused by name.

    Read RFD66606-2292 next, the organization domain this workspace’s RFDs render into.

    Where it lives

    It is its own repository on the interactor side, placed when it is created, and the planner revision it builds against is recorded in its manifest.

    What landed

    The persona is a Lean package of its own: a domain of state variables, a codebook and actions, a goal over the planner’s own node space, and a search that composes the plan. The landing subject is “Compose the persona in Lean over the planner library”.

    Its gate is a witness exe with a positive and a negative control per invariant: the codebook’s size, basis and mixed-radix index; a code past its level and a code of the wrong arity both refused; a plan that executes to the goal; and three refusals, an unreachable goal, an undeclared variable and zero fuel.

    The codebook is the vocabulary

    Eight levels over four dimensions is 4096 codes a stage, and four stages of those is 281474976710656 codes from thirty-two small integers. A code is what a goal argument binds, and a number is the other half of the surface.

    The codec is the one this workspace already certifies for the residual-FSQ recommender: a mixed-radix index over per-dimension levels, injective and bounded at the real scale.

    References

    The codebook’s shape and the stages it stacks come from this lineage.

    • Zeghidour et al., SoundStream (doi 10.1109/TASLP.2021.3130651)
    • Défossez et al., EnCodec (doi 10.48550/arXiv.2210.13438)
    • Mentzer et al., Finite Scalar Quantization (doi 10.48550/arXiv.2309.15505)
    • Zhu et al., Robust Residual FSQ (doi 10.48550/arXiv.2508.15860)
    • Liu et al., VQTalker (doi 10.48550/arXiv.2412.09892)

    The design’s other half

    The persona is the half that answers from a program. The other half is a language model, and the design keeps a place for it until the model has a home (operator, 2026-10-29).

    Code as data, and what a persona says back

    A caller gives category and numeric instructions, and the persona walks the programs it holds: “you did not even weight paint”, then what face tracking costs. The caller is given options, and a choice fits the input shape rather than arriving in words. A failure and a success each point at a guide, baked in or linked (operator, 2026-10-29).

    What is not known

    • How a persona composes with this workspace’s rendered problems, which the organization domain answers today through the planner’s Elixir consumer.
    • The temporal reading of a domain that declares no reads and no writes: the plan order is exact, and the timeline parallelizes what the domain leaves undeclared.

    The problem

    A persona cannot answer a question that is not a goal.

    The tuples

    rfd-2339--provides--persona-goal-task-planner
rfd-2339--is-a--model-pipeline-stage

    RFD66606-2337: a garment fit at MESH on the GPU L-BFGS-B

    State: discussion Feature: the pen’s MESH stage moves a garment that clips the body out of it Scope: the fit in the drape guest, its kernels, and the pen’s MESH stage

    Can the pen’s skirt leave the body without a wider clearance on the strokes?

    On the statue avatar’s body, the scripted skirt’s surface sits 12 to 17 mm inside the cone its rings are sized for, about an AA battery’s width, between the front and back seams.

    • MESH ends with a fit. A garment surface that clips the body is moved out of it by the fit, not by a wider clearance on the strokes (operator, 2026-10-27).
    • The fit follows the intersection-free retargeting fork’s start: the body begins shrunk along its vertex normals, so the drawn surface is outside it, and grows back to full size in steps.
    • Each step is one solve by contract-lbfgsb (2-contract/lbfgsb) on the GPU: the shape term keeps the drawn surface’s shape, and the IPC barrier keeps every vertex outside the body at that step’s size. Every iterate stays intersection-free.
    • The fit runs in the guest of interactor-drape (3-interactor/drape), which already drives the solver on RenderingDevice and holds the IPC kernels. drape.elf comes back to transport-meshing-pen (1-transport/meshing-pen) (operator, 2026-10-27).
    • The pen’s check that no garment vertex is inside the body reads the fitted mesh. The scripted skirt’s ring clearance goes back to 1 cm, a little more than a pencil’s width.

    Read the gates and controls below, then run the pen’s check that no garment vertex is inside the body on the fitted skirt.

    The problem

    Nine of 1910 vertices end up 3 to 12 mm inside the body, from two pennies to nearly a AA battery’s width. A 2 cm ring clearance, two AAA batteries side by side, hides it without moving the surface.

    The solve

    For grow fraction a from 0 to 1 in N steps, the body is B(a) = B − (1 − a) d0 n, with n the area-weighted vertex normals of the body and d0 the shrink depth. At each step the solver minimises over the garment vertices x:

    E(x) = ks * sum over edges (|xi − xj| − lij)^2
     + kl * sum over vertices |L x − L x0|^2
     + kappa * sum over vertices, candidate triangles of B(a): b(d^2)

    lij and L x0 are the drawn surface’s edge lengths and Laplacian coordinates, and b is the IPC log barrier of the drape kernel, zero beyond dhat. The step starts from the last step’s result.

    What exists, and what is new

    • L-BFGS-B on the GPU: contract-lbfgsb vec_rd, in the drape guest, run by its solver tests.
    • IPC point-triangle barrier: drape IpcPointTriangle.lean, gradient and Hessian, no energy.
    • IPC step bound: drape IpcStepClamp.lean, written, not emitted or wired.
    • Shape term and normal shrink: new.
    • Fit entry points in the guest: new. New in the kernels:
    • The barrier’s energy, summed per vertex, because a line search compares energies.
    • The step bound inside the line search: the solver’s largest step is capped so no vertex moves more than a fraction of its distance to the body. Candidate triangles for each vertex come from the body mesh on the guest’s CPU, once per step.

    Gates and controls

    • No vertex inside: 0 inside, by winding number, after the fit. Control that must fail: the fit off, where the statue skirt has 9 inside.
    • Every iterate outside: 0 inside after every step. Control: the step bound off.
    • The start: 0 inside against the shrunk body. Control: d0 = 0 on the statue skirt.
    • The shape kept: the move of each vertex is reported. No control, because it is a measurement. Each runs on the scripted skirt (two avatars), the replayed skirt and dress, and the two hand-drawn skirts. The fit runs on RenderingDevice only. The solver’s vector ops keep their CPU-against-GPU unit tests.

    What is not known

    • ks, kl, kappa, dhat, d0 and N: measured on the fixtures first.
    • Time per fit on the GPU for about 2000 garment vertices.
    • Whether float32 vectors converge with the barrier near a 1 mm dhat, about a card’s thickness.
    • The statue’s body is open (870 boundary edges, 28 components): whether its normals give a clean shrink.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2293, which cut the fit from the pen; RFD66606-2294, where compute runs.

    RFD66606-2321: the autobattler fields Frames that wear

    State: committed Feature: each fighter in the SolidCraft autobattler is a Frame put together from guest solids, rolled on survey tables, and it carries wear from round to round Scope: the SolidCraft autobattler: its game script, its page and its zone version

    Autobattler fighters are Frames that carry wear from round to round.

    Each unit was one bare solid with no identity, and every round started from zero. Nothing on screen said which unit was hurt or why a round ended.

    Each squad in the SolidCraft autobattler fields five Frames. A Frame’s body is put together from solids the guest kernel builds, and its species, presentation and age come from three d100 rolls on the population survey tables of our appendix-E dataset. A Frame that survives a round stays with wear and leaves after five rounds, and each side earns scrip per round, as in the Gyre setting. The operator asked for more Frames, game feel, the Gyre flavour and readability on 2026-10-17.

    Run the game script with --selftest and --rounds=N to read a sim of the rounds.

    Roles, props and the zone as requested

    Each Frame also has one of three roles, melee, range or cyber, that beat each other as in rock, paper, scissors. The operator requested the roles on 2026-10-18. Each role and the plant also need a prop in a mirrored arena: cover, a relay per side or soil. The operator requested them the same day. On 2026-10-19 the operator requested that the game also run as a fabric zone that headsets join, with the store kept off every frame and every tick.

    Sources

    Drafted on 2026-10-17 from the game script as shipped, its self-test logs on each system and the operator’s requests of the same day.

    What a Frame is

    The guest builds 18 solids while the game loads: 12 whole solids and six parts (a head, a limb, a torso, a ring, a cube and a base). A Frame places parts by species and merges them into one mesh, so a Frame is one draw call. The parts become separate pieces only when it breaks. The bounds of the parts set health, damage, speed and reach, as the single solid did before.

    • Species: humanoid 1-50, semi-humanoid 51-88, synthetic 89-94, uplifted animal 95-96, plant 97-98, exotic 99-100.
    • Presentation: feminine 1-71, masculine 72-89, other 90-100.
    • Age: youth 1-58, juvenile 59-75, adult 76-87, no age 88-99, infant 100.

    The bands are the raw survey distribution, tables E.8 to E.10. Age scales the body and the head. Each species but humanoid adds one trait: semi-humanoid is fast, uplifted animal is very fast with less health, synthetic is plated and slower, plant regrows and is slow, and exotic is one bare whole solid that hits hard.

    Wear and scrip

    A Frame that survives a round gains one point of wear, and its maximum health drops by a tenth of its base for each point. At five points it leaves. New drafts fill the empty places. Each side earns two scrip per round plus one per Frame left, and the winner three more.

    Feel and readability

    A hit flashes the Frame and plays a short generated sound. A Frame that breaks throws its parts and shakes the camera. Each Frame has a health bar and a name tag, a little of its side’s colour shows even in shade, and the end of a round shows the Frames left and the scrip earned.

    Roles

    Melee beats range, range beats cyber and cyber beats melee. A hit on the role the attacker beats does 1.6 times its damage, a hit on the role that beats it does 0.6 times, and a hit on the same role does its normal damage. Reach puts the roles in order: melee hits at the reach of its body, cyber at 3.8 m and range at 7 m, so a range Frame shoots a cyber Frame before the cyber Frame can answer, and a melee Frame has to close the gap to a range Frame.

    • Melee: 1.25 times the health, 1.15 times the speed, an attack every 0.8 s, and a shield in front. Its hits push the target back.
    • Range: 0.75 times the health, 0.8 times the damage, 0.9 times the speed, an attack every 1.1 s, and a barrel at the shoulder. Each shot is a small sphere that flies to the target.
    • Cyber: 0.95 times the health, 0.7 times the damage, an attack every 1.0 s, and a dish on top. Each hit adds 0.7 s to the target’s next attack and shows a ring that spreads over the target.

    The role’s parts come from the same catalog of guest solids and merge into the Frame’s one mesh, but they do not count toward its health, damage or reach. Each squad’s draft holds every role at least once, so every round shows the triangle. The other two places draw a role at random from the round’s seed. The name tag shows the role before the species.

    What the world gives each role

    Each role and the plant now need something in the arena, so a sim shows what the world adds and what it takes away. The operator requested these props on 2026-10-18, for every role at once so that no role is the only one that depends on the world.

    • Range needs a clear line. Five cover blocks stand in the middle. A range Frame does not shoot through cover. It walks around the block until the line is clear. Every Frame walks around cover, not through it.
    • Cyber needs its relay. Each side has a relay mast, with its reach drawn as a faint disc on the floor. A cyber Frame jams only within 6.5 m of its own standing relay; away from it, the hit does half damage and no jam. A cyber Frame waits at the edge of the disc while friends who are not cyber still fight. Any Frame can attack the enemy relay (160 health). A relay that goes down stays down until the next round.
    • Melee needs open ground. Within 0.9 m of cover a melee Frame moves at 0.6 times its speed and its hits do not push the target back.
    • A plant needs soil. It regrows (4 health per second) only on one of four soil patches. Below half health it walks to the nearest patch and stays until it is nearly whole.

    Equity is a property of the layout: each prop has a twin of the same shape at the mirror place across the middle line, side 0’s relay is on side 0’s half, and a tie in which way to walk round cover goes the same way for both sides. The self-test checks the mirror and fails when one block is moved 0.5 m (the control). It also checks that a line through the middle block is blocked and a line past the blocks is clear. Each round prints a WORLD line: seconds range Frames spent with no clear line, cyber hits with and without the relay, seconds melee Frames spent beside cover, seconds plants spent on soil, and each relay’s health. --rounds=N with --selftest runs N rounds for a longer sim.

    Zone server and VR mode

    The round is deterministic: one seed gives the same ROUND, DAMAGE and WORLD lines on the web and on the three desktop systems. That makes the game a fit for an authoritative zone. The zone server runs the round headless, and every client shows the same round.

    Three loops run at three rates, and only the last touches the store.

    • The headset renders at 144 Hz, a frame every 6.9 ms. It predicts poses locally and never waits on the network or on a commit.
    • The zone runs the round at a fixed tick. At the start of a round it sends the seed and both drafts on a reliable stream. Each tick it sends every Frame’s place and health as datagrams, where the next tick replaces a lost one, and hits, breaks and the round’s end on the reliable stream. The zone and transport are those of interactor-fabric-zone (3-interactor/fabric-zone).
    • After a tick, the zone hands its SQLite journal image to a save thread if it changed. The save thread writes the image to SQLite on FoundationDB (datasource-store (6-datasource/store)) and keeps only the newest one: a save that is still in flight when the next is ready is replaced, not queued. A slow commit makes the stored image older. It never holds a tick or a frame.

    The store’s place in the third loop comes from a measurement. On 2026-10-19, sixteen players committing one row 20 times a second waited 5.5 to 6.0 ms for the median commit on the Windows desk’s FoundationDB under WSL, and over one player-day the worst waits reached 3.3 to 4.7 s. A typical commit is already a whole frame at 144 Hz, and the worst is hundreds of frames.

    The zone version lives in a new interactor repository, named interactor-solidcraft-zone and placed in the goal manifest when it is made. The game’s Godot project moves there as the one source, with a zone-server mode and a headset mode. The Space keeps the web build and the downloads, built from that repository. The guest kernel and the zone repository stay as they are and are used as dependencies.

    Each step has a check, and each check has a control.

    • The Space’s web build prints the same lines after the move as before it.
    • Two headless clients beside a zone server print the server’s ROUND, DAMAGE and WORLD lines. A client given another seed must differ.
    • The headset mode runs under the XR Pilot desktop runtime, which an agent drives with no person in a headset.
    • The save thread reports the age of the newest stored image over a player-day: its worst and how often it passes 1, 2 and 5 s. The planted slow commit must raise it.

    The zone simulates at 60 Hz and sends rows under RFD66606-2326’s byte budget. Two choices are open: whether the headset client is the V-Sekai client or a scene in the game’s own project, and which host runs FoundationDB in production. A run on a plain Linux runner, pending on 2026-10-19, says whether the multi-second waits come from the WSL host.

    The autobattler is the network test bench

    RFD66606-2326’s numbers so far come from walkers generated for the test, whose rows never repeat. The autobattler gives real traffic with an answer key. One seed fixes every round, so the server’s replay of a seed is the truth for every row a client receives, at every tick.

    • Scale. One zone runs many arenas side by side, from one to a few hundred, each a round of ten Frames on its own seed, with headless players placed so their view holds from tens to thousands of Frames. Arenas start a few ticks apart, so hits, breaks and round ends spread over time.
    • Classes. The zone carries what the game carries, not one kind of mover: Frames on scripted moves, players’ tracked heads and hands, props at rest that change only when touched, and crowds of pedestrians who stop, start and walk in pairs. Headless players replay recorded head and hand tracks, since tracked motion has sensor jitter a script lacks. Every report is split by class.
    • Scenes. Crowds come as the scenes people make: a shopping street, a standing concert, a seated stadium with a wave, a queue, a scramble crossing, a dance floor, a parade, a festival plaza, a theatre, a picnic lawn, an exit through one door, and a ring of players talking. Each scene’s density and pace come from footage counted the way the blue-hour street walk was, and in social scenes most of the crowd is tracked players.
    • Oracle. Each headless client decodes its rows, moves Frames along their sent velocity between rows, and compares what it holds with the server’s replay of the same seeds. It reports the worst position error and how long a Frame stayed wrong. A client must never hold a Frame the replay says has left, or a value that was never sent.
    • Link. Between server and clients sits a relay that drops and delays datagrams: no loss, 1% and 5%, at 50, 100 and 200 ms of round trip.
    • Record. The relay writes every message it passes. The recordings are the corpus for the static zstd dictionary: dictionaries built from them at 1, 8, 64, 256 and 1024 MB are measured on held-out recordings in bytes per row, and the size stops growing where the gain flattens.
    • Report. Bytes per player per second against the budget, bytes per row for plain zstd, for patch-from against the last row the client acknowledged, and for each dictionary size, and the oracle’s errors. Saves go through the store’s latest-wins thread and report save age.

    On rows generated for the test, sent as the gap from the client’s own prediction, props at rest cost 0.31 bytes a row, pedestrians 2.16 and tracked points 3.96. Walkers that never stop cost 0.47, which flatters prediction, so the bench uses pedestrians and never zombies. Scripted scenes flatter it the same way: a scripted queue, wave or crossing cost 0.31 to 0.34, the price of a prop at rest, and a scripted concert 2.04. Scenes are replayed from recorded motion where a licence allows, and a scene full of players costs what their tracked heads and hands cost. The budget gives players near each other the first share, and the bench sets the split from recorded traffic.

    Each measurement has a planted defect that must show in the report:

    • the budget ignored, which must push bytes per second over it;
    • a client holding another dictionary version, which must fail to decode and never decode wrong values;
    • the clock counter per row, which must make a client order rows wrong past 256 rows in a tick;
    • the velocity scale read per tick, which must raise position error;
    • a dropped leave message, which must leave a Frame the replay has removed;
    • the store’s slow commit, which must raise save age and nothing else.

    What was measured

    The change is in the game script only, so the guest and every translation hash stayed valid. On 2026-10-17 the web build and the macOS, Windows and Linux zips each started translated, built 18 solids and printed RESULT PASS. The script cost per physics frame rose from about 0.23 ms to about 0.3 ms on the Mac. The web game’s slowest frame in the first round read 139 to 145 ms before and after. Native frame times on the Mac were not compared: other jobs on the same machine made them vary more than the change.

    On 2026-10-18 the roles changed the game script only, again. The self-test first checks the triangle: every role beats exactly one other and loses to exactly one. A control table in which melee loses to both others must fail the same check, and it does. The macOS, Windows and Linux zips and the web build in a desktop browser then printed the same two rounds, with the same winners and the same damage per pair of roles, and RESULT PASS. In round 1, range did 303 damage to cyber and cyber did 57 to range. The web game’s slowest frame in round 1 read 150 ms with the roles and 134 ms without them, one run each in the same browser, so the difference is not measured past noise. The release kept its tag, because the guest did not change. Its zips and SHA256SUMS were replaced.

    On 2026-10-18 the world props changed the game script only, a third time. The self-test printed WORLD mirror=true control=false line_through=false line_beside=true on each system. The macOS, Windows and Linux zips and the web build in a desktop browser printed the same ROUND, DAMAGE and WORLD lines for the four rounds they share. The web run went on to nine rounds and the macOS run to twelve. Over the twelve rounds each side won six. Per round, range Frames spent 0.3 to 3.0 s with no clear line, melee Frames spent 1.2 to 9.0 s beside cover, and cyber Frames landed 1 to 17 hits with the relay and 0 to 13 without it. Plants stood on soil in four of the twelve rounds, for up to 8.0 s. Plants are 2 in 100 of the species rolls, so a sim that wants to read the soil rule needs many rounds. No relay went down in the twelve rounds (the lowest read 103 of 160). The first version moved a blocked range Frame sideways only, and in one round two range Frames stayed blocked for 34 s until the 45 s limit ended it. A blocked range Frame now walks around the block, and no round of the twelve reached the limit.

    The problem

    Each unit was one solid: a box, a cylinder, a sphere or a torus.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2379, where the desktop builds ship: the release that carries this game.
    • RFD66606-2085, RFD66606-2091 and RFD66606-2120, the Gyre setting (abandoned): the source of Frames, wear and scrip.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2321-the-autobattler-fields-frames-that-wear.exs

    RFD66606-2320: an agent drives the OXRSys simulator through cua-driver

    State: committed Feature: an MCP agent session on the Mac launches, sees and drives the OXRSys Simulator through cua-driver, in the background Scope: XR Pilot’s oxrsys/docs/xr-cua-oxrsys.md and oxrsys/scripts/xr-cua-oxrsys-register.sh

    An agent sees and drives the OXRSys Simulator on the Mac without taking the operator’s focus.

    The simulator is a desktop window. Without a way for an agent to see it and give it input, every simulator run needed a person at the keyboard.

    An agent drives the OXRSys Simulator on the Mac through cua-driver’s own MCP server, registered under the name xr-cua-oxrsys. It launches the simulator, reads the decoded preview as pixels and the control row as accessibility elements, and sends keys, clicks, typing and scrolls into the view. Every call runs in the background: no focus change and no cursor move, so the operator keeps working in another window. The operator ruled it done on 2026-10-17.

    Run scripts/xr-cua-oxrsys-register.sh to register xr-cua-oxrsys; it prints the diff.

    Setup

    cua-driver is installed once on the Mac and reused across projects. Its accessibility and screen-recording grants belong to the driver app, not to the terminal that runs the agent. scripts/xr-cua-oxrsys-register.sh writes the xr-cua-oxrsys entry (command cua-driver, argument mcp) into the agent’s MCP settings, keeps every other server and prints the diff. A running session picks the entry up when it reconnects its MCP servers.

    Where it landed

    XR Pilot’s repository, commit “Add xr-cua-oxrsys as the automation surface for the simulator” (2026-10-01): the document and the installer, 91 lines in two files. The plan tool landed there in “Add a plan tool that acts out a taskweft RECTGTN task network” (2026-10-04).

    What it leaves out

    • The headset side, a second server reached over SSH, is not on main. The document places it on the Flow 2 branch, and docs/platforms/ does not exist on main (read 2026-10-17).
    • The simulator does not ship with cua-driver.
    • The name ends in -oxrsys so it does not clash with the headset-side server.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2235, the agent that plans with taskweft through the editor, done in desktop mode through XR Pilot’s plan tool.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.
