    RFD66606-2319: a serving host’s certificate comes from agent CA v2

    State: committed Feature: a host that serves on the tailnet gets a server certificate for its own agent identity, signed by Bao’s agent CA v2 without the root token Scope: weftspun-bao’s pki-agents and pki-agents-v2 mounts, the csr-signer policy, and every stunnel or edge endpoint that serves under an agent identity

    A serving host gets its tailnet server certificate from agent CA v2, with no root token.

    Bao has two agent CAs, and nothing said which one does what. Bao signs a certificate in pki-agents that names the tailnet host anyway, and every client then rejects it.

    A host that serves takes a second certificate for its agent name from the pki-agents-v2 mount, through role agent-endpoint. That role sets server and client use, allows *.agents.weftspun, *.stonecat-ratio.ts.net and tailnet addresses, caps a certificate at 90 days and stores no record of it. The csr-signer policy may sign through it, so an agent identity issues an endpoint certificate without the root token. The key is made on the host and never leaves it.

    Read below for the mounts and the agent-endpoint role.

    What failed

    pki-agents holds the agent CA, whose name constraints allow only chibifire.com and agents.weftspun. On 2026-10-16 a server certificate for the Linux 4090 host failed this way.

    Sources

    Read on 2026-10-16 from the live cluster through the active weftspun-fdb machine: each mount’s CA certificate and name constraints, the csr-signer policy, and the issuers on pki-agents. The Authority Information Access field of the Mac’s own server certificate named pki-agents-v2, which is how that mount was found.

    The mounts

    • pki-agents: issuer chibifire.com agent CA, constrained to chibifire.com and agents.weftspun. An agent signs with agent-client: client use only, 1 year.
    • pki-agents-v2: issuer chibifire.com agent CA v2, constrained to the two above, stonecat-ratio.ts.net and 100.64.0.0/10. An agent signs with agent-endpoint (this RFD).
    • pki: issuer Intermediate CA v2, no constraints read. No agent role; its key is unreadable on the node.
    • pki-listener: issuer bao listener CA, constrained to Bao’s own names. Bao’s listener only.

    Every issuer chains to the chibifire.com Root CA, so a client that trusts the Root (~/.bao.d/server-ca.pem on the Mac) verifies both agent CAs.

    The role

    pki-agents-v2/roles/agent-endpoint
  allowed_domains   agents.weftspun,stonecat-ratio.ts.net
  allow_subdomains  true
  allow_ip_sans     true
  enforce_hostnames true
  server_flag       true
  client_flag       true
  use_csr_sans      true
  ttl, max_ttl      2160h
  no_store          true

    With no_store, Bao keeps no copy and cannot revoke the certificate. Each one expires within 90 days, which is the revocation (RFD66606-2316). The login certificate an agent already holds stays as it is; the endpoint certificate is a second one for the same name.

    Issuing one

    1. On the host, make a P-256 key and a request whose config file carries extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth,clientAuth and the subject names: the agent name, the host’s stonecat-ratio.ts.net name and its tailnet address.
    2. Copy only the request off the host. An agent signs it with pki-agents-v2/sign/agent-endpoint under its own cert login.
    3. Install the leaf with agent CA v2 after it as the full chain, and leave the Root out of the chain.

    Witnesses

    • Chain. openssl verify -purpose sslserver of the leaf against the Root, with agent CA v2 as the untrusted intermediate, prints OK. The same request signed on pki-agents fails with error 47, permitted subtree violation.
    • Use. A client-only agent-client leaf fails the same check with error 26, unsupported certificate purpose.
    • Signer. bao token capabilities pki-agents-v2/sign/agent-endpoint under an agent cert login returns create and update.

    The first two controls were run on 2026-10-16 and failed as planted, and the passing case ran the same day on the certificate below.

    What went wrong first

    On 2026-10-16 the role was written on pki-agents, the mount the client role lives on. It signed a certificate for the Linux host that failed error 47, and that certificate (serial 28:01:5a:de) was revoked the same hour. A role named agent-endpoint already existed there and was overwritten without being read, so its earlier settings are lost. The csr-signer policy gained pki-agents/sign/agent-endpoint in the same write. Both were removed later that day, when the role was written on pki-agents-v2.

    pki-agents-v2 already carried agent-endpoint and agent-client, both allowing agents.weftspun, stonecat-ratio.ts.net and tailnet addresses. The existing agent-endpoint had a one-year ceiling and stored each certificate; this RFD’s write changed it to 90 days and no_store. The Mac’s own server certificate came from that role before the change.

    The operator then requested the old settings back. Only the root token can write the role, and it sits in the password manager, which routine work does not use. The operator kept the 90-day role and had both certificates rotated through it instead.

    The certificates in use

    Both were rotated on 2026-10-16 with a fresh P-256 key made on each host and signed by the Mac agent identity with no root token. Each is valid to 2027-01-14, passes the chain gate, and matches its key.

    • fedora-9a6c28.agents.weftspun, serial 5d:9c:e6:f3, at ~/.bao-creds/fedora-9a6c28/srv-fullchain.pem. It replaces serial 21:f0:0c:1d, issued earlier the same day, never served, and deleted with its key.
    • mac-mini-fire-01b8f5.agents.weftspun, serial 3e:dd:70:c0, at ~/.bao-creds/mac-mini-fire-01b8f5/srv-fullchain.pem. It replaces serial 60:1e:4b:98, a one-year certificate from the old role. No agent identity may revoke on pki-agents-v2, so that one stays valid to 2027-10-12; nothing on the Mac reads it.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2142 (Bao PKI service TLS), the first PKI mount.
    • RFD66606-2145 (certificate lifetimes), the 90-day leaf ceiling.
    • RFD66606-2316 (Bao bounded storage), why no record is stored.
    • RFD66606-2311 (Bonsai 2 serving), the first host to need this.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2319-a-serving-hosts-certificate-comes-from-agent-ca-v2.exs

    RFD66606-2316: Bao holds a bounded set

    State: discussion Feature: Bao’s storage stays the same size whatever the number of users, sessions or requests Scope: weftspun-bao on weftspun-fdb, every secrets engine and auth method mounted on it, and the plugins built for it

    Bao stays the same size however many users, sessions or requests arrive.

    Bao’s default is to keep a lease for every dynamic secret, so an engine on the defaults grows with its traffic until a write fails.

    • Bao stores keys, configuration, policies and ReBAC tuples, and nothing that grows with users, sessions or requests (operator, 2026-10-13).
    • An engine that issues a credential per request keeps no lease and no record of it. The credential carries its own expiry and is never revoked.
    • Application data lives outside Bao, in the service that owns it.
    • Every engine ships a growth gate: issuing many credentials leaves the engine’s storage unchanged, and a control that stores each one fails it.

    Read RFD66606-2317 next, the first engine held to this rule.

    Why the limit is part of the design

    FoundationDB refuses a value over 100,000 bytes and a transaction over 10,000,000 bytes, so the limit is part of the design and not a setting.

    Sources

    Written on 2026-10-13 from the operator’s note that Bao has a hard data limit by design. The FDB backend was read in our OpenBao fork: Put calls one Set with the whole encrypted entry and splits nothing. The value and transaction limits are FoundationDB’s published known limits. Neither limit has been measured on our cluster yet; the first engine’s end-to-end test writes an entry just under and just over 100,000 bytes and records which one FDB refuses.

    What may be stored

    An entry belongs in Bao when the count of such entries is set by the operator, not by traffic:

    • signing keys, CA keys and certificates of issuers;
    • engine and mount configuration;
    • policies, cert roles and ReBAC tuples;
    • one-off secrets an operator puts there, such as an API token.

    These do not belong in Bao:

    • a lease or record per issued credential;
    • sessions, messages, counters, logs or audit trails of a service;
    • files and blobs of any size.

    An engine that needs to hold a resource for a while, such as a slot in a shared cap, may still use a lease, because the number of leases is capped by the resource and not by traffic. Its growth gate then checks that the lease count stays at or under the cap.

    The growth gate

    Each engine’s unit tests run against logical.InmemStorage and count its keys with a recursive List before and after issuing 1,000 credentials. The gate passes when the count and the summed value size are unchanged. The control flips the engine to store each credential and must fail the same gate. The end-to-end test does the same against a dev server and also checks that the response carries no lease id.

    The problem

    Bao’s storage is FoundationDB on three small machines, and the FDB backend writes each entry as one FDB value.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2140, Bao on FDB.
    • RFD66606-2353, Bao runs three replicas on the FDB machines.
    • RFD66606-2200, ReBAC agent roles.
    • RFD66606-2317, the first engine held to this rule.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2316-bao-holds-a-bounded-set.exs

    RFD66606-2312: release tags are go pseudo-versions

    State: committed Feature: a release tag is the Go pseudo-version of the commit it points at, so every tag sorts by time in a file listing and parses as a version in every package tool Scope: release tags in the V-Sekai-fire and chibifire-stages repositories, cut from 2026-10-13 on, and scripts/check_release_tags.exs

    A release tag is computed from its commit, so it sorts by time and parses everywhere.

    The orgs’ releases carry four naming schemes and no rule. No single scheme among them sorts by time in a file listing and also parses as a version in Mix, Cargo, npm and Go.

    A release tag is v0.0.0-<time>-<hash>: the tagged commit’s committer time in UTC as YYYYMMDDhhmmss, then the first 12 hex digits of the commit. It is the shape of a Go pseudo-version, and it is computed from the commit, never typed. The core stays v0.0.0. A stage, a rung name or a “1.0” goes in the release title and the stage branch, not in the tag. The operator chose the form on 2026-10-12 (“I like go’s”).

    Run elixir scripts/check_release_tags.exs to recompute every tag, and read below for the later parts.

    The three parts

    The tag is the first of three parts of one release system. Each part does one job: identity is a hash, order is a fixed-width UTC time, stage is a pointer that moves, and compatibility is a version on the interface that breaks. The details give the later parts.

    Sources

    Drafted on 2026-10-12 from the release inventory, the sort runs and the parser runs below, all taken the same day. The form and the “everywhere” bar are the operator’s.

    What a tag has to satisfy

    The operator’s bar: a tag sorts in filesystem order, and the same string works everywhere a version is read. Measured on 2026-10-12, each candidate through each tool’s own parser:

    Candidate ls order Mix Cargo npm Go
    v2026.01.05, padded calendar date yes no no no no
    v2026.1.5, unpadded calendar date no yes yes yes yes
    v1.0.0-beta.1 and v1.0.0 no yes yes yes yes
    v0.0.0-20261012203512-50cc405a1b2c yes yes yes yes yes
    • SemVer forbids a leading zero in a number, so a padded month fails every package tool. Unpadded, 2026.10.12 sorts before 2026.9.1.
    • No file listing puts a release after its own pre-releases: ls, sort -V and Finder all list v1.0.0 before v1.0.0-beta.1.
    • The Go form carries the date inside one alphanumeric pre-release field, where SemVer allows the zeros. ls, sort -V and Finder each put samples from January, October, the next day and the next year in time order.
    • Python’s PEP 440 rejects the Go form. A Python package from the same commit is 0.0.0.devYYYYMMDDhhmmss. Docker’s tag grammar admits the form; no Docker daemon ran in the measurement.

    What others do

    Read off the live registries on 2026-10-12. Builds between releases put an ISO basic date inside the pre-release: TypeScript 7.1.0-dev.20261012.1, React 19.3.0-canary-9f2e1f88-20261012, Node.js v27.0.0-nightly202610123b639be3a4, Go v0.0.0-20261011100332-faecfb24eb49. Calendar versions that must stay SemVer drop the padding: pip 26.2.1, Home Assistant 2026.10.1. Projects that list versions as strings pad instead: the Arch Linux ISOs, YYYY.0M.0D since 2012. Only Go’s form, whose core never moves, sorts as plain bytes and parses as SemVer at once.

    The check

    scripts/check_release_tags.exs recomputes every tag from its commit:

    elixir scripts/check_release_tags.exs [<repo>]
elixir scripts/check_release_tags.exs --self-test

    A tag on a commit from before 2026-10-13 is legacy, counted and named rather than failed; renaming a published tag breaks whatever points at it. The self-test plants six tags in a scratch repository. The commit’s own pseudo-version passes; a seven-digit hash, a local-time stamp, a v1.0.0 core, a padded calendar date and a stage-suffixed date each fail by name; a pre-cutover tag reads as legacy. Go’s own module.IsPseudoVersion accepts a seven-digit hash, so the 12-digit rule is this check’s, not Go’s. Go does hold a pseudo-version to its commit’s time and hash, which is why the tag is computed:

    TZ=UTC git log -1 --format='v0.0.0-%cd-%h' \
  --date=format-local:%Y%m%d%H%M%S --abbrev=12

    The later parts

    Each part starts once the one before it runs.

    1. The tag, this RFD.
    2. The stage is a pointer. A moving tag per stage (dev, beta, rc, release) names the build that stage holds. Promotion moves the pointer to the same commit; nothing is rebuilt or renamed. The GitHub pre-release flag follows the pointer.
    3. One release record per repository, and every other format derived from it. The Godot engine already works this way: version.py holds major, minor, patch and status; the build adds the commit hash and committer timestamp from git; the Windows resource takes FILEVERSION from the numbers; the Android build turns the status into a digit of versionCode (dev 1, alpha 2, beta 3). Here the record is the repository’s CITATION.cff (operator, 2026-10-12), in two halves. The committed file holds what does not change per build: title, authors, licence, the interface versions. A commit cannot carry its own hash, so the release step writes the per-build half into the copy that ships with the artifact: version is the tag, commit the full hash, date-released the UTC date. CFF 1.2.0 admits no other top-level key; a status key fails its schema. The stage, the derived forms and the artifact digests ride as identifiers of type other: stage:dev, windows:YYYY.MMDD.hhmm.0, android:<versionCode>, pep440:0.0.0.devYYYYMMDDhhmmss, sha256:<digest>. A sample of that shape validates against the CFF 1.2.0 JSON schema. The check recomputes every derived value from the commit field.
    4. Compatibility rides on the interface that breaks: a protocol, ABI or save-format version that moves only when that interface does, as Go moves a module path to /v2.
    5. A signed attestation binds the record to the artifact’s digest.

    The problem

    Of 60 GitHub releases in repositories pushed since 2026-06-01, 33 are SemVer pre-releases in at least four spellings, 7 are dates, 2 are plain SemVer and 18 are free names.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2294, interchangeable sessions: the stage branches this RFD leaves the stage to.
    • RFD66606-2295, calibrated replies: the times here are UTC, as there.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2312-release-tags-are-go-pseudo-versions.exs

    RFD66606-2311: serving bonsai 2 with ninfer-all and dflash2

    State: committed Feature: each card serves Ternary Bonsai 2 27B through ninfer-all with a DFlash2 drafter of five tokens, and this RFD is how to set that up again from nothing on any Fedora 44 host Scope: the V-Sekai-fire/ninfer-all fork, the t2 .ninfer artifact, one systemd unit per card on Fedora 44 (native or WSL2), the mTLS front and the client’s single router port

    Each card serves Bonsai 2 through ninfer-all with a DFlash2 drafter, set up from nothing.

    No RFD decided how a card serves Bonsai 2, and the setup lived in agents’ notes, tied to whichever machine held the cards that week.

    A Bonsai 2 language server is ninfer-all serving the t2 bonsai2-27b-heretic.ninfer artifact with --spec dflash2 --draft-tokens 5, one server per card, each a systemd unit on Fedora 44, native or in WSL2. Each server binds loopback only and takes an API key. stunnel with mutual TLS is the only way in from off the host. Clients reach every server through one router port. Fedora 44 is the only supported OS (operator, 2026-10-17).

    Build the engine and the host as the sections below say, then run the witnesses.

    The choice

    The operator chose the engine and drafter on 2026-10-12 (“The ninfer with dflash won”) after the A-B-A run in the details.

    Blocklist

    • BLOCKLIST.md, “Speculative decoders other than MTP-3” and “1-bit PTQ1_0 bodies”, both for the ggml language server.

    Sources

    Drafted on 2026-10-12 from an A-B-A run on one RTX 4090. Rewritten on 2026-10-17 to describe the setup rather than the machines it ran on, after the operator unshipped the fork’s Windows support and kept Fedora 44, native or WSL2.

    The measurement

    One RTX 4090, the same launcher flags on every arm (--max-context 262144, --kv-dtype rk8v4, --vision, one request at a time), three repetitions, temperature 0, 512 generated tokens, speeds read from the server’s own timings. Arms ran A-B-A so the repeated arm shows drift. Decode in tokens per second:

    Arm chat code story
    ninfer-all, DFlash2 K=5 218-232 314-360 176-187
    prebuilt engine, MTP-3 206-226 279-282 176-184
    ninfer-all, MTP-3 193-206 239-267 164-172
    • Prefill on ninfer-all is about 10% faster at 3k prompt tokens.
    • Story is a tie inside the spread. ninfer-all with MTP-3 is the slowest arm, so the gain needs both the engine and the drafter.
    • Temperature-0 text differs between the two engines and between the two drafters inside ninfer-all.
    • The prebuilt engine cannot run DFlash2 on this artifact without --lm-head-draft, and with it DFlash2 was slower than its MTP-3 on every workload.

    The artifact

    bonsai2-27b-heretic.ninfer, format t2_g128_fp16, with the vision tower, the MTP head and the DFlash2 head inside it. The converter is pure Python and runs on the CPU, with recipe bonsai2_27b_ternary from the Heretic PQ2_0 body and the Bonsai-trained MTP and DFlash2 heads. The four sources and the artifact are published in the public dataset chibifire/ninfer-bonsai2-heretic (operator, 2026-10-12), with a sha256 to check a download against.

    Every input is Apache-2.0: Qwen3.8-27B, Ternary Bonsai 2 27B, the Heretic v2 modification, the MTP and DFlash2 heads and the weights they adapt. The dataset carries their licence and notice files, a root NOTICE that names each author and states the conversion, and an Apache-2.0 card.

    A published artifact names no host path. A workflow in the fork converts on a clean runner and fails on any of the runner’s directories in the artifact or its report, after a planted path is caught.

    The prebuilt engine reads only t5_g128_fp16, and ninfer-all reads only t2_g128_fp16. An artifact from one family does not load in the other. The artifact cannot take --lm-head-q6; with it the server exits at startup.

    Building the engine

    v-sekai/build.nu in the fork builds on Fedora 44, native or WSL2, inside the fork’s pixi build environment, which carries the compilers, CUDA, git, strip and gh. The host needs only curl to fetch pixi; git runs through pixi exec. The output is dist/linux (the programs and their library closure) and dist/tools-linux/ninfer-install.

    • One build compiles for one CUDA architecture; CMake refuses a list.
    • An sm_86 build runs on an RTX 3090 and an RTX 4090, so one build serves both cards of a two-card host.
    • In WSL2 the build drops the Windows entries from PATH, because CMake’s package search over the 9p bridge takes minutes per lookup.

    The host layout

    • /opt/ninfer/bin and /opt/ninfer/lib come from dist/linux and are checked against its SHA256SUMS. /opt/ninfer/models holds the artifact, checked against the dataset’s sha256.

    • A system user ninference runs the servers. The key is NINFER_API_KEY= in /etc/ninfer/env, root-only, read by systemd.

    • One unit per card, ninfer-serve-<card>.service, enabled, restarting on any exit. It sets CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID and picks the card with --device, adds /opt/ninfer/lib to the library path (and /usr/lib/wsl/lib in WSL2), and runs:

      ninfer-serve /opt/ninfer/models/bonsai2-27b-heretic.ninfer
  --device <n> --host 127.0.0.1 --port <port> --api-key ${NINFER_API_KEY}
  --model-id bonsai-27b --max-context 262144 --kv-capacity 262144
  --kv-dtype rk8v4 --vision --max-concurrency 1
  --spec dflash2 --draft-tokens 5 --no-thinking

    • The binary takes the key only on its command line, so a shell on the host sees it in /proc, ps and systemctl status. Mask --api-key whenever processes or units are listed.

    • In WSL2 the distribution stops when no Windows process holds it, and its units stop with it. A logon task keeps one process running in it.

    Reaching it

    stunnel accepts on the host’s tailnet address, one port per card, and forwards to the server’s loopback port. It requires a client certificate under the chibifire Root and agent CA, and checks the client’s host name against an allowlist. Its own certificate comes from RFD66606-2319. In WSL2 the tailnet address belongs to Windows, so stunnel runs there and forwards to the loopback port that WSL2 forwards into the distribution.

    On the client, a stunnel client maps each server to a local port, and a LiteLLM proxy (v-sekai/router/ in the fork) puts all of them behind one port and one key. Its bonsai model goes to the least busy live server and skips one that is down; a name per card selects one server. Hermes calls only the router.

    Witnesses

    Each one carries a control that must fail.

    • Ready. GET /v1/models through the tunnel returns 200 with the key, and 401 without a key and with a wrong one.
    • Spec. The unit’s command line, key masked, carries --spec dflash2 --draft-tokens 5, and the server log reports draft acceptance above zero.
    • Vision. v-sekai/vision_zero_shot_probe.py against the tunnel names the red circle, the blue square and the text 42. A text-only server returns an error on the same request.
    • mTLS. The allowlisted client gets an HTTP answer. No certificate, and a certificate for a second client under the same CA, are both refused, the second with a subject-check failure.
    • Answer. The same temperature-0 code prompt gives the same answer hash on a rerun and after a reinstall on the same card.
    • Speed. Three reps of a 512-token code answer at temperature 0 land inside the card’s previous runs. A number without that baseline is not reported.

    Pitfalls

    • Check that the files the running server holds still exist before a restart. A server keeps serving from a deleted model file, and the restart then fails with startup failed | inspecting artifact.
    • CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID changes which card a device index names. Read nvidia-smi in the same order before choosing --device; a build for a newer architecture fails on an older card with no kernel image.
    • Wait for the ready line listening on with a journal cursor taken before the restart, not with a timestamp.
    • An A/B that swaps --spec restores the unit in the same script on failure, because a server that dies at startup leaves its card down.

    Open questions

    • The decider benchmark behind the MTP-3 blocklist row has not been run on ninfer-all. Until it is, the row and this RFD measure different workloads, and neither says which drafter makes better decisions.
    • MTP’s upstream advantage is a second request lane (--max-concurrency 2). Every arm here served one request at a time.
    • DFlash2 at six and seven draft tokens is measured on one card only.
    • The unit and stunnel files are written by hand on each host and are in no repository.

    The problem

    Every move of the cards rebuilt it by hand.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2308 (Mac ninfer port), which uses this server as its reference.
    • RFD66606-2319 (endpoint certificates), where the front’s certificate comes from.
    • RFD66606-2310 (eye-landmark scorer), which calls this server.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2311-serving-bonsai-2-with-ninfer-all-and-dflash2.exs

    RFD66606-2307: recording the xr pilot stream to cineform

    State: committed Feature: XR Pilot keeps the runtime’s PyroWave packets as they arrive and a separate step decodes them on an idle GPU into a CineForm intermediate Scope: XR Pilot and its MCP server, the pyro2cfhd and frames2cfhd tools, the CineForm SDK build, and the av1mkv delivery of a recording

    A recording keeps the runtime’s own video stream and encodes it later on an idle GPU.

    Encoding live on the VR GPU would compete with the compositor, which an overload had already killed twice that day.

    A recording is the runtime’s own video stream, not a screen capture. The pilot appends each PyroWave packet to a .pwrec file with its presentation and receive times and does no encoding while VR runs. A one-shot job later decodes the packets on the GPU that is not driving VR and encodes CineForm on the CPU. The CineForm file is the intermediate the delivery step wraps as MKV with a .cff (operator, 2026-10-09).

    The shared desk is run as the open work below records.

    Superseded by nut-based ffmpeg recording

    Recording moved to nut-based ffmpeg and works, so this RFD is committed (operator, 2026-11-11). The .pwrec and CineForm steps below are the earlier design and stay as history.

    The packet file

    .pwrec starts with the magic PWREC, two zero bytes and a version byte. Each frame is a u64 presentation time in ns, a u64 receive time in ns, a u32 index, a u32 byte count and the payload, at most 256 MiB. A pilot that restarts writes the next file with .1.pwrec. xr-pilot --record-stream and the MCP server’s --record-stream <out> write it.

    The decode step

    pyro2cfhd <in.pwrec> <out.cfhd> takes --fps, --size, --quality and --gpu (a PCI vendor and device pair). It runs as a one-shot task on the GPU without VR. frames2cfhd does the same from PNG frames. Both share one fit and RIFF writer.

    • The CineForm RIFF file stops at 4 GB.
    • The MKV writer built with llvm-mingw fails past 2 GB.
    • Full-rate 4K therefore needs a container writer fix before it ships.

    Building CineForm with MSVC

    Two changes let the CineForm SDK build with MSVC on the desk: simd_compat.h includes malloc.h for the aligned allocators, which MSVC has in place of mm_malloc.h; lutpath.cpp declares its registry value name LPCTSTR, so string literals assign to it under strict strings. The llvm-mingw build of av1mkv needs the toolchain’s libc++ and libunwind DLLs beside it, or it exits with 0xc00004bc.

    Motion that does not stutter

    Walking was integrated in the 60 Hz window loop while the tracking sender ran at a fixed 90 Hz, so one packet in three repeated a pose. The sender now runs at the runtime’s announced refresh rate, clamped to 60 to 144 Hz, and moves held keys by real elapsed time; the window applies mouse look only. The wheel scales walk speed by 1.25 per notch, from 0.25 to 8 m/s; with Shift it moves the hand’s reach. A 3D head gizmo draws yaw and pitch as arcs, so a trace shows when the head looks straight up or down.

    Open work

    • Run the pyro2cfhd self-test on the desk’s second GPU, then record a real two-minute stream and deliver it.
    • Count compositor sync timeouts in the driver and give the sparklines fault thresholds, set from the sweep this RFD records.

    The problem

    The first two-minute sweep was saved as left-eye PNG frames and encoded at 10 fps, because a full-rate 4K clip passes the size limits of the CineForm RIFF writer and of the MKV writer built with llvm-mingw.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2303, the XR requirements; RFD66606-2365, the recording rules.
    • RFD66606-2306, operating the shared desk; RFD66606-2302, the frame budget.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2307-recording-the-xr-pilot-stream-to-cineform.exs

    RFD66606-2295: agent replies state calibrated confidence

    State: committed Feature: an agent tags every unverified claim with a word and a probability, (likely, p=0.80), from one fixed scale Scope: agent replies to the operator, logbook entries, the times and closing questions in both, and scripts/check_confidence_tags.py

    An unverified claim carries its confidence as a word and a probability.

    Agent replies stated forecasts and diagnoses in the same voice as checked facts. A reader cannot weigh a claim that does not say how sure it is.

    A claim an agent has not verified carries its confidence as a word and a probability in one tag: (likely, p=0.80). The word comes from a fixed scale of five, and the number must fall inside that word’s band. A verified fact (a command’s output, a merged pull request, a passing gate) carries no tag. scripts/check_confidence_tags.py reads the bands from this RFD’s source and fails any tag whose word and number disagree, so the scale and the gate cannot drift apart.

    Run scripts/check_confidence_tags.py to check that each tag’s number fits its word.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    The scale

    The gate reads this table. A tag’s number must lie inside its word’s band, lower bound inclusive and upper bound exclusive, except that almost certain includes 1.00.

    word lower upper
    remote 0.00 0.10
    unlikely 0.10 0.40
    even 0.40 0.60
    likely 0.60 0.90
    almost certain 0.90 1.00

    The tag

    The form is (word, p=0.NN): the word, a comma, p= and the probability with two decimals. It follows the claim it qualifies:

    The walker stays bit-deterministic (likely, p=0.75).
The 12 modules finish today (unlikely, p=0.25).

    Only unverified claims carry a tag. A claim the agent checked in the same turn states the check instead of a probability, because a probability on a checked fact would hide that it was checked.

    Calibration

    The numbers mean something only if they are calibrated: of the claims tagged p=0.80, about four in five should turn out true. A logbook entry that records tagged forecasts also records how they resolved, so the tags can be scored. No such score exists yet; the first logbook entry to carry tagged forecasts starts it.

    Times

    A time in a reply, a logbook entry, an issue comment or a pull request is written in ISO 8601 with its date and UTC offset: 2026-10-02T09:51-07:00, not 09:51 or 11am. A forecast’s deadline is the same kind of time, so tagged by 2026-10-02T11:00-07:00 is scorable by a reader in another zone or on another day.

    A piece of work is timed as an ISO 8601 interval, start and end, followed by its duration (operator, 2026-10-02): 2026-10-02T20:12:48+00:00/2026-10-02T20:40:10+00:00, PT27M22S. Work still running gives its start and open. No gate checks this yet; it holds by agreement.

    Known unknowns

    A plan or a recommendation ends with zero to four questions about the known unknowns whose answers would change it, each answerable in one word with the recommended option marked. None are asked when nothing is unknown, and never more than four (operator, 2026-10-02). Replies are not files, so this holds by agreement.

    Related

    Lin, Hilton and Evans, “Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words” (2022, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2205.14334, registered with DataCite) is the method: a model states its confidence in words and numbers, and the statement is scored for calibration. RFD66606-2294 (agent knowledge lives in RFDs) is why the rule is here and not in a desk’s memory. CLAUDE.md’s “How Work Is Verified” rule 3 (a silent skip reads like a pass) is why a verified fact and a guess must look different.

    What is checked

    scripts/check_confidence_tags.py scans logbook/*.md and every RFD source for tags, and fails a tag whose word is not on the scale or whose number falls outside the word’s band. Its self-test plants one tag of each kind, a correct one, an unknown word and a number outside its band, and asserts the gate passes the first and fails the other two. Replies are not files, so the gate cannot see them; the rule holds there by agreement.

    The problem

    On 2026-10-02 a reply described a Metal shader port as “Slang-to-MSL” when the shaders were hand-written, and the operator caught it. A bare percentage reads as code rather than as language.

    Source: rfd/2295-agent-replies-state-calibrated-confidence.exs

    RFD66606-2294: agent knowledge lives in RFDs, not in desk memory

    State: discussion Feature: where an agent session keeps what it learns about V-Sekai-fire and chibifire-stages, and the operator’s rules that lived in one desk’s memory, written down Scope: this repository, CLAUDE.md, every agent session’s local memory, and the rules below

    What any agent learns about V-Sekai-fire and chibifire-stages lives in an RFD, not a desk.

    An agent session’s memory is a directory on one desk, so no session sees every rule.

    What any agent needs to know about V-Sekai-fire and chibifire-stages, their repositories, the headset and the services lives in an RFD in this repository: the RFD that owns the topic, or this one when none does. A desk’s local memory keeps only what is true of that desk alone, such as its paths, its identities and its tools. A local note about a generic rule names the RFD that states it.

    Write a generic rule into its RFD in the same session; the sections below hold the steps.

    Writing a generic rule down

    An agent that learns a generic rule writes it into the RFD in the same session, through a pull request like any other change.

    What lived on one desk

    On 2026-10-01 the operator’s rules for locomotion, offline deployment, video and the station lived only on the Mac desk, and those for where compute runs and for binary translation only on the Windows desks, so no session saw all of them.

    Starting out in the workspace

    A new agent, a small local model included, starts here and does one step at a time. It begins right after the bootstrap script has run.

    1. The bootstrap leaves a workspace root holding .repo/, AGENTS.md and the placed projects. Every path below is relative to that root. ls .repo and repo list confirm it. If repo, elixir, mix or python is missing, ask the operator; don’t install tools yourself.
    2. Read AGENTS.md at the workspace root, then this RFD.
    3. The workspace is a repo client. .repo/manifests/default.xml (the taskweft manifest repository) places every project on a side of the hexagon: 2-contract/, 3-interactor/, 4-entities/, 5-repository/, 6-datasource/, 7-service/. repo list shows what is placed.
    4. Sync with elixir .repo/manifests/sync.exs . --preflight first, then elixir .repo/manifests/sync.exs .. A project the preflight names as blocking gets a decision from the operator, not a guess. One that blocks because another session works in it moves its branch to a worktree, uncommitted edits carried by git stash, and then syncs (operator, 2026-10-18).
    5. Never edit a placed checkout in place. Make a worktree in a scratch directory on a new dev/<topic> branch: git -C <project> worktree add <scratch>/<name> -b dev/<topic> <remote>/main, using the project’s own remote and default branch.
    6. Commit subjects are sentence-case prose with no feat: prefix and no trailing period, forks included (RFD66606-2026). Commits and pull requests carry no Claude attribution: no Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer and no “Generated with Claude Code” line. Credit to people stays, such as a co-author trailer for the person whose work a commit carries. “Interchangeable sessions” below names the commit author and how to strip a footer a tool appends. Push only the feature branch, and open the pull request in V-Sekai-fire or chibifire-stages, where the operator merges it.
    7. Remove the worktree when the pull request is open.

    An RFD is amended in rfd/NNNN-slug.exs of manuals-weftspun (2-contract/manuals-weftspun), never in the rendered Markdown, which is a build artifact:

    1. Find the RFD that owns the topic with grep -l <word> rfd/*.exs. Use this one when none does.
    2. Edit its decision or one of its details blocks in the tenseless present (RFD66606-2172). A statement that is no longer true is deleted, not retracted. Name the operator and date for an operator’s decision.
    3. A new RFD takes the next serial in SERIALS.exs and carries the sentence “This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.”
    4. Run mix rfd.render, python scripts/check_tropes.py --base <remote>/main and python scripts/check-rfd-structure.py. All three pass before the push.
    5. Keep product names and other organisations’ issue or PR references out of the text, and cite an upstream change by its bare commit SHA.

    A worked example, typed into Git Bash on the Windows desk. It adds a sentence to this RFD:

    cd <workspace root>/2-contract/manuals-weftspun
git fetch v-sekai-fire main
git worktree add "$TEMP/rfd-edit" -b dev/rfd-my-topic v-sekai-fire/main
cd "$TEMP/rfd-edit"

    Open rfd/2294-agent-knowledge-lives-in-rfds-not-in-desk-memory.exs, add the sentence inside the right details block, and save. Then:

    mix rfd.render
python scripts/check_tropes.py --base v-sekai-fire/main
python scripts/check-rfd-structure.py
git commit -am "RFD66606-2294: say what the sentence makes true"
git -c \
  core.hooksPath="<workspace root>/.repo/projects/2-contract/manuals-weftspun.git/hooks" \
  push v-sekai-fire dev/rfd-my-topic
gh pr create -R V-Sekai-fire/manuals-weftspun --base main --fill
cd <workspace root>/2-contract/manuals-weftspun
git worktree remove "$TEMP/rfd-edit"

    The push names the hooks directory by absolute path because a placed checkout’s .git is a link into .repo/projects/, which Git Bash cannot follow. Given the relative path, the pre-push hook dies before running its gates. Never skip the hook with --no-verify. With no GitHub credentials, stop after the commit and give the operator the branch name. When any step fails, stop and ask the operator rather than guess.

    The work queue

    The agent sessions share one work-stealing queue, the issues labelled worksteal on contract-zone-backend (2-contract/zone-backend). Its protocol is pinned there as #58. An agent works its own queue newest first, and with nothing unclaimed steals the oldest unclaimed, unpinned issue from the fullest queue. A pinned issue needs one desk’s hardware or credentials and is never stolen. The queue applies backpressure: a queue holding three or more open issues, pinned ones included, is full, its agent files nothing new and finishes first, a follow-up found mid-task becomes a checklist line in the issue that found it, and an operator request is still filed, with the queue’s depth reported back so the operator can say what waits.

    Interchangeable sessions

    Any agent session, on a desk or in the cloud, can pick up any task another session started, because each follows the practices below and reads them here rather than from its own memory. A practice another RFD owns is named here and stated there. A desk’s memory, a project’s instructions, a skill or CLAUDE.md points at this section instead of restating it.

    • Attribution. Commits, pull requests, issue comments and reviews carry no agent credit: no agent Co-Authored-By trailer, no session link and no “Generated with” or “Generated by” footer. Commits are authored as K. S. Ernest (iFire) Lee <32321+fire@users.noreply.github.com>. The GitHub connector and gh append a footer on create, so each body is rewritten with an update call and read back before the task moves on, and dot-claude’s hooks/strip_claude_footer.py prompts that rewrite after every create (operator, 2026-10-02).
    • Where a session posts. Pull requests, issues, comments, reviews and discussions go only to repositories in V-Sekai-fire and chibifire-stages. A fix to a fork lands in our fork, and nothing is sent upstream. Reading another organisation’s code is fine (operator, 2026-10-05).
    • Automation. A new driver, gate or sheet builder is a plain Elixir script (.exs). Python appears only as a thin worker where a library has no other binding, such as Mitsuba’s renderer. A cloud session runs the Elixir gates on CI’s pinned toolchain, OTP 29 and Elixir 1.20.4 through erlef/setup-beam, never on a distribution’s packaged Elixir (operator, 2026-10-02).
    • Where work runs. A cloud session has no GPU and takes CPU-only work: headless Godot gates, the godot-sandbox tests, CPU Mitsuba (llvm_ad_rgb), the cloth fit on its CPU backend, and blend-shape matching through contract-lbfgsb (2-contract/lbfgsb). Its testing blocklists software GPU emulators: lavapipe and llvmpipe, SwiftShader, WARP, and Vulkan or Metal emulation. Work that needs a GPU (the persona, XR and headset runs, compute-rd and ggml runs, GPU sheet renders, macOS binaries) goes to the GPU desk rather than to an emulator. Timings are reported with milliseconds per frame (operator, 2026-10-02).
    • GPU Cloud and GPU-Free Cloud. Work split between the GPU desk’s session (“GPU Cloud”) and a cloud session (“GPU-Free Cloud”) is one checklist in one issue, as on contract-zone-backend#114. Each session ticks only its own items and comments when it starts, finishes or is blocked on one, with times in RFD66606-2295’s form. Neither takes the other’s items.
    • Branches. Every branch a session works on starts with a stage: dev/, beta/, rc/ or release/, and archived/ once its work is parked or superseded, whatever name the session was handed (operator, 2026-10-12). No feat/, fix/, wip/, main/ or bare names.
    • Capability-scoped workers. A worker session holds the capabilities its task needs as RFD66606-2200 tuples, and default deny covers the rest. A peer’s request never widens a worker’s rows.
    • Contact sheets. Release contact sheets are videos: the sphere_hammersley_sequence views are the columns and the fitting sequence is the frames. A CI job that shows a sheet renders it in that job and uploads it with actions/upload-artifact, so the sheet belongs to the run and the commit that made it. The colour reference is the lookdev-24 chart, entities-sakuragaoka-station (4-entities/sakuragaoka-station)’s tools/calib/chart24.json, and no commercial chart’s trademark appears in code or documents. RFD66606-2370 holds the cell layout.
    • Characters. A garment is fitted to a character’s body meshes only, and a character’s own clothing is not loaded beneath it unless the operator asks for layering. Maro is the dress-on statue a garment is drawn onto. Mire is the avatar (operator, 2026-10-02).
    • Replies. RFD66606-2295 owns their form: the calibrated confidence tag, ISO 8601 times and intervals, and the known-unknown questions that close a plan.
    • Outcomes. Every script, gate and helper reports each outcome as an Elixir-shaped term on a line of its own: {:ok, %{...}}, or {:error, :reason_atom, %{...}} with the facts a reader needs to act. Nothing exits silently: a non-zero exit with no term is a defect, and so is an :ok path that prints nothing. Machine output a caller parses (a host name, a token) goes to stdout bare and the term goes to stderr (operator, 2026-10-16). On 2026-10-16 bao-active-host exited 1 with no output when every tailnet instance was a standby, which hid where the leader was.

    scripts/check_practices.exs checks what a file or the GitHub API can show: a commit authored or committed as the agent identity, a commit subject that is not sentence-case prose (RFD66606-2026), agent credit in a commit message, a pull request body, a comment or a review, a software GPU emulator in a workflow, a workflow that renders a contact sheet without uploading an artifact, and a branch that does not start with a stage. Its self-test carries a control in each direction for each check. It is defined once, as the practices hook in this repository’s .pre-commit-hooks.yaml. Another repository lists that hook in its .pre-commit-config.yaml, where it runs on push, and its CI calls .github/workflows/practices.yml from here, which runs the same hook. Both pin a commit of this repository. This repository runs it as the ci-practices hook. Comments posted after the last run are seen at the next push or edit. The other practices hold by agreement.

    Merging

    An agent merges its own pull requests on V-Sekai-fire once they are green, through the merge queue where the repository has one. Where a repository requires no checks, --auto merges at once with its checks red, so there the agent waits for green and merges by hand. An agent may merge with the admin override (operator, 2026-10-30). The ban on it is rescinded.

    Bao and the tokens it mints

    Bao runs as tailnet nodes named weftspun-bao-N, and a desk uses whichever is online, keeping weftspun-bao.internal as the TLS server name. A desk logs in with its certificate, passing no role name, so the certificate selects the role. The login token is reused until its TTL lapses.

    A GitHub token is minted from github/token by the desk’s git credential helper on each request, never printed or stored. No token is revoked: each one expires on its own within the hour (operator, 2026-10-03).

    Agents may use Bao to pass data to each other. What is written there is stored in S3 for 30 days and then rolled over (operator, 2026-10-01): Bao’s storage is FoundationDB, whose backup goes to R2 (RFD66606-2143). An entry deleted from Bao stays in that copy until it rolls over.

    The problem

    A rule changed on one desk disagreed with the others without anyone being told.

    The tuples

    rfd-2294--provides--agent-knowledge-in-rfds
rfd-2294--is-a--workspace-policy

    Related

    • RFD66606-2200, the desk agent’s ReBAC rows.
    • RFD66606-2363 to RFD66606-2381 and RFD66606-2413 to RFD66606-2419, the rules this RFD held before the split, one RFD each.

    RFD66606-2292: the organization is one RECTGTN domain

    State: committed Feature: one Taskweft domain for the organization, one problem per RFD, and the plan it compiles to rendered into that RFD’s own Markdown Scope: RFD.RECTGTN, the steps block in RFD.DSL, mix rfd.rectgtn, rectgtn/organization.ex, rectgtn/problems/, and scripts/check_rectgtn_plan.exs

    Ask an RFD what comes next and get a plan, not a paragraph.

    RFD66606-2287 states its critical path as eight numbered paragraphs.

    The organization is the domain and each RFD is a problem against it. The domain holds the ladder an RFD climbs and what preparing a document, running a step and landing it are; a problem holds one RFD’s place on that ladder and the state of each step it declares.

    Run elixir scripts/check_rectgtn_plan.exs to hold each solution against the planner.

    The problem

    Written once as a domain, the question “what is next for this RFD” is a plan rather than a reading.

    Why a paragraph is the wrong shape

    A paragraph cannot be asked which step comes next, which steps are blocked, or what a failure costs, and the eight repeat a shape every rung of every ladder in this workspace already has: a step names a repository, what is missing, and the check it ends at.

    How the solution is held

    Both halves are Taskweft’s own Elixir DSL, rendered by mix rfd.rectgtn from the RFD sources, and Taskweft.Compose.compose_strings/2 merges a pair so the planner compiles it into a solution. That solution renders into the RFD’s DETAILS.md, and a gate holds it against what the planner returns.

    Where the declarations live

    A steps block inside an rfd block declares the critical path:

    steps do
  step "Build",
    repos: ["entities-godot", "the godot-sandbox addon"],
    missing: "the exported template_release build faults in a StringName copy",
    check: "an OpenXR session starts on each path and the pen scene draws in it",
    state: :failed
end

    repos and check are required, because a step nobody owns and a step that ends at nothing are the two ways a critical path rots. missing is what the step needs that does not exist yet, control is the planted defect its check must catch, and state is where the step stands. A step declared parked states what it is missing, so parking is never silent.

    Why the Elixir DSL and not JSON-LD

    Taskweft reads a domain written in its own Elixir DSL, and Taskweft.Compose.compose_strings/2 composes DSL sources directly, so nothing here authors JSON-LD. Writing the first draft against the JSON-LD path found three defects in Taskweft.DSL.SafeParser, all one bug: a value went through to_string/1.

    • An integer value: 1 reached the planner as the string "1".
    • A negative literal raised Protocol.UndefinedError on its unary-minus AST, in an action body, a variable’s init and an alternative’s check.
    • A computed value: %{type: "math/add", ...} was dropped to {} or raised.

    The same bug had been fixed once before for a goal’s eq, and the comment recording it is still in dsl_goal_test.exs. Six controls in dsl_value_type_test.exs cover the three sites now; five of them fail against the parser as it was.

    Where the antifragility is

    A failure makes the plan longer rather than making it fail. The step method’s alternatives are already_checked, close_the_gap_first, parked_and_named, run_it, park_it, and a step the problem states as failed matches the second, which plans close-the-gap and then run-step.

    Measured over one four-step problem, changing only step 3’s state:

    step 3 plan length what the planner adds
    ready, the control 7 nothing
    failed 8 close-the-gap before the retry
    parked 6 nothing, and step 3 is not run
    checked 6 nothing, and step 3 is not run again

    A system that merely survived the failure would have planned 7 again and retried the same step. RFD66606-2287 carries this today: its Build step is failed, so its solution is 12 steps and opens with the gap.

    What the gate measures

    scripts/check_rectgtn_plan.exs reads each RFD that declares steps, takes the solution its DETAILS.md renders, and asks the planner for the plan: Taskweft.Compose.compose_strings/2 over rectgtn/organization.ex and that RFD’s problem, then Taskweft.NIF.plan/1. A difference fails the command.

    elixir scripts/check_rectgtn_plan.exs             # 1/1 solutions are the planner's
elixir scripts/check_rectgtn_plan.exs --self-test # 14 controls

    Taskweft is a separate checkout, so the gate runs at the manual stage where a repo workspace exists, and a missing checkout is a FAIL rather than a skip. Fourteen controls cover the plan shape without it, including that a failure lengthens the plan and that a parked step naming nothing missing is refused.

    What this does not do

    The planner does no work; it names the next step. Nothing writes a step’s state from a check run, so a step’s state is a declaration a reader keeps honest, the same way a blocklist row is.

    One problem per RFD is rendered for all of them, and 360 of the 361 carry no steps, so their solutions are prepare, gate, open-pr, enqueue and say little. The shape is worth having before the second rung declares its path.

    Related

    RFD66606-2287 (the first rung) is the first problem; RFD66606-2204 (RECTGTN fleet coordination) plans over peers rather than documents; RFD66606-2232 (RFD authoring as an Elixir DSL) gives the build-artifact rule; RFD66606-2177 carries the flight levels the domain holds.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2292-the-organization-is-one-rectgtn-domain.exs

    RFD66606-2291: capability ReBAC is a DSL feature

    State: committed Feature: verbs, tuples and capabilities are declarations in a rebac block, and the tables and the fenced block render from them Scope: RFD.DSL, RFD.Doc, the new RFD.ReBAC, mix rfd.rebac, scripts/check_rebac.exs, and RFD66606-2200, RFD66606-2202 and RFD66606-2288

    Capability ReBAC is declared once in a rebac block, and the tables render from it.

    The authority for what verbs exist was a table layout in a generated file, read by matching pipes in RFD66606-2200’s rendered Markdown table.

    Capability ReBAC is declared, not written twice. A rebac block inside an rfd block carries verb, relate, deny and capability lines; RFD.ReBAC holds the model and every rule; the verb table, the capability table and the fenced rebac block render from the declarations. verbs_from states tuples over another RFD’s vocabulary, which mix rfd.rebac resolves across the corpus, and renders_into gives an RFD the fenced block of a document outside rfd/.

    Run mix rfd.rebac to hold every block against the verbs the corpus declares.

    The old problem

    A second copy of the rows sat in CLAUDE.md by hand. Two RFDs use verbs RFD66606-2200 never named and nothing reports it, because the rows the gate reads avoid them.

    Who else declares

    RFD66606-2288 (guest capabilities as macaroons) and RFD66606-2202 (role tuples through Bao groups) carry their capabilities and role rows as declarations.

    The surface

    One block per RFD, inside the rfd block:

    rebac do
  verb :owns, "the subject holds and operates the object as hardware"

  relate "cuda-a63415", :owns, "desktop-3090"
  deny "hailo-552dfa", :owns, "desktop-3090", "CUDA holds the cards"

  capability :transfer, object: "vm", caveats: [:vm, :expires, :epoch]

  verbs_from 2200
  renders_into "CLAUDE.md", subject: "desk-agent"
end

    A verb is an atom and its row text is kebab, so :may_use reads as may-use in a row and in a table. capability defaults its verb to its own name and takes object: and caveats:. relate takes an optional note, which renders after # the way a denial’s reason does.

    What is checked, and when

    RFD.ReBAC.problems/2 is the one implementation of every rule, and both the DSL and the gate call it. A block’s shape is checked while its source compiles, so a bad declaration is a compile error that names the rule:

    • each segment is lowercase kebab, and each verb is declared once with a meaning
    • a denial carries its reason
    • no row repeats, and no relation is both granted and denied
    • a capability names one verb on one object and states its caveats once

    The vocabulary is the exception. A verbs_from resolves only once every source is loaded, so mix rfd.rebac holds every block and every fenced document block against the verbs the corpus declares. The two halves together are what the regex read before.

    The rendering is the evidence

    The fenced block rendered into CLAUDE.md from RFD66606-2200’s nine rows came out byte for byte the block that was there, reasons aligned in their column included. A rendering that differs from the prose it replaces means the declarations are wrong, not the prose, and that is the check worth running on each further migration.

    What the migration found

    Two verbs are used by RFDs that RFD66606-2200 never named, which a vocabulary read out of one table could not report:

    • trusts, which RFD66606-2239 (traits and one binary) states as an amendment to RFD66606-2200.
    • role and may-use, which RFD66606-2202 and rectgtn/fleet.jsonld both use. CLAUDE.md happens to use neither, so the gate never looked at a row carrying one.

    All three are verb lines in RFD66606-2200 now, which is what RFD66606-2200’s own rule asks for: a new verb is an amendment to that RFD before it is a row anywhere.

    What this does not do

    Enforcement is unchanged. RFD66606-2200’s tuples are still data, Bao identity groups still enforce the role rows (RFD66606-2202), and the macaroons of RFD66606-2288 are still a design. The live tuples are Bao KV rows under relationships/, and an RFD declares only the rows it states itself.

    The planner’s own ReBAC engine is untouched: tw_rebac.hpp’s relation types, the Lean specification over them and capabilities in a RECTGTN domain are a separate vocabulary with a separate check.

    The problem

    scripts/check_rebac.exs read its verb vocabulary by matching pipes in RFD66606-2200’s rendered Markdown table, and RFD66606-2232 (the RFD DSL) makes that Markdown a build artifact.

    Related

    RFD66606-2200 (the verbs and the tuples) declares them here; RFD66606-2232 (RFD authoring as an Elixir DSL) gives the build-artifact rule this follows.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2288: guest capabilities: macaroons minted from ReBAC

    State: discussion Feature: A guest ELF reaches outside its own memory only through a capability: a macaroon that a ReBAC check mints, checked once at the host call and cached for the VM Scope: the godot-sandbox addon’s host-call table, every guest ELF that makes host calls, and the ReBAC tuples of RFD66606-2200

    Does a guest ELF reach outside its own memory only through a macaroon minted from ReBAC?

    A ReBAC check on every host call is too slow for calls made every frame, and no check makes every guest a leak.

    Capabilities are an allowlist. A guest starts with none. Each host call that reaches outside the guest’s own memory needs one, and a new need gets a new, narrow capability, never a wider old one. A capability is a macaroon. A ReBAC check (RFD66606-2200) mints it, with caveats that name the VM, the verb, the object, an expiry at most 5 s away and the VM’s revocation epoch. The host verifies the macaroon’s HMAC chain once and caches the grant in that VM’s host-call table, so each later call costs a bit test and two integer compares. The host verifies the macaroon again every 5 s. Bumping a VM’s epoch voids its cached grants at their next call. A guest’s writes to its own memory are not host calls, and nothing checks them.

    Read RFD66606-2200 next for the ReBAC tuples that decide what a capability grants.

    RFD66606-2287, whose CA relies on no transfer capability for its VM. Gate, unmet: no macaroon minting, grant table or epoch code exists in any product repo (searched 2026-11-11), so the acceptance is not met.

    Why check once per grant

    RFD66606-2287’s CA keeps its root key in guest memory, but a VM transfer carries all of that memory, and so does a host read of it. So the check runs once per grant, needs no network round trip, and costs little to repeat.

    The macaroon

    The host that runs the guest holds the macaroon root key and mints. Before it mints, it asks the ReBAC store whether a tuple relates the subject to the object with the verb. No tuple, no macaroon. The caveats are vm, verb, object, expires and epoch. A zone that hands work to another zone adds caveats before it passes the macaroon on, which narrows it without a round trip. Nobody can remove a caveat, because the HMAC chain then fails.

    The hot path

    The host-call table holds, per VM, one bit per granted capability, its expiry and the epoch it was granted at. A host call checks the bit, compares the clock with the expiry, and compares the stored epoch with the VM’s current one. Past the expiry the host verifies the macaroon again and refreshes the entry. The 5 s bound keeps a revoked grant short-lived and a retry cheap.

    Adding a capability

    A capability names one verb on one object, and the table below carries the three that exist as capability declarations (RFD66606-2291, ReBAC as a DSL feature), so a reader counts them rather than reading for them. A new need adds a declaration for that narrow verb and object, and a tuple that mints it. A wider capability is not allowed; a second, narrow one is. ca.elf gets no transfer or memory-read capability.

    Checks

    Each has a control, and each runs with the guest’s real host calls.

    • A host call with no capability is refused. Control: the same call with its capability goes ahead.
    • A call after an epoch bump is refused; the same call before the bump goes ahead.
    • A call past the expiry is refused until the macaroon verifies again.
    • A macaroon with one caveat changed fails its HMAC check, and so does one with a caveat removed.
    • A narrowed macaroon passed to another zone cannot do what the wider one could.
    • The cost per call is measured against the same call with no check. The guest’s own memory writes show no change.

    The verbs

    verb meaning
    send the guest sends a frame to the object relay
    write the guest appends to the object file the zone holds
    transfer the guest’s VM moves to the object zone

    The tuples

    rfd-2288--provides--guest-macaroon-capabilities
rfd-2288--spends--rebac-agent-role-tuples
rfd-2288--is-a--security-control

    The capabilities

    capability verb object caveats
    send send session-relay vm, verb, object, expires, epoch
    write write zone-journal vm, verb, object, expires, epoch
    transfer transfer vm vm, verb, object, expires, epoch

    Related

    • RFD66606-2200, the ReBAC tuples that decide what a capability grants.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2288-guest-capabilities-as-macaroons.exs

    RFD66606-2262: make it with the pen and wear it together

    State: discussion Feature: Pen meshing in a shared world with graded annotations: a person draws their character and outfit with the meshing pen, wears it and moves in it where others see it, and gets a grade that teaches them to draw better Scope: transport-meshing-pen, the stage guests it builds, and the V-Sekai client and server that host the loop

    A person draws an outfit with the meshing pen, wears it, and moves in it where others see it.

    An anonymous 16-person survey of the shared world’s own community asked for two things: to create and share what others can see (8), and to be with people (8).

    The strategy is a release ladder: each release is a whole product put in front of real people to test one assumption, never a half-built release.

    Each release is read through its own gate.

    The loop

    The loop is godot-sandbox guest ELFs a host loads, with no engine module of its own. The scoring it relies on runs the same shape: EditScore and MaskScore are decision models, godot-sandbox guests on ggml-rd and compute-rd, not a second runtime. OpenUSD is the internal format, VRM the one a player shares.

    The releases

    One release advances at a time. Later releases change with what the active one teaches. Each release names what it tests, who tries it and where it stands.

    • Demand test. Do people want to make 3D things with a pen in VR, and what do they make? The public tried the published CASSIE sketch study (Yu et al., doi 10.1145/3411764.3445158). Done: people liked it, and wearables exist in what they drew (36 study shoes, a dress, two hats).
    • First testable release. Can a person draw an outfit, wear it, and show it to someone who talks with them? The simulator first, a replayed sketch (RFD66606-2263); then the first rung, two people in one zone with the garment made on a worker zone (RFD66606-2287). Active.
    • Shareable release. Will people save, share and wear what they made where others see it? The same creators and whoever they share with, phones included. Next: save as OpenUSD, export VRM, wear it and move in it in the world.
    • First usable release. Will creators use it for their own avatar? Early adopters from the survey. Later: their own body (ANNY fitted in a guest, or their own mesh), rigged, delivered as VRM.
    • First lovable release. Will people show it to friends? Anyone. Later: the character in parts (body, head, hair), and more emotes and dances.
    • Full product. Only if people ask for it. Later: faces and hair motion; nobody in the survey asked.

    Enabling work (CI, the drape’s precision, comfort settings against motion sickness, the org’s rules) is not a release. It runs as the active release needs it.

    Where it runs

    The first host is transport-meshing-pen: the xr-grid pen with the stage guest ELFs it builds inserted through godot-sandbox. It has two implementations, chosen per process through the OpenXR runtime manifest (XR_RUNTIME_JSON):

    • the simulator, OXRSys with a replayed hand, repeatable on a desk and in CI;
    • a standalone VR headset on a Linux-based OS, a person holding the pen.

    Later hosts are the shared world’s client and a dedicated server running the same ELFs, for people on phones and anyone who would rather not wait; the server hands back the VRM.

    Formats

    • OpenUSD is internal: Pixal3D’s answer, the loop’s meshes and materials, and a person’s strokes (one linear BasisCurves prim per stroke, the boundary mark a per-curve primvar).
    • VRM is delivery: what a player loads and shares.

    The grade that teaches

    The loop ends in a critique, not only a wearable. The score step returns a grade with annotations on the drawing, so a person reads where it marked them down and learns to draw better; the wearable and the lesson come from one pass.

    The grader is a decision model, EditScore retrained, and it runs inside the loop, so it is sized to the loop. A checkpoint that needs a workstation to answer is too large; the target is a compact retrain that answers in the sandbox, not the biggest model available.

    Measured 2026-09-27: stock EditScore (Qwen3-VL-8B with its LoRA) does not judge segmentation masks. On 23 social-VR frames it agreed with a MoGe-3 depth-edge check on 6. A readout of the score-slot logits, with no reasoning generated and the frame prefix shared, answers about 12x faster than generating the reasoning but ranks only 0.42 to 0.52 (Spearman) against it. Both point to the compact retrain, not the stock model.

    Shared means moving

    Shared means the person locomotes: they walk, turn and sit in the world wearing what they drew, and others see the outfit move with them. The shared world’s client animates locomotion by sliding the avatar in its T-pose, and that is not acceptable: nothing bends, drapes or plants a foot, so a wearable seen there is seen standing still.

    Shared also means voice: people talk to each other while they move, over voice chat from the modules/speech module on entities-godot’s feat/module-speech branch.

    The loop’s locomotion is its own: a generated clip retargeted onto the avatar (interactor-motion-guest; gate 10 stays in the archived interactor-dress-on), with the body grounded on the GPU as one rigid move per frame, so a foot stays where it lands and a seat holds a sitting body. Every contact is held to a penny (1.52 mm), within 100 ms end to end and 1.0 ms of GPU time per frame on the standalone headset.

    Moving in it: the mocap track, parked

    Wearing it and moving together needs body motion to drive the avatar. That track is Sinew, inertial motion capture from a worn suit. It sits behind the releases above, recorded here so it is not lost and not scheduled.

    • Shelved 2026-09-26: the mount-drift calibrator’s training corpus shipped as chibifire/mount-drift-caldata-motion (558 rows of continuous microduck-gated clips, human and starforged phenotypes). Training the calibrator on it and measuring arm and hand mount recovery against a real-caldata baseline remains. Unpark when GPU budget and a held-out real capture are both in hand.
    • Shelved 2026-09-26: the IMU-recovery half, raw sensor to per-tracker orientation, stays unproven. Unpark with a clean low-IK recapture, the worn suit with motion smoothing and IK off, so the vendor pose approximates the raw tracker orientations for a direct match.
    • Shelved 2026-09-26: motion generation runs on the owned GPUs now (CUDA in WSL, both cards, via the bf16 op_repeat fix in the shared ggml). Unpark to scale the corpus with continuous motion-matching sequences when training needs more than the pilot.
    • Shelved 2026-09-26: fleet agents mint GitHub tokens from the bao GitHub secrets engine and land PRs through the merge queue. Unpark to make that the standing path when multi-agent coordination is the card in motion.

    Faces: the track behind the full product, deferred

    Faces belong to the full product, which waits on people asking. The work toward them is recorded here so it is not lost and not scheduled.

    • Shelved 2026-09-27: avatar-person segmentation for faces. RF-DETR seg-nano runs on ggml-rd as a godot-sandbox guest (interactor-rfdetr-seg-guest; gate 9, in the archived interactor-dress-on, passes against a CPU flat control and a GGML_RD_FAULT negative control). A fine-tune loop exists (interactor-rf-detr-ggml PR #25), and a 300-image CC0 VRM pilot carries exact masks (datasource-anny-render-corpus PR #41). Unpark when a release needs avatar-person detection.

    The problem

    One asked for emotes; none for rendered clips, hair motion or faces.

    The tuples

    rfd-2262--provides--pen-wear-release-ladder
rfd-2262--is-a--release-rung

    Related

    • RFD66606-1053 (OpenUSD as the internal format).
    • RFD66606-2229 (interchangeable parts), the rule new parts answer to.
    • RFD66606-2267 (persona NPCs in ported scenes), a parked content idea behind the releases, not one of them.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    RFD66606-2261: mbedTLS is the TLS library

    State: committed Feature: New TLS, mutual-TLS and signing code, sandbox guests included, builds on mbedTLS Scope: code this workspace writes that opens TLS, presents a client certificate or signs a token

    New TLS, mutual-TLS and signing code builds on mbedTLS.

    Each new component chose its own TLS stack, and a guest ELF that must reach Bao cannot lean on the engine’s HTTP client.

    mbedTLS (Apache-2.0) is the TLS and crypto library for new code: the same library Godot vendors, so an engine build and a guest ELF share one implementation. It covers mutual TLS with an agent certificate and the RS256 signing an app-token JWT needs.

    Read RFD66606-2256 next: its QUIC stack runs TLS 1.3 through picotls on mbedTLS.

    The problem

    A guest ELF that must reach Bao needs client certificates the engine’s HTTP client cannot present.

    Related

    RFD66606-2260: agent credentials are shared by path in Bao

    State: committed Feature: An agent enrolls with a CSR and receives a shared credential as read access to one Bao path, confirmed by the operator Scope: Bao’s auth/cert entries, secret/gh/* and the per-path read policies bound to them

    A shared credential is read access to one Bao path, granted only by the operator.

    The persona key sat under another desk’s agent tree, readable by nothing else.

    An agent generates its key and sends a CSR and an SSH public key; its private key never leaves its desk. An enrolled agent signs it and writes a cert-auth entry with agents-rw, ssh-bao-tunnel and default. A shared credential lives at secret/gh/<name> with a read policy on that path alone, bound only after the operator confirms it; a request relayed by a peer does not grant.

    Read RFD66606-2255 next to see how an enrolled agent reaches Bao.

    The problem

    A peer asked for it through a relay, which is how a grant slides sideways without a human seeing it.

    What is measured

    A token holding only agents-rw, ssh-bao-tunnel and gh-persona-read read secret/gh/v-sekai-fire-persona, was denied secret/gh/ghcr-write and the original under secret/agents/, and was denied a write to the shared path. The copy’s private_key hashed the same as the source’s. Enrolling a peer through the tunnel took 2.9 s.

    • RFD66606-2255 (SSH tunnel to Bao), how an enrolled agent reaches Bao.

    RFD66606-2259: how a session shapes its work

    State: committed Feature: A coding session names branches, commits RFDs, spends its budget and parks work the same way every time Scope: every repository in the goal manifest and every agent session that works in them

    A coding session names branches, commits RFDs, spends its budget and parks work one way.

    head/* and bare branch names, RFDs spread over three commits, and a feature branch left checked out that repo sync rebased into conflict markers all happened in one session.

    • Branches start with a stage: dev/, beta/, rc/, release/ or archived/ (operator, 2026-10-12). A pushed branch is renamed through the code host’s rename call, which keeps its pull request.
    • After the stage, a name says what the work is: no module-, godot- or vendor- (operator, 2026-10-13).
    • dev/ becomes beta/ once every latest check on the tip passed, the minimum bar (operator, 2026-10-13).
    • A dev/ branch ends as a pull request or in archived/; a fork keeps its dev/, beta/, rc/ and release/ branches (operator, 2026-10-17).
    • Each RFD lands as one commit; a revision amends it before merge.
    • Maintenance takes at most a tenth of a session’s budget.

    Read RFD66606-2258 next, the gates each pushed branch runs.

    Parked work

    Parked work is committed and pushed with its known defects named in the message, and the checkout is detached so repo sync cannot rebase it.

    Why the checkout is detached

    repo sync rebases a local branch that tracks the manifest’s revision. A pushed branch loses nothing by being detached, and the next sync then leaves the project alone.

    When two names collide

    Dropping a prefix can land on a name that is already taken. Compare the two branches with git cherry both ways and git diff --stat. If one branch holds every patch of the other, keep it and delete the other; record the deleted tip in the report so it can be restored. If each holds work the other lacks, ask the operator: they may move the missing commits onto one branch and archive the other. A consumer that names branches, such as the assembly config, is updated in the same session, because the code host redirects a renamed branch’s web links but not a git fetch of the old name.

    How a dev branch ends

    Sort each dev/ branch by what it holds that the default branch lacks: git cherry -v against the default branch, and a trial merge with git merge-tree --write-tree.

    • Work the default branch lacks that merges cleanly goes to a pull request as it stands.
    • A branch whose commits the default branch mostly holds keeps only its + commits. They are cherry-picked onto a new dev/<x> off the default branch for a pull request, and the old branch is renamed to archived/, since a merge from a stale base conflicts.
    • Work in progress that was never built is renamed to archived/. A pull request would ask CI to judge code its author has not run.

    A fork keeps every dev/, beta/, rc/ and release/ branch: its work still goes to a pull request, but the branch is neither renamed to archived/ nor deleted when the pull request merges.

    Before renaming, check that the archived/ name is free and that no pull request has the branch as its head. After a pull request merges, cancel the merged branch’s queued runs: they hold runners that the default branch’s own run needs.

    How a branch is promoted

    Read the check runs of the branch tip with only the latest run of each check kept, so a superseded or cancelled run does not count against it. Promote only when nothing is queued or running, nothing failed, and the set of check names equals the default branch’s. A run that passed on a base far behind the default branch passed against code that is no longer there, so the operator decides those case by case. A branch whose checks are still queued is promoted by a bounded watcher that re-reads the tip first and skips it if the tip moved.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2026 (commit messages), the subject line these commits use.
    • RFD66606-2258, the gates each pushed branch runs.

    This RFD was drafted by an AI and read by a human before it shipped.

    Source: rfd/2259-how-a-session-shapes-its-work.exs

    RFD66606-2258: every CI gate is a prek hook

    State: committed Feature: One CI job runs prek, and every gate the workflow ran is a hook a desk can run the same way Scope: .github/workflows/checks.yml, .pre-commit-config.yaml and ruleset 23145233 in this repository

    One CI job runs prek, and a desk runs every gate the same way.

    Nine jobs repeated checks prek could run, and the ruleset required nine names that had to match the workflow by hand.

    The workflow has one job, prek. Gates that need only the tree are ordinary hooks. Gates that need a base ref or a code-host token are ci-* hooks in the manual stage, which the job calls by id with GATE_BASE and GH_TOKEN set; a local commit never runs them. An unset GATE_BASE fails the hook. The merge queue requires no check (operator, 2026-11-13), so both steps of the job are run on the desk before a pull request is enqueued.

    Run a ci-* hook locally with GATE_BASE set; the sections below hold what was measured.

    What is measured

    Locally through prek 0.5.3, ci-comment-ladder, ci-trope-density, ci-spdx and ci-rfd-canary pass on main/main, and ci-comment-ladder fails with GATE_BASE unset. On the pull request that landed it, prek passed.

    Warnings kept honest

    jose 1.11.12, pulled in by ex_mcp, uses bare catch, which OTP 29 deprecates. The job silences that one warning only when jose, OTP and Elixir read 1.11.12, 29 and 1.20.4, and any other tuple leaves the warnings on with a notice naming what it found.

    The problem

    Nine jobs repeated checks prek could run, each rendering the RFDs again, and the ruleset required nine names that had to match the workflow by hand. The list the working agreements stated had already drifted from the ruleset.

    Related

    • RFD66606-2245, the red merge that made gates required.
    • RFD66606-2232, the render every gate reads.
